At the first level she objects to the practice; at the second level she has reasons, which she judges to be weightier, for not interfering with it: that adults have authority over their own lives, that her own judgement might be wrong, that a society in which everyone enforced their disapproval on everyone else would be unbearable. Consider a mother who thinks her grown son's choice of career foolish and tells him so, but would never dream of threatening to cut him out of her will to force him back. She has not abandoned her objection. She has ranked it beneath something she values more.", "Toleration so understood has limits, and they follow from the same structure. Where the second-level reasons give out, as when a practice inflicts harm on people who have not agreed to bear it, the case for restraint weakens and may disappear. A tolerant society is not one that permits everything.", "Some critics find the whole idea condescending: to be tolerated, they point out, is to be told that one is disapproved of and merely endured, and they propose that a just society should aim higher, at the positive recognition and affirmation of different ways of life. There is something in this complaint, since nobody enjoys being put up with. Yet the modesty of toleration is also its strength. It asks citizens who disagree deeply to share a political life without first requiring them to approve of one another, which is fortunate, because in a diverse society such approval is not going to be forthcoming. A demand for universal affirmation sounds more generous, but it may ask for what people cannot sincerely give."]
difficulty_reason: A conceptual clarification with a familiar example and an explicitly signalled reply to critics; the argument is easy to follow.

subtopic: The expressive theory explains what deterrence theories miss about punishing the innocent, but since its measure of severity is conventional it needs an independent limiting principle.
paragraphs: ["Theories of punishment have long been divided between those that look forward and those that look back. Forward-looking theories justify punishment by its effects: it deters, it incapacitates, perhaps it reforms. Their persistent embarrassment is that they seem to license too much. If the point of punishment were simply to discourage crime, then punishing an innocent person whom the public believed guilty might serve that point as well as punishing the guilty one, and sometimes better, since it would be quicker. Most people regard this conclusion as monstrous, which suggests that the effects of punishment, however important, cannot be the whole of its justification.", "An expressive theory offers to supply what is missing. On this view punishment is, before anything else, a form of communication: the community's way of declaring that an act was wrong and that the person who did it is answerable for it. This explains at once why the innocent may not be punished. To condemn someone who did nothing is not an inefficient use of punishment but a lie told in its language. It also explains why we distinguish a fine from a tax, though both take money: the tax carries no message of blame, while the fine carries little else.", "The obvious objection is that condemnation can be expressed in words. If the point of a prison sentence is to say that an act was wrong, why not simply say so, in a formal judgement solemnly delivered? The expressive theorist's reply is that words alone are too cheap to carry the message. A declaration that costs the offender nothing would be heard as a declaration that the wrong did not matter much; only something that is felt as a burden registers the seriousness of what was done.", "This reply is ingenious, but it has an uncomfortable implication. If hard treatment communicates because of the meanings a society attaches to it, then how much hard treatment is needed depends on those meanings, and meanings can drift. A society accustomed to long sentences will hear a short one as a shrug; the same sentence elsewhere might sound like thunder. The expressive theory, in other words, cannot by itself tell us how severe punishment should be, because severity is fixed by convention, and conventions can escalate without limit. That is not a reason to abandon the theory, which captures something the forward-looking view plainly misses. It is a reason to think that the theory needs a partner: some independent principle, perhaps of proportion or of humanity, that sets limits the language of condemnation cannot set for itself."]
difficulty_reason: Claim, objection, reply and a critique of the reply; the final paragraph turns on a metaphor and an implication that must be followed.

subtopic: The luck objection refutes the claim that rewards measure moral desert but not the practice of honouring entitlements earned under fair rules.
paragraphs: ["The defence of meritocracy rests on a simple and appealing idea: that positions and rewards should go to those who earn them, through talent and effort, rather than to those born into the right family. Against the background of aristocratic privilege this was a revolutionary thought, and it remains a powerful one. Yet it has been attacked, with increasing force, on the ground that talent and effort are themselves largely matters of luck. No one chooses the abilities they are born with. And the capacity to work hard, to persist through failure and to defer gratification, is shaped by upbringing, health and circumstance in ways that no one controls. If this is so, the critic concludes, nobody deserves the rewards that meritocracy hands out, and the language of merit is a flattering fiction.", "The premises of this argument are difficult to deny, but its conclusion moves too fast. It runs together two different claims that a person might make about a reward. One is that she deserves it in a deep moral sense, that the world would be unjust if she did not have it. The other is that she is entitled to it, because she has met the conditions that a fair set of rules laid down in advance. A runner who wins a race under fair conditions is entitled to the prize even if her speed owes much to her genes and her coaching; to take the prize away on the ground that she was lucky would itself be a wrong, because she trained and competed on the understanding that winning would bring it. Entitlement of this kind does not depend on the winner being the author of her own talents. It depends only on the fairness of the rules and her compliance with them.", "Seen in this light, a society can reward productive contributions, and honour the expectations its rules create, without pretending that the rewards measure the moral worth of those who receive them. It also leaves open, as it should, the question of whether the rules themselves are fair, including how much inequality of reward they ought to permit. What the luck argument undermines is not the practice of rewarding achievement but a particular story told about it, the story in which the successful have simply earned their place and the unsuccessful have simply failed to earn theirs. That story is corrosive. It encourages the winners to regard their advantages as wholly their own, and it adds to the losers' material disadvantage the further injury of being told that they deserved it. The remedy is not to abolish merit but to hold it more lightly."]
difficulty_reason: Turns on a conceptual distinction (desert versus entitlement) that has to be grasped and applied; the stance is a partial rejection of the critic.

subtopic: The ideal of public reason is best read as a test that coercive laws must pass rather than a restriction on what citizens may say, though insincere advocacy remains a real worry.
paragraphs: ["In a society whose members hold different and often incompatible views about the meaning of life and the sources of value, on what basis may some of them use the power of the state to make others comply with laws? One influential answer holds that coercive laws must be justifiable by reasons that all reasonable citizens could accept, whatever their wider convictions. A law defended solely by appeal to a doctrine that many of one's fellow citizens reject, whether that doctrine is religious or secular, treats them as subjects to be managed rather than as equals to be persuaded. The requirement to offer such shared, or public, reasons is usually called the ideal of public reason.", "Critics have objected that the ideal asks too much of ordinary citizens. People do not keep their deepest convictions in a compartment separate from their political views; for many, their sense of what justice requires flows directly from a philosophical or religious outlook. To tell such citizens that they may vote, campaign and argue only on grounds detachable from that outlook is to ask them to enter public life as strangers to themselves. Worse, the demand seems to fall unevenly, since those whose convictions already happen to resemble the shared vocabulary are asked to give up nothing.", "Much of this objection depends on reading the ideal as a rule about what citizens may say. It is more plausible to read it as a test that laws must pass. On this reading a citizen may give whatever reasons move her, in the street, in the press or in the voting booth, and the ideal is satisfied so long as the law that is eventually enacted can also be supported by reasons that do not depend on any one contested doctrine. The burden then falls most heavily on those who exercise official power, on legislators drafting statutes and judges explaining decisions, rather than on citizens in conversation with one another.", "This reading does not remove every difficulty. If a citizen offers public reasons she does not herself find convincing, merely because she knows they are the only reasons that will count, her contribution begins to look less like persuasion and more like strategy. The ideal was meant to express respect for others as fellow reasoners, and insincere argument is a poor vehicle for respect. But this worry, though real, tells against a particular style of advocacy rather than against the test itself. A law can be justified in shared terms even if some of its supporters were moved by other considerations, just as a bridge can be sound though some of those who voted to build it understood nothing of engineering."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract comparison of two readings of an ideal, with an objection, a reinterpretation and a residual worry; the stance is indirect.

subtopic: A persistent minority shows not that majority rule is unjust in itself but that a condition of its fairness has failed, so remedies should aim first to restore that condition.
paragraphs: ["The case for deciding by majority is usually made on grounds of fairness rather than wisdom. Majorities are not reliably right, but a procedure that counts each vote equally treats each voter as an equal, and no rival procedure seems to do so as well. There is a second, less often stated part of the case. Majority rule is tolerable to those who lose because losing is expected to be temporary. Today's minority may be tomorrow's majority, since coalitions shift as issues change, and a citizen who is outvoted on one question can reasonably expect to be on the winning side of another. Over time, the losses are spread around.", "This second condition does not always hold. When the issues that matter most to people line up with a stable division in the society, by language, region or ancestry, for instance, the same group may find itself outvoted on question after question for generations. Its members cast their votes, and their votes are counted equally, but the counting never changes the result. Formal equality at the ballot box then coexists with something very like permanent exclusion. To tell such a minority that it has been treated fairly because each of its votes weighed as much as anyone else's is to mistake the form of fairness for its substance.", "Various remedies have been proposed: requirements of supermajorities for certain decisions, the devolution of some powers to regions where the minority is concentrated, electoral systems that give smaller groups a share of seats, and constitutional rights that no majority may override. Each has costs. Supermajority rules protect minorities by making change difficult, which also protects whatever injustices the status quo contains. Devolution can create new minorities within the regions it empowers. Entrenched rights shift power from elected bodies to courts, whose members the minority usually has no means of holding to account.", "None of these costs settles the matter, but together they suggest that the problem should be framed differently. The persistent minority is not evidence that majority rule is unjust in itself. It is evidence that one of the conditions under which majority rule is fair has failed. The aim of a remedy, accordingly, should be to restore that condition where possible, for example by encouraging cross-cutting associations that loosen the grip of a single division on political life, rather than to replace majority rule with a different principle of decision. Where the condition cannot be restored, stronger protections may be needed, but they should be understood as repairs to a damaged procedure, not as a rival theory of legitimacy."]
difficulty_reason: Problem, survey of remedies with costs, and a reframing; the final paragraph draws a distinction that the questions rely on.

subtopic: Freedom as non-domination exposes an unfreedom that counting interferences misses, though it works better as a diagnosis of where to look than as a measure of how free people are.
paragraphs: ["For much of modern political thought, to be free has meant to be left alone. On this view a person's liberty is diminished whenever someone interferes with her choices, by force, by threat or by the closing off of options, and it is enlarged whenever such interference is removed. The view has the merit of simplicity, and it gives a clear direction to political argument: other things being equal, less interference means more freedom. An older tradition, recently revived, holds that this account misses something essential. What makes a person unfree, it says, is not interference as such but dependence on the will of another who could interfere at pleasure, whether or not he ever does.", "The point is easiest to see in a case where the two accounts come apart. Imagine a tenant whose lease allows the landlord to evict her at any time and for any reason, and whose landlord happens to be a mild man who has never troubled anyone. On the non-interference view the tenant is perfectly free, since nobody is stopping her from doing anything. Yet she knows her position. She will think twice before complaining about a broken boiler, she will keep her opinion of the landlord to herself, and she may find herself anticipating his preferences in matters he has never raised. The absence of interference in her life is not evidence that she is free; it may be, in part, an effect of her unfreedom, since a person who must stay in another's good graces learns to make interference unnecessary. The rival tradition calls her condition domination, and it defines freedom as the absence of domination.", "The shift has striking consequences. Interference, on this view, does not always reduce freedom. A law that restrains me, but that I and others like me can contest through courts, elections and other channels that force those who make it to take our interests into account, does not subject me to anyone's arbitrary will, and so does not make me less free, even though it limits what I may do. Conversely, a benevolent ruler who chooses to interfere very little may still leave his subjects unfree, because what they are permitted to do depends on his continued goodwill.", "Critics reply that the notion of arbitrary power is too elastic to do the work asked of it. Almost every relationship, from employment to marriage to the ordinary dealings of neighbours, contains some capacity of one party to make the other's life worse. If all such capacities count as domination, then domination is everywhere and the concept loses its edge; if only some do, we need a criterion, and the obvious candidates seem to smuggle back the very judgements about interference that the theory hoped to avoid. Defenders answer that power is arbitrary when it is not forced to track the interests of those subject to it, and that whether it is so forced is a question about institutions: about rights of exit, of appeal and of collective voice.", "This answer is better than the critics allow, but it is not quite enough to turn non-domination into a measure. It tells us where to look rather than how much freedom we will find there. That may be its real value. The non-interference view, by counting acts, trains attention on what happens; the rival view, by asking about standing, trains it on what could happen, and on the structures that make some things unthinkable to attempt. Even if it cannot yield a neat scale, the second view identifies a kind of unfreedom that a tally of interferences would never register."]
difficulty_reason: Five dense paragraphs contrasting two conceptions, with a counterintuitive consequence, an objection, a reply and a carefully balanced verdict.

subtopic: The levelling-down objection can be answered, but only by making equality an impersonal value; a relational account of equality escapes it while still owing an account of distribution.
paragraphs: ["Egalitarians hold that there is something wrong with inequality as such: that when some people are much worse off than others through no fault of their own, the situation is bad, and bad in part simply because of the gap. The most famous objection to this view asks us to consider what follows from it. Suppose that the only way to remove an inequality were to make the better off worse off, with no benefit to anyone, as if a town in which some households had gardens and others had none could reach equality only by paving over every garden. If inequality is bad in itself, then such a change would remove something bad, and so would be in one respect an improvement. Yet the change helps no one and harms many. To call it an improvement in any respect, the objectors say, is absurd.", "Many philosophers have been moved by this objection to give up equality as a fundamental value. Some have adopted the view that benefits matter more the worse off their recipient is, so that a gain to a poor person counts for more than the same gain to a rich one; others hold that what matters is that everyone should have enough, after which differences cease to be of moral concern. Neither view is troubled by levelling down, since on neither does reducing the well-being of the better off, by itself, improve anything. Both also capture much of what drew people to equality in the first place, which was a concern for those who are badly off.", "Yet the objection is less decisive than it is usually taken to be. The egalitarian need not claim that a levelled-down world is better all things considered, only that it is better in one respect while much worse in others. Plural values often pull apart in this way. We can think that a promise kept at terrible cost was in one respect admirable without thinking that it should have been kept. Seen this way, the levelling-down case shows only that equality is not the only thing that matters, which almost no egalitarian ever believed.", "This defence succeeds, but at a price. It keeps equality as a value only by making it a strangely impersonal one: something that can make a state of affairs better while making it better for no one at all. Many will find such a value hard to care about. There is, however, another way to understand what egalitarians were after. On a relational view, the core of equality lies not in how goods are distributed but in how people stand to one another: in the absence of rank, servility and contempt, in a society where no one must bow and no one may command another merely by virtue of birth or wealth. Inequalities of resources matter on this view chiefly because, beyond some point, they turn into inequalities of standing, as when wealth buys influence over others or poverty forces deference to them.", "The relational view is untouched by the levelling-down objection, because paving over gardens neither creates nor abolishes any relation of rank between neighbours. Whether it can say enough about distribution is a further question. A society might abolish titles and deference while leaving vast differences in income intact, and the relational egalitarian owes us an account of when such differences begin to corrode equal standing. But the view has at least located the value of equality in a relation between persons, which is where most of its defenders always felt it to be."]
difficulty_reason: A layered argument: objection, two retreats, a defence, the cost of the defence and an alternative with its own open question; the author's position emerges only at the end.

subtopic: The usual payment and consent arguments do not justify general workplace monitoring, which should be limited to responses to specific, identifiable risks.
paragraphs: ["The case for monitoring employees at work usually rests on two claims. The first is that the employer is paying for the worker's time and is therefore entitled to know how that time is spent. The second is that the worker has agreed to the arrangement: the monitoring policy was set out in the contract, and nobody was forced to sign it. Both claims sound reasonable, and both, I think, prove much less than their defenders suppose.", "Take the argument from payment first. An employer buys a worker's labour, not the worker; the wage secures a certain kind of effort over a certain period, and it has never been understood to include a right to observe everything a person does while that effort is being given. A firm that pays a carpenter by the day may inspect the cabinets she builds, but it does not thereby acquire a claim to read her letters during lunch. The argument from consent fares little better. Agreement given by someone who needs the job, in a market where most comparable employers impose similar terms, tells us that the terms were accepted, not that they were fair. Consent of this kind can settle a dispute about what was agreed; it cannot settle whether the agreement should have been offered.", "The deeper difficulty is what continuous monitoring does to work itself. When every keystroke and pause is recorded, the employee learns to perform for the record rather than for the task. A support worker whose calls are timed will cut short a conversation with a confused customer even when a longer one would solve the problem; an office worker whose idle minutes are logged will keep the screen busy instead of stopping to think. The record begins to replace the judgement it was supposed to check, and the trust on which most skilled work depends, the expectation that a person will use discretion well when no one is looking, quietly erodes. There is an irony here as well: the information that monitoring yields grows less useful the more thoroughly it is collected, because what it captures is increasingly a display staged for the watcher.", "None of this means that employers may never watch. Where a job carries a specific and serious risk, such as handling cash, operating dangerous machinery or opening confidential records, targeted checks are a reasonable response to that risk, and most employees understand them as such. The test I would propose is therefore not whether monitoring was agreed to, but whether it is tied to an identifiable hazard and limited to what that hazard requires. General surveillance, justified only by the employer's wish to know, fails that test, however clearly it has been written into the contract."]
difficulty_reason: Clear claim and objection structure with signposted replies and a concrete closing test; vocabulary is plain.

subtopic: The difference between lying and misleading with true words carries moral weight only where listeners are expected to be on guard, not in relationships of trust.
paragraphs: ["Many people who would never tell a lie are perfectly comfortable misleading. Asked whether he has finished a report, an employee replies that he has been working on it all morning, which is true, and which he says precisely so that his manager will conclude that the report is nearly done. He has not lied, he tells himself; if his manager draws the wrong conclusion, that is her inference, not his assertion. The intuition behind this self-defence is widely shared, and it is not merely self-serving. Ordinary moral thinking, many legal systems and a long tradition of moral reasoning have treated the outright falsehood as a graver matter than the true statement artfully deployed.", "Yet when we ask what is wrong with lying in the first place, the distinction begins to look thin. The harm of a lie consists chiefly in two things: the listener ends up with a false belief that he did not choose, and the trust he extended to the speaker has been turned against him. Both harms are present in the case of the employee. His manager now believes something false about the report, and she believes it because she assumed, reasonably, that a colleague answering her question was trying to answer it. The employee exploited exactly that assumption. That he did so by selecting true words rather than inventing false ones changes the technique, not the result.", "There is, however, one setting in which the distinction earns its keep. In a negotiation over the price of a used car, both parties know that the other is pursuing its own advantage, and each is expected to read the other's statements with suspicion. A seller who says that several people have asked about the car, when several have indeed asked but none has made an offer, leaves the buyer free to discount the remark, and a competent buyer will. Where the listener is on guard by convention, the responsibility for drawing inferences is genuinely shared, and the misleader has exploited much less trust than the liar, who asserts something false that even a wary listener has no means of checking.", "What this suggests is that the moral line runs less between lying and misleading than between relationships in which listeners are entitled to rely on a speaker's cooperation and those in which they are not. In the first kind, which includes most of our dealings with doctors, colleagues, friends and family, the careful choice of true but misleading words offers almost no moral shelter. In the second, it offers some. The employee who congratulates himself on never having lied has simply mistaken the setting he is in."]
difficulty_reason: Concrete examples carry each step; the concession in paragraph 3 is clearly signposted with 'however'.

subtopic: Substituted judgement should be confined to cases where an incapacitated patient's wishes are actually known; otherwise surrogates should openly decide on her best interests.
paragraphs: ["When a patient can no longer decide for herself, someone else must decide for her, and the question is on what basis. The answer favoured in much of modern medical ethics is that the surrogate, usually a close relative, should choose as the patient would have chosen had she been able to. This standard of substituted judgement has an obvious appeal. It extends the patient's autonomy beyond the point at which she can exercise it, so that even when she is unconscious, her values rather than anyone else's continue to govern what is done to her body. The older alternative, that the surrogate should simply choose whatever is in the patient's best interests, looks paternalistic by comparison, since it invites others to put their idea of a good outcome in place of hers.", "The appeal is real, but it depends on there being something for the surrogate to reconstruct. Sometimes there is. A patient who said repeatedly, while healthy, that she would never want to be kept alive on a ventilator has left a clear instruction, and a daughter who honours it is doing exactly what the standard asks. Far more often, however, the situation that arises is one the patient never considered. She may have had firm views about dying at home but none about a trial of dialysis that offers a modest chance of recovery and a large chance of prolonged discomfort. To ask what she would have chosen here is to ask a counterfactual question to which there may be no fact of the matter. The surrogate who answers it confidently is not discovering the patient's will; he is extrapolating from scraps, and the extrapolation is shaped, inevitably, by his own hopes and fears.", "This would matter less if the fiction were harmless, but it has two costs. The first is that it hides the surrogate's own judgement behind the patient's name, so that a decision which ought to be open to discussion, with doctors and with other relatives, is presented as beyond discussion: this is simply what she would have wanted. The second is subtler. Families often find substituted judgement consoling precisely because it seems to relieve them of responsibility, and that consolation is not to be despised. But a consolation bought by pretending is fragile, and relatives who later doubt that they read the patient correctly may suffer more than they would have if they had been told, from the start, that they were being asked to judge what was best for her.", "The remedy is not to abandon substituted judgement but to confine it to cases where the patient's own wishes are actually known and actually bear on the decision, and to say plainly, in all other cases, that the surrogate is choosing on the patient's behalf what seems best for her. Honesty about which standard is in play is itself a form of respect for the patient."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common standard with a concession, a counterfactual argument and two distinct costs; moderately abstract.

subtopic: Offsetting is incoherent for wrongs directed at particular persons but coherent for aggregate, interchangeable harms such as emissions, where the real questions are practical.
paragraphs: ["Few practices attract scorn as readily as offsetting. A traveller who pays a fee to have trees planted in compensation for the emissions of her flight is compared, almost by reflex, to the sinner who once bought a pardon: she has not stopped doing the harmful thing, the critic says, she has merely paid to feel better about it. A sharper version of the objection imagines a man who wishes to be unfaithful to his wife and pays a friend to remain faithful to his own, so that the total quantity of fidelity in the world is unchanged. If that arrangement is absurd, and it plainly is, why should paying for trees be any different?", "The comparison is instructive, but not in the way the critic intends. Infidelity wrongs a particular person, and the wrong consists in what is done to her; another couple's faithfulness does nothing to repair it, because she was never interested in the global supply of fidelity. The harm of greenhouse emissions has an entirely different structure. It does not fall on anyone in particular by virtue of a relationship with the emitter; it arises from the total concentration of gases in the atmosphere, to which every tonne contributes equally regardless of where it came from. A tonne removed in one place cancels a tonne added in another as far as the eventual damage is concerned. Where a harm is aggregate and interchangeable in this way, compensation elsewhere is not a moral sleight of hand. It is, at least in principle, a genuine undoing.", "What the fidelity case shows, then, is that offsetting is incoherent for directed wrongs and coherent for aggregate ones. One cannot offset an insult to a colleague by being kind to a stranger, but one can offset a contribution to a shared stock of harm by subtracting an equal amount from it. The serious questions about carbon offsetting are therefore not philosophical but practical: whether the trees would have been planted anyway, whether they will survive long enough to hold the carbon they are credited with, whether the accounts of the scheme can be trusted. An offset that fails these tests is not a pardon; it is simply a fraud, and the right response to it is an audit, not moral disdain.", "I do not want to claim that nothing remains of the critic's unease. A person who comes to regard every harm as purchasable may lose the habit of asking whether she should be doing the harmful thing at all, and a culture of easy offsetting may slow the changes in conduct that will ultimately be needed. These are real worries. But they concern the character of the offsetter and the politics of reform, not the question of whether the harm itself has been undone, and they should not be dressed up as proof that offsetting is a confidence trick."]
difficulty_reason: Turns an opponent's analogy against him through an abstract distinction between directed and aggregate harms, then concedes residual worries.

subtopic: Special obligations in giving arise from relationships, not from mere proximity, so the usual case for local charity rests on a confusion.
paragraphs: ["Arguments about charity tend to divide into two camps. On one side are those who hold that money given to help others should go wherever it will do the most good, which, given the vast differences in what a sum can buy in different places, often means far from home. On the other are those who insist that we owe something special to our own: our town, our region, our country. The first camp accuses the second of parochialism dressed up as loyalty; the second accuses the first of a cold arithmetic that would dissolve every bond that makes moral life recognisable. Each has hold of something, and each, I think, misidentifies what it is.", "Begin with what the defenders of local giving get right. There really are special obligations. A parent owes more to her own children than to children in general, and no plausible ethics of giving asks her to fund a stranger's schooling before her son's. We also owe more to those we have harmed, and to those with whom we share institutions that we sustain and from which we benefit, such as a school we attended or a cooperative to which we belong. These obligations do not arise from distance. They arise from relationships: from dependence, from history, from reciprocity.", "The trouble is that the case for local giving usually trades on these relationships while asking for something else. The resident who prefers to give to a shelter in his own city rather than to a health programme abroad rarely stands in any special relation to the people in the shelter. He has not harmed them, does not depend on them and shares no institution with them beyond the accident of living within the same municipal boundary. What draws him is proximity, and proximity by itself has little moral force. A sick stranger in the next street does not matter more than a sick stranger in another country simply because she is closer, though I may be better placed to help her.", "That last qualification points to the strongest argument for local giving, which is not about loyalty at all but about knowledge. Near home, donors can see whether their money is used well, and can withdraw it if it is not. This is a serious consideration, but it is an empirical one, and it cuts in both directions: where reliable assessments of distant programmes exist, the advantage of proximity shrinks, and where the local charity is opaque, it disappears. What remains, once relationships and knowledge are set aside, is often a preference for help whose results one can watch, a preference that is understandable but that should not be mistaken for an obligation."]
difficulty_reason: Adjudicates between two camps by separating relationships, proximity and knowledge; the stance is explicit but the distinctions are fine.

subtopic: Uncertainty about whether insects can suffer, combined with their vast numbers, justifies modest precautions where we farm and kill them, not indifference.
paragraphs: ["Whether insects can suffer is a question on which serious people disagree, and on which the evidence is likely to remain inconclusive for a long time. Their nervous systems are tiny and organised very differently from ours; some of their behaviour looks like nothing more than reflex, while some looks uncomfortably like the behaviour that, in a dog or a bird, we would take without hesitation as a sign of pain. Faced with this uncertainty, the usual response is to treat it as permission. If we cannot know that insects feel anything, the thought runs, we need not worry about how we treat them.", "This inference is much weaker than it looks. Uncertainty about whether a being can suffer is not the same as confidence that it cannot, and in other contexts we do not treat it so. A builder who is unsure whether a house is occupied does not demolish it on the grounds that no one has proved anyone is inside. What uncertainty calls for is a weighing: the probability that harm is occurring, multiplied by how bad the harm would be and by how many beings it would affect. With insects, the last factor is overwhelming. The numbers involved in agriculture, pest control and the growing industry that farms insects for animal feed run to many billions, so that even a modest probability of sentience yields a large expected total of suffering.", "The obvious objection is that this style of reasoning proves too much. If any probability of suffering above zero, multiplied by a sufficiently large number of beings, can generate an overriding moral demand, then we might find ourselves obliged to reorganise our lives around bacteria, or around the remote chance that plants feel pain. That objection has force against arguments resting on probabilities so small that they amount to mere logical possibility. It has much less force here. The case for insect sentience is not a bare possibility of the kind that could be raised for any organism; it rests on specific behavioural and physiological features that insects share with animals whose capacity for pain we already accept, even if they share them only partially.", "What follows is not that insects should be accorded the same consideration as mammals, nor that every crushed ant is a tragedy. It is that where we deliberately bring insects into existence in vast numbers and kill them, as in insect farming, we should prefer methods of rearing and killing that would minimise suffering if suffering is present, provided the cost of doing so is modest. Precautions of this kind ask little of us. To refuse them on the grounds that sentience has not been proved is to mistake the absence of certainty for the presence of a licence."]
difficulty_reason: Reasoning under uncertainty with an anticipated objection and a limited practical conclusion; the probabilistic argument needs careful reading.

subtopic: The discount rate applied to far-future harms is not a neutral technical parameter but an ethical verdict, since only some of its components survive scrutiny.
paragraphs: ["Any decision whose costs and benefits are spread over time requires some way of comparing what happens now with what happens later, and the standard device is the discount rate. A benefit expected in a year is counted as worth somewhat less than the same benefit today; one expected in ten years, less again; and so on, at a compounding rate. Within a single human life, and over horizons of a few decades, the practice is largely uncontroversial. Its consequences become startling only when the horizon stretches across centuries. At a rate of five per cent a year, a harm that will occur two hundred years from now is valued today at a tiny fraction of one per cent of its full size, so that a policy which spared our descendants a catastrophe would barely register against even modest present costs. Whether we owe the future anything substantial thus turns, in practice, on a number that is usually set by technical convention.", "It helps to separate the reasons that have been given for discounting, because they do not stand or fall together. One is pure time preference: the view that well-being simply matters less the later it occurs. Another appeals to growth. If future people will be considerably richer than we are, then a given sum of money, or a given quantity of goods, will make less difference to their lives than it would to ours, much as a rupee means less to a wealthy person than to a poor one. A third appeals to uncertainty: the further away an outcome, the less sure we can be that it will happen at all, or that there will be anyone for it to happen to.", "Pure time preference is the weakest of these, at least when it is applied across generations. A person who prefers a pleasure today to a larger one next year may be imprudent, but the impatience is his own and so are its costs. To discount the well-being of people not yet born merely because they will be born later is a different matter: it is to treat a position in time as a reason for counting someone's suffering as less, in just the way that it would be indefensible to count suffering as less because it occurs in a distant country. The growth argument is more respectable, because it does not deny the equal standing of future people; it says only that the same resources will do them less good. But it is respectable only on its own assumptions. It presupposes that the future will in fact be richer, which is precisely what is in doubt if the harm in question is severe enough to undermine prosperity, and it applies only to losses for which wealth can compensate. A flooded coastline or an extinct species is not made good by a larger economy, and to discount such losses at the rate at which consumption grows is to treat them as though they could be bought back.", "The argument from uncertainty deserves more sympathy than critics of discounting usually allow it. It is reasonable to give some weight to the possibility that there will be no future people at all, and a small discount for that possibility is defensible. But the rate this argument supports is far lower than the rates commonly used, and it has nothing to say about harms we are confident will occur. What emerges from these distinctions is that the choice of a discount rate is not the technical matter it is often taken to be. Each component encodes a substantive view: about whether time itself diminishes moral standing, about how confident we are in continued growth, about which losses money can repair. A rate presented as a neutral parameter is, in effect, a verdict on what the present owes to the future, reached without the argument such a verdict requires."]
difficulty_reason: Dense analytic essay that separates three rationales and grades each differently; the stance emerges only from the cumulative distinctions.

subtopic: The preference for rescuing identified people is partly a bias but also secures a real assurance, which justifies rescue without excusing our neglect of prevention.
paragraphs: ["When a child falls into a disused well or a group of miners is trapped underground, communities will spend almost without limit to bring them out. Engineers are flown in, machines are diverted from other work, and no one asks whether the money might have been better used. The same communities, meanwhile, routinely decline measures that would save far more lives at far lower cost: safer road junctions, better lighting on rural highways, routine screening for common diseases. To many economists and policy analysts, the contrast is simply an error. A life saved by a guardrail is no less a life than one saved by a rescue shaft; that we cannot name the person in advance makes no difference to the value of what is saved. On this view the preference for identified over statistical lives is a bias, and a costly one, to be corrected by accounting that treats every life saved alike.", "Much of this critique seems to me correct. The people whose deaths a guardrail prevents are not abstractions; they are as real as the trapped miners, and they would have suffered and been mourned in the same way. If we spend a hundred times more per life on rescue than on prevention, a great many people die who need not have, and the fact that we never learn their names does not make their deaths any less our doing. It is worth noticing, too, that the identified lives we rush to save are often identified by chance: they are the victims whose plight happens to be reported, while others in similar danger elsewhere receive nothing, because no one is watching.", "Yet the critique moves too quickly when it concludes that the impulse to rescue has no rational content. What a community expresses when it refuses to abandon a known person in peril is a commitment that has value beyond the life in question: an assurance, to everyone, that if they are ever in that position they will not be left to die because the arithmetic was unfavourable. This assurance is a real good, and it is one that statistical accounting, which counts only lives saved, has no column for. It is enjoyed by people who are never in danger, and it shapes how the members of a community regard one another.", "Nor need this good conflict with the analyst's preferred standpoint. The strongest case for prevention is made from the position of someone who does not yet know whether he will be a victim: from there, each of us would prefer the policy that most improves our own chances, and that is usually prevention. But someone in that position would also want the assurance that rescue provides, and would be willing to pay something for it. Properly understood, then, the choice made under that uncertainty is not between rescue and prevention but about the proportion in which to buy them, and it is hard to believe that the proportion would resemble our present spending, in which prevention is starved while rescue is limitless.", "The lesson is not that rescue should be abandoned in the name of consistency, a policy that would purchase a few more statistical lives at the price of a community in which no one could count on being saved. It is that the scandal lies on the other side of the ledger. We do not rescue too much; we prevent too little, and the impulse to rescue, rightly valued, gives no excuse for that neglect."]
difficulty_reason: Partial agreement with a critique, a defence of the criticised practice, a reconciliation from the critic's own standpoint and a reversal of where the fault lies; the stance is nuanced.

subtopic: The deliberate falsehoods in scientific models are best read as testable claims about which factors make a difference, not as convenient fictions.
paragraphs: ["Students meeting physics for the first time are often unsettled to learn that the planes in their textbooks have no friction, the pendulums swing without air, and the planets are treated as points. Economics and population biology are worse offenders: their agents calculate perfectly and their populations are infinitely large. A natural response is to say that science, at least in its models, trades truth for convenience, and that a model is a useful fiction whose only virtue is that it lets us calculate. On this view the idealisation is a debt to be repaid later, when better methods allow the missing details to be added back.", "This response gets the matter backwards. An idealisation is not usually a lapse in description but a claim about relevance. To leave friction out of an account of a stone sliding down a smooth slope is to assert, implicitly, that friction makes no appreciable difference to the feature one is trying to explain, namely the way the stone's speed grows with time. If that assertion is correct, the idealised model is not a fiction about the stone; it is a true statement about what the stone's motion depends on. The model is false about the world in its details and accurate about the structure of dependence, and the second is frequently what we wanted to know. Adding every missing factor would not improve such a model; it would bury the very pattern the model was built to display.", "This does not mean that every idealisation is innocent. The claim of irrelevance can be wrong, and it is often wrong in a particular way: an assumption that holds well within one range of conditions fails outside it. Treating air as absent is harmless for a stone dropped from a window and disastrous for a feather, or for a parachutist. The danger lies less in the falsehood itself than in forgetting that it was a bet about relevance, so that a model calibrated in one setting is carried into another where the bet no longer pays.", "The sensible test, then, is not whether a model is literally true, since almost none are, but whether its conclusions survive when the idealisation is relaxed. If a result about a population holds whether the population is taken to be infinite or merely very large, the assumption of infinity was doing no harm. If the result vanishes as soon as the assumption is loosened, it was an artefact of the simplification rather than a discovery about the world. Read in this way, the frictionless plane is less an embarrassment than a hypothesis, and like any hypothesis it can be checked."]
difficulty_reason: A clearly signposted argument (rejected view, reply, concession, test) with concrete physical examples and moderate vocabulary.

subtopic: Explanation and prediction are not symmetrical: prediction needs only a reliable connection, while explanation must identify what the outcome depends on.
paragraphs: ["A long tradition in the philosophy of science treats explanation and prediction as two faces of one achievement. To explain why an event happened, on this view, is to show that it could have been expected, given the relevant laws and the conditions that held beforehand; to predict an event is to perform the same derivation before the event rather than after it. The symmetry is attractive because it makes explanation answerable to something. An explanation that could not, even in principle, have served as a prediction would seem to be no more than a story told after the fact. The view also promised a single standard for the whole of science, from astronomy, where eclipses are calculated centuries ahead, to clinical medicine, where a diagnosis is expected both to account for a patient's symptoms and to anticipate their course.", "Yet the symmetry fails in both directions. A falling barometer reading is an excellent predictor of a coming storm, and anyone who knows the correlation can forecast the weather with it; but no one supposes that the barometer explains the storm. Both are effects of a drop in atmospheric pressure, and the reading earns its predictive power by riding on that common cause. Conversely, we can often explain what we could never have predicted. A geologist can say why a particular hillside gave way, pointing to saturated soil and a weakened layer of clay, without having been able to say beforehand that it would fail that week rather than in some other year. The explanation is sound even though the forecast was out of reach.", "What these cases suggest is that explanation and prediction answer to different demands. A predictor need only be reliably connected with what it predicts; it does not matter how the connection arises. An explanation must identify what the outcome depends on: the factors such that, had they been different, the outcome would have been different too. The barometer fails that test, since a broken barometer would not have prevented the storm; the clay passes it, since firmer clay would have held the slope.", "None of this makes prediction irrelevant to explanation. A claim about what an outcome depends on usually implies something about what would happen under other conditions, and checking those implications is how such claims are tested. A theory that explains everything and forbids nothing should make us suspicious. But the test is a check on an explanation, not its substance. To confuse the two is to mistake the evidence that an account is right for the thing that makes it an account at all."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract argument built on two counterexamples running in opposite directions, followed by a criterion and a concession; requires tracking which case supports which half.

subtopic: Inductive inference is licensed by particular knowledge of particular domains rather than by a general principle, and the resulting regress does not make science irrational.
paragraphs: ["The sceptical argument about induction, usually traced to David Hume, has a disarming simplicity. Every inference from observed cases to unobserved ones assumes that the future will resemble the past, or more generally that nature is uniform. That assumption cannot be proved by logic, since its denial involves no contradiction, and it cannot be supported by experience without circularity, since the support would itself be an inference from observed cases. Philosophers have spent a long time looking for a way out, usually by searching for a single principle that would license inductive inference in general.", "The search may be misconceived, because there is no such thing as inductive inference in general. Consider two investigators. One measures the melting point of a newly prepared sample of a pure compound and concludes, from a single careful trial, that every sample of that compound will melt at the same temperature. Another measures the height of one adult and draws no conclusion at all about the heights of adults. Both are reasoning well, and they differ not because one has found the universal principle and the other has not, but because each knows something about the kind of thing being studied: that pure compounds are uniform in their melting points, and that people are not uniform in their heights.", "On this picture, what licenses an inductive step is not a principle of uniformity but particular facts about particular domains, which tell us how far a sample can be trusted to stand in for the whole. The obvious objection is that this merely relocates the problem. Our confidence that compounds are uniform in their melting points was itself acquired by induction, and so the sceptic can ask what licenses that.", "The objection is fair, but it is less damaging than it looks, because it trades on an ambiguity between justifying each belief and justifying all of them together. The regress it describes is real, yet it never requires us to justify all our inductive habits at once. At any moment we lean on some background knowledge in order to test some other part of it, and any item can in turn be questioned while the rest is held fixed. This does not answer the sceptic on the sceptic's own terms, which demand a foundation lying outside experience altogether. It does show that the demand is not one that science, as actually practised, needs to meet in order to be rational, any more than a household needs to audit every account on the same afternoon in order to keep honest books."]
difficulty_reason: A classic problem is restated, a localist reply offered, an objection granted in part and answered; the reader must see exactly how much the reply claims.

subtopic: The best justification for preferring simpler theories is statistical protection against fitting noise, which makes simplicity a context-dependent policy rather than a mark of truth.
paragraphs: ["Faced with two theories that fit the evidence equally well, scientists usually prefer the simpler, and they rarely feel the need to say why. When pressed, they tend to offer one of two answers. The first is that simplicity is a convenience: simpler theories are easier to state, to teach and to calculate with, and so they deserve priority in the way that a tidy desk deserves priority over a cluttered one, without any suggestion that tidiness is truer. The second is that nature itself is simple, so that a simple theory is more likely to have captured how things are. Neither answer is satisfactory. The first explains why we might enjoy simple theories but not why we should believe them, and the second asserts, with no evidence that could be independent of the very preference in question, exactly what needed to be shown.", "A more promising answer comes from an unglamorous source, the practice of fitting curves to data. Any finite set of measurements, each carrying some error, can be fitted perfectly by a sufficiently complicated curve, one that bends to pass through every point. Such a curve is usually a worse guide to the next measurement than a smoother one that passes near the points without touching them all, because much of what it has faithfully reproduced is noise. Additional adjustable parameters let a model accommodate the accidents of a particular sample, and the price of that accommodation is paid when the model meets new data. Seen in this light, a preference for simplicity is a policy for estimating well from limited and imperfect evidence, not a belief about the architecture of the world.", "This answer has a cost that its admirers do not always acknowledge. If simplicity earns its keep by protecting against noise, then its value should shrink as data become more abundant and more precise, and statistical practice broadly bears this out: with enough clean data, more complex models often predict better, because they can capture real structure that a simple model would smooth away. Simplicity, on this account, is not a standing virtue but a discount applied in proportion to our ignorance. Nor is it clear that simplicity can even be measured independently of how a theory is written. Counting parameters seems objective until one notices that a relation expressed compactly in one set of variables may require several parameters when it is rewritten in another.", "None of this returns us to the view that simplicity is mere taste. The statistical argument shows that, in the situations scientists usually face, favouring the simpler of two well-fitting hypotheses is a reliable way to be less wrong. What it does not show is that the simpler hypothesis is, for that reason, more likely to be true; and the habit of speaking as though it did has lent the principle an authority it borrowed rather than earned."]
difficulty_reason: Dense abstract argument that rejects two answers, adopts a third, then limits it twice; the final stance (useful policy, not a mark of truth) is a fine distinction.

subtopic: Keeping a theory in the face of an anomaly can be rational, but no rule tells us in advance when tenacity becomes dogma.
paragraphs: ["It is often said that a scientific theory can never be proved but can always be refuted: no number of successful predictions establishes it, while a single failed one brings it down. The slogan captures something real about the asymmetry between confirmation and refutation, but as a description of how theories should be treated it is too simple. A prediction is never derived from a theory alone. It depends also on assumptions about the instruments used, the conditions of the experiment and the other bodies or forces that might be at work. When a prediction fails, logic tells us that something in this whole bundle is wrong; it does not tell us which part.", "The history of astronomy offers a well-known illustration. In the first half of the nineteenth century, the observed orbit of Uranus departed from what Newtonian mechanics predicted. Astronomers did not abandon Newton. They supposed instead that an unseen planet was pulling on Uranus, calculated where it would have to be, and in 1846 Neptune was found close to the predicted position. The anomaly, far from refuting the theory, became one of its most celebrated successes.", "The same strategy, however, does not always succeed. A small discrepancy in the orbit of Mercury was also attributed to an undiscovered planet, which some astronomers even named, but no such planet was ever found. The discrepancy was finally accounted for only by Einstein's general theory of relativity, which replaced Newton's account of gravitation rather than adding to it. In hindsight, the two anomalies look entirely different. At the time, they looked much the same, and the decision to treat both in the same way was reasonable.", "The lesson is not that anomalies should be ignored, nor that theories should be given up at the first sign of trouble. It is that there is no rule which tells us in advance when an anomaly is a puzzle to be solved within a theory and when it is a sign that the theory is failing. Tenacity is a virtue in science, since a theory abandoned at the first difficulty would never have the chance to show what it can do; but tenacity shades into dogma when a theory is protected by one convenient assumption after another, each invented for no reason except to save it. Telling the two apart is a matter of judgement, informed by how many anomalies have accumulated and by whether the assumptions used to explain them away have earned independent support."]
difficulty_reason: Concrete historical cases, a clear contrast and an explicitly stated lesson; the stance is direct.

subtopic: Because accepting a hypothesis means judging the evidence sufficient, and the cost of error is a matter of value, values properly help set the evidential bar but must never alter the evidence.
paragraphs: ["A familiar picture of scientific objectivity confines values to the edges of inquiry. Values may legitimately decide which problems are worth studying and how results are used, but in the central act of science, deciding whether the evidence supports a hypothesis, they are supposed to have no place. A researcher who lets personal hopes affect whether a conclusion is accepted is, on this picture, simply doing bad science, and the remedy is a stricter separation between the laboratory and the world outside it.", "The trouble is that evidence rarely settles a question outright, and so accepting a hypothesis always involves deciding that the evidence is strong enough. How strong is strong enough? Consider a laboratory testing whether an industrial solvent damages the liver. If it wrongly concludes that the solvent is safe, workers may be harmed; if it wrongly concludes that the solvent is dangerous, a useful product may be withdrawn and money wasted. Which error is worse, and therefore how much evidence to demand before declaring the solvent harmful, is not something the data can decide. It depends on how one weighs injured workers against lost revenue, which is a question of value. Two laboratories examining identical data could therefore set the threshold in different places, and neither would have misread a single measurement.", "A natural reply is that scientists need not accept or reject anything. They could report the probability that the hypothesis is true, given the evidence, and leave the decision to those who must act. The reply is attractive but harder to carry out than it sounds. Before any probability can be reported, the investigators must decide how to classify ambiguous tissue samples, which measurements to discard as faulty and which statistical model to fit, and each of these decisions can err in either direction, with the same uneven consequences. The weighing of errors does not disappear; it moves to a stage where it is less visible.", "It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that anything goes. The argument shows that values can properly bear on how much evidence to require, given what is at stake if one is wrong. It does not show that values can bear on what the evidence is, or license a researcher to discount an inconvenient result because it is unwelcome. The distinction is between setting the bar and moving the evidence, and the integrity of science depends on keeping the two apart, not on pretending that the bar sets itself."]
difficulty_reason: A standard view, an argument against it built on a concrete case, a reply and a counter-reply, then a limiting distinction; moderately abstract.

subtopic: Thought experiments teach by bringing tacit expectations into conflict with explicit theory, so they are neither disguised arguments nor direct insight, and are only as reliable as the experience behind them.
paragraphs: ["Thought experiments occupy an awkward place in the theory of knowledge. Scientists and philosophers have long used them to settle questions, and some of the most admired episodes in the history of physics turn on an imagined scenario rather than an actual measurement. Yet a thought experiment, by definition, collects no new data. The experimenter sits still and imagines. If we learn something about the world this way, it is not obvious where the information comes from, and two answers have dominated discussion.", "According to the first, a thought experiment is an argument in disguise. Its vivid scenario can always be rewritten as a set of premises and a conclusion, and whatever it teaches, it teaches because the premises were already believed and the conclusion follows from them. The imagery is persuasive packaging, useful perhaps for teaching, but adding nothing to the logical content. According to the second, the best thought experiments give us something no argument could: a kind of direct intellectual insight into the necessary structure of nature, as if the mind could see a law of physics in the way the eye sees a colour.", "Neither answer fits the most celebrated example well. Galileo asked his readers to imagine a heavy body and a light one tied together and dropped. If heavier bodies fall faster, as the received physics of his day held, the light body should hold back the heavy one, so that the pair falls more slowly than the heavy body alone; but the pair is heavier than the heavy body, so it should fall faster. The supposition contradicts itself, and the natural way out is that all bodies fall at the same rate, at least in the absence of a resisting medium. The argument reading can reconstruct this, but only by writing in premises that no one had formulated before the scenario was imagined: for instance, that the speed of a composite body must lie somewhere between the speeds of its parts. The insight reading, for its part, makes the result mysterious, as though Galileo had glimpsed a law rather than noticed a contradiction in what he and his readers already believed.", "A better account is that thought experiments work by drawing on knowledge we have but have never made explicit. Everyone who has carried a load or watched things fall has a large stock of tacit expectations about how bodies behave. A well-constructed scenario brings these expectations to bear on a case where they collide with an explicit theory, and so exposes a tension that was there all along. What is new is not the information but its arrangement. This explains why thought experiments can be genuinely informative without new data, and also why they cannot be reduced to an argument that someone might have written down beforehand: the premises are found by running the scenario, not before it.", "It also explains when they should not be trusted. Our tacit expectations were formed in a narrow band of experience, among objects of moderate size moving at moderate speeds. A thought experiment that asks us to imagine the very small, the very fast or the very distant invites us to apply those expectations where they were never tested, and the resulting conviction, however vivid, carries only the authority of the experience behind it. The method is neither a trick of rhetoric nor a window onto necessity. It is a way of interrogating what we already know, and it is exactly as reliable as that knowledge."]
difficulty_reason: Two rival views are set out, tested against one example and replaced by a third with a stated limit; the structure is clear but the distinctions between the views are fine.

subtopic: The reference class problem afflicts both frequency and propensity views because chance is relative to a specification of circumstances, which makes it incomplete without one but not subjective.
paragraphs: ["Statements of chance are among the most familiar in science and ordinary life, and among the hardest to interpret. When we say that a fair coin has a chance of one half of landing heads, what are we saying? The most influential answer identifies chance with frequency: the chance of heads is the proportion of heads in a long run of tosses, or the limit towards which that proportion tends as the run is extended without end. The answer has the great merit of tying chance to something that can be counted, and it explains why observed frequencies are our main evidence about chances.", "Its difficulties begin with the single case. A particular coin may be tossed once and then melted down; a particular patient either will or will not recover from a particular operation. Yet we speak readily of the chance that this toss lands heads or that this patient recovers, and such judgements guide real decisions. The frequency view can treat them only by placing the single case in a class of similar cases and borrowing the frequency of the class. And here a second difficulty appears, because every case belongs to many classes. The patient is a man of sixty, a non-smoker, a resident of a particular city, someone treated by a particular surgeon, and the recovery rates in these classes may differ considerably. Which frequency is the patient's chance?", "Dissatisfaction with this reference class problem has led many to prefer a propensity view, on which chance is a physical tendency of a particular set-up to produce a given outcome, a property the single toss or the single operation possesses whether or not any long run ever occurs. The propensity view handles the single case gracefully, but at a price. It is unclear what a propensity is, beyond a name for whatever it is that frequencies are evidence of, and the view does not escape the problem it was meant to solve. The tendency of a set-up depends on how the set-up is described: the toss described as a toss of a fair coin has one propensity, while the toss described down to the exact force and angle of the flick may have another, close to certainty.", "The persistence of the problem across both views suggests that it is not a defect peculiar to either but a feature of chance itself. A chance is not a property an event has simply, but a property it has relative to a specification of the circumstances. Asking for the chance of an event, full stop, is like asking for the speed of a train without saying relative to what: the question is not unanswerable but incomplete. What remains open, and must be settled by our purposes rather than by the world, is which specification to use. For a gambler who cannot measure the flick, the description 'fair coin' is the relevant one; for a physicist with a high-speed camera, it is not.", "Some will feel that this concedes too much, making chance a matter of perspective rather than a feature of the world. But relativity to a description is not the same as subjectivity. Once the specification is fixed, the chance is fixed too, and two observers who adopt the same description and disagree about the chance cannot both be right. Velocity is no less objective for being relative to a frame. What the account gives up is only the idea that there is a single privileged description, the one nature itself would choose, and it is far from clear that anything in science requires such a description."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract comparison of two interpretations, a diagnosis that the shared problem is a feature of chance, and a reply to a subjectivity objection; the stance is reached only in the last two paragraphs.

subtopic: Life-satisfaction scores measure people's evaluations of their lives, which depend on their expectations, so they should be one measure of wellbeing among several rather than a complete one.
paragraphs: ["Governments that once judged their success almost entirely by output have lately begun to ask citizens a different question: all things considered, how satisfied are you with your life these days? The answers, usually given on a scale from zero to ten, are collected, averaged and compared across regions and years, and a rising average is increasingly cited as evidence that policy is working. The appeal of this approach is easy to understand. Income is at best a means to living well, and a measure that asks people directly about their lives seems to cut out the middleman.", "Yet the question is less direct than it looks. To answer it, a respondent must do something quite unlike reporting a sensation. She must call to mind her life as a whole, choose the standards by which it is to be judged, and compare the one with the other. The number she gives is therefore an evaluation, and evaluations depend on the standards brought to them. Two people whose days contain the same mixture of pleasure, worry and boredom may give very different scores because one expects more from life than the other. A person who has learned to expect little can report contentment with circumstances that would dismay a neighbour, and a population whose expectations rise quickly can report falling satisfaction even as its conditions improve.", "None of this makes the surveys worthless. Evaluations matter in their own right: how people judge their lives shapes what they choose, whom they blame and whether they think change is possible. The scores also move in ways we would expect, dropping when people lose their jobs or fall seriously ill. The error lies not in collecting the numbers but in treating them as a complete reading of how well people are living. A measure of judgement is not a measure of experience, and neither is it a measure of whether a life contains the goods, such as health, friendship and freedom, that most traditions of thought have held to be worth having whatever one happens to feel about them.", "A sensible policy, then, would treat satisfaction scores as one instrument among several, read alongside measures of how people actually spend and feel their days and of what they are really able to do. Used alone, the scores reward whatever lowers expectations as readily as whatever improves lives, and a government that steered by them alone could succeed by teaching its citizens to want less."]
difficulty_reason: A single clear thesis with a signposted concession in paragraph 3; vocabulary and argument are accessible.

subtopic: The Stoic distinction between what is and is not up to us is a demanding claim about where a person's good lies rather than a technique for calm, though its two-way division fits poorly with outcomes that are partly in our control.
paragraphs: ["The handbook of Epictetus's teachings opens with a distinction that has outlived nearly everything else in ancient ethics: some things are up to us and some are not. Our judgements, intentions and desires are up to us; our bodies, our possessions, our reputations and the offices we hold are not. In its modern popular form the distinction is offered as a technique for calm. Worry, it is said, comes from caring about what one cannot change, so the remedy is to stop caring about it, and the person who masters this will be undisturbed by traffic, criticism and bad news alike.", "This reading is not exactly wrong, but it inverts the order of the original argument. For the Stoics, tranquillity was a consequence, not the goal. The goal was to place one's good where it actually lay, in the quality of one's own choosing, and the distinction between what is and is not up to us was a claim about value before it was advice about feeling. To say that a friend's illness is not up to me is not to say that I should be indifferent to it; it is to say that my goodness as a person does not depend on whether she recovers, but on whether I act well toward her. The Stoic was expected to visit the sick, serve in public life and keep his promises with full seriousness, while declining to stake his worth on how any of it turned out.", "Read this way, the doctrine is more demanding than the popular version, not less. It asks for constant attention to one's own judgements, which the Stoics thought were the real source of most distress, and it offers no permission to withdraw. Someone who uses it to stop voting because elections are not up to him has learned a convenient half of the lesson and discarded the half that mattered.", "There is, however, a genuine difficulty that the more careful reading does not remove. The line between what is up to us and what is not is drawn more sharply in the doctrine than in life. Whether I pass an examination is not wholly up to me, but it is hardly independent of my effort; whether my child grows up kind is partly my doing and partly not. Most of what we care about lies in this middle region, and a doctrine that sorts everything into two bins must either treat such outcomes as indifferent, which seems false to how they matter, or admit that our worth is, after all, partly hostage to fortune. The Stoics chose the first answer. One can admire the clarity of that choice and still doubt that it describes a life anyone actually leads."]
difficulty_reason: The author corrects a popular reading, then raises an objection the correction does not answer; the stance has two layers that must be kept apart.

subtopic: The Zhuangzi story of the useless tree is less prudential advice than a critique of seeing things only in terms of their usefulness, though it does not reject usefulness as such.
paragraphs: ["Among the stories collected in the Zhuangzi, one of the best known concerns an enormous tree. A master carpenter passes it without a second glance, and when his apprentice asks why so magnificent a specimen has been ignored, he explains that its wood is good for nothing: boats made from it would sink, coffins would rot and tools would split. That night the tree appears to the carpenter in a dream and rebukes him, pointing out that trees bearing fruit are stripped and broken and never live out their natural years; its own uselessness, it explains, is precisely the reason it has lived so long and grown so large.", "The usual moral drawn from the story is a prudent one: in a dangerous world, conspicuous talent invites exploitation, and the wise keep their heads down. That reading has support in the text, which elsewhere praises figures who survive by escaping notice. But it makes the story smaller than it is. The carpenter's mistake is not merely that he underrates the tree; it is that he assumes the only question worth asking about a tree is what it is good for to a carpenter. The tree's reply amounts to the observation that usefulness is always usefulness to someone, for some purpose, and that a thing seen only through that lens is not really seen at all.", "This point has lost none of its edge. We are surrounded by institutions that measure things by their contribution to some further end, and we have grown skilled at the carpenter's glance. A subject of study is asked to justify itself by the jobs it leads to, a stretch of land by the revenue it can produce, an hour of a person's time by what it yields. Each of these questions is reasonable on its own, and institutions that never asked them would be failing in their responsibilities.
