What the story warns against is letting one of them become the only question, so that whatever cannot answer it, a friendship, a landscape, an afternoon of unhurried conversation, is passed by as if it were not there.", "It would be a mistake, though, to read the story as a rejection of usefulness as such. Boats and coffins must be made from something, and a world of nothing but magnificent useless trees would be a hard place to live. The story's target is narrower and more interesting: the habit of mind that cannot see a tree as anything other than timber not yet cut, and that mistakes the list of its own purposes for an inventory of what the world contains."]
difficulty_reason: A familiar story is retold and then reinterpreted in plain language; the turn and the concession are clearly marked.

subtopic: The Lucretian symmetry argument dissolves the fear of being dead as a state but not the fear of losing future goods, which reflects a legitimate concern for one's own future.
paragraphs: ["Epicurus held that death is nothing to us, since where death is, we are not, and his Roman follower Lucretius added an argument that has been discussed ever since. Look back, Lucretius suggests, at the endless stretch of time that passed before you were born, which did not trouble you then and does not trouble you now. The time after your death is a mirror held up to that earlier time, and it would be inconsistent to dread the one while feeling nothing about the other. If non-existence before birth is no evil, non-existence after death can be none either.", "The argument has a pleasing economy, and against one target it is decisive. Many people who fear death picture it, half consciously, as a condition they will find themselves in: a darkness, a silence, an interminable wait. Against this picture the mirror works admirably: nobody imagines that they spent the centuries before their birth sitting patiently in the dark, and the comparison exposes the fear of being dead as a confusion, since there will be no one there to suffer the darkness.", "But most people who fear death are not chiefly afraid of a condition; they are afraid of losing what they would otherwise have had: the next conversation, the completion of their work, the sight of their children grown. Here the symmetry breaks down, because our attitudes to past and future are not symmetrical even in ordinary life; we look forward to pleasures and dread pains that are still to come in a way that has no counterpart for those already over. More importantly, the goods we stand to lose by dying are goods that this very life would have contained had it continued, whereas the goods of the centuries before our birth were never ours to lose. A person could hardly have been born a hundred years earlier and remained the same person, with the same parents and history; but the same person can very easily die later than he in fact does.", "This does not mean that Lucretius has nothing to teach. If the fear of death is partly a fear of a condition, then his argument removes part of the fear, and that is no small gift. What remains is better described as grief in advance for a life cut short, and grief of that kind is not a confusion to be argued away. It is the shadow cast by caring about one's own future, and a consolation that worked perfectly against it would have to work by teaching us to care less."]
difficulty_reason: A classical argument is granted partial success and then limited by an objection resting on a fine distinction between fearing a state and fearing a loss.

subtopic: The Gita's teaching of action without attachment to its fruits asks for a relation to consequences that improves action rather than ignoring results, though whether that relation can be sustained remains open.
paragraphs: ["On the eve of a battle, the Bhagavad Gita relates, the warrior Arjuna loses heart at the prospect of fighting his own kinsmen, and his charioteer Krishna answers him in a long discourse. One of its central teachings is that a person has a claim on his action but not on its fruits: he should act, and act well, without making the outcome the motive of what he does, and he should meet success and failure with the same evenness of mind. The teaching has been admired across many centuries and many traditions, and it has also been accused of something close to moral recklessness. An agent who does not care about outcomes, the objection runs, is an agent who will not count the cost of what he does.", "The objection rests on running together two different things: attending to consequences and depending on them. Nothing in the idea of acting without attachment forbids a person from considering what his action is likely to bring about; a physician who acts in this spirit still chooses the treatment most likely to help. What the teaching asks is that the physician's steadiness, and his sense of having done what he should, not be held hostage to whether the patient recovers. Consequences enter into deciding what to do. They do not enter into the agent's claim to a reward, or into the anxious craving that so often bends judgement toward whatever promises to be noticed and praised.", "Seen this way, detachment is less a withdrawal from the world than a condition for acting well in it. Anxiety about results is notoriously bad for performance; the craftsman watching the clock and the speaker imagining the applause both tend to do worse work than the one absorbed in the task. More seriously, an agent fixed on fruits is tempted to choose the action whose success will be visible over the one that is right, and to abandon a just course the moment it begins to fail. The teaching guards against both distortions.", "It would be too quick, however, to declare the tension dissolved. Consequences cannot be considered in choosing and then set aside entirely in acting, because most actions unfold over time and must be adjusted as their effects appear. The physician has to watch whether the treatment is working. What the teaching can sensibly ask is not blindness to results but a particular relation to them, in which they are information to be used rather than verdicts on one's worth. Whether that relation can be sustained by ordinary people under real pressure is a question the teaching poses rather than settles."]
difficulty_reason: An objection is answered by a distinction, then the author qualifies the answer; the argument is abstract but well signposted.

subtopic: Solitude is a distinct good from which loneliness should be distinguished, so efforts to cure loneliness should improve connection rather than aim simply to reduce time spent alone.
paragraphs: ["Public discussion tends to treat time alone as a problem to be solved. Loneliness is described, rightly, as a source of real suffering, and the remedies proposed, from neighbourhood programmes to ever more ingenious ways of connecting online, share an assumption: that the less time a person spends unaccompanied, the better. On this view solitude and loneliness are a single condition seen from two angles, the first merely a polite name for the second.", "The assumption confuses a fact about circumstances with a fact about experience. Loneliness is the painful sense that one's connections are fewer or thinner than one needs; it can be felt in a crowded room, and some of its most persistent forms occur within marriages and among colleagues who see each other every day. Solitude is simply being alone, and its quality depends on what one brings to it. For someone who is lonely, an empty evening confirms a lack. For someone who is not, the same evening may be the only time in the week when attention is not divided, when a thought can be followed to its end, or when grief or pleasure can be felt without being performed for anyone.", "Many traditions have valued this second kind of aloneness. Hermits, monks and contemplatives have sought it deliberately, sometimes for years at a time, and periods of withdrawal into wilderness or retreat recur in the stories told about religious teachers in very different cultures. One need not share their aims to see the point they grasped: a person who can never bear his own company depends on others in a way that makes his relationships less free. Friendship is richer between people who could survive without it.", "This is not an argument for withdrawal. Solitude is good largely because it is chosen and because it comes to an end; a solitude imposed by exclusion, or one that stretches on with no prospect of return, turns into the very loneliness from which it was supposed to be distinct. Nor is the capacity to be alone a substitute for company; it is a companion skill to it. But if the two conditions really are distinct, then policies and technologies that aim only at reducing time spent alone may, without anyone intending it, crowd out a good that most people need in some measure and few are ever taught to use. The cure for loneliness is better connection, not the abolition of solitude."]
difficulty_reason: A conceptual distinction is drawn and defended with a qualification; the final policy point needs the distinction to be held firmly.

subtopic: Treating leisure as recovery for work lets the standards of work take over free time; Aristotle's view of leisure as activity chosen for its own sake survives the just objection that he reserved it for a privileged few.
paragraphs: ["In ordinary speech leisure is what is left over when work is done. It is time off, and its value is usually explained by reference to the work it interrupts: we rest so that we can return refreshed, and an employer who grants generous holidays is said to be investing in productivity. Even our defences of free time tend to be framed in these terms. Leisure, on this picture, is the pause that makes the next effort possible, and a person who takes too much of it is quietly suspected of having failed at something.", "Aristotle saw the relation the other way round. In the Nicomachean Ethics he argues that we are busy in order to have leisure, much as we make war in order to have peace, and the Greek word for leisure, schole, is the ancestor of our word 'school'. Leisure in his sense was not rest or idleness. It was the condition of being free to engage in activities chosen for their own sake, of which he held contemplation to be the highest, though he also counted the cultivated enjoyment of music among its proper occupations. Amusement, by contrast, belonged with work. We need relaxation because we cannot labour continuously, and amusement provides it, so amusement exists for the sake of further activity rather than as an end in itself; to toil for the sake of amusement struck him as childish.", "The modern inversion has a consequence that is easy to miss. Once leisure is understood as recovery for the sake of work, it inherits the standards of work. Free time becomes something to be used well, which increasingly means used productively: hobbies are pursued for the skills they build, exercise for the stamina it sustains, even sleep for its effect on the next day's performance. The result is not merely that people have too little time off, though many do, but that the time they have is colonised by the logic it was supposed to interrupt. Aristotle would have recognised the pattern. A life organised entirely around work and the recovery it requires has, in his terms, no leisure at all, however many holidays it contains.", "The obvious objection is that Aristotle's leisure was a privilege resting on the labour of others. The citizens free for philosophy and politics were supported by slaves, by women whose sphere he confined to the household, and by labourers and artisans whom he considered unsuited to full citizenship in the best city. A conception of the good life that excludes most people from it can hardly serve as a model for a society in which nearly everyone must work. This objection is just, and it should not be softened. But it tells against the distribution of leisure in Aristotle's city, not against his account of what leisure is. One can reject the arrangement that gave a few men freedom from necessity while still holding that freedom from necessity is valuable for what it makes possible, and that what it makes possible is not simply more work.", "What follows for us is less a programme than a question. If the value of leisure lies in activities worth doing for their own sake, then the measure of a society's free time is not only how much of it there is but whether people have the means, the education and the settled habits to fill it with such activities, rather than with recovery alone. That is a demand on schools and cities as much as on employers, and it is one that the language of rest and productivity has no words to state."]
difficulty_reason: Five paragraphs that move from a common view through a historical contrast to an objection whose scope the author limits; several distinctions (leisure, rest, amusement; nature versus distribution) must be held at once.

subtopic: The Buddhist no-self teaching is chiefly a practical exercise against craving and so escapes the easy refutation, but it still rests on a contestable claim about the self that deserves philosophical scrutiny.
paragraphs: ["Few doctrines have been more often misunderstood by sympathetic outsiders than the Buddhist teaching of anatta, usually translated as 'no-self'. Stated baldly, as the claim that there is no self, it seems to invite an easy refutation: someone, after all, is entertaining the doctrine, and someone will be disappointed if it turns out to be false. Critics who press this point imagine that they have found a contradiction at the heart of the tradition. In fact they have mostly found a problem of translation, and behind it a mistaken assumption about what kind of claim the teaching was meant to be.", "In the early discourses the teaching typically appears not as a thesis about what exists but as an exercise. The listener is led through the components that make up a person, which the tradition groups as bodily form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, and is asked of each whether it is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it is under one's control. Since none of them passes these tests, none, the discourse concludes, should be regarded as 'mine', as what 'I am', or as 'my self'. The point of the exercise is practical. According to the tradition's own account of suffering, its origin lies in craving, and craving is sustained by the habit of treating changing and uncontrollable processes as possessions one must defend. To see that nothing in experience is fit to be owned in that way is to loosen the grip of the habit.", "Read in this light, the easy refutation misses its target. The teaching does not deny that there is a stream of experiences, nor that the stream has a history, makes choices and bears their consequences; the same tradition has a great deal to say about all three. What it denies is that there is, in addition to the stream, an unchanging owner standing behind it, and it denies this chiefly because belief in such an owner is what makes us cling. A later dialogue makes the point with a chariot: the word names an assembly of axle, wheels and frame, and nothing is lost by admitting that there is no further chariot over and above the parts, arranged as they are. The person, likewise, is a convenient name for a functioning whole, not a hidden thing to which the whole belongs.", "It would be too convenient, however, to conclude that the doctrine is purely therapeutic and therefore immune to philosophical scrutiny. A therapy that works by inducing a belief earns its authority only if the belief is warranted; otherwise it is a comforting fiction, and the tradition has never presented its teaching as a fiction. The exercise succeeds, by its own standards, because it reveals how things are. So the metaphysical question cannot be set aside; it can only be stated more precisely. The question is not whether anyone exists but whether a person is anything more than the organised stream, and on that question the doctrine takes a position that some philosophers in other traditions have also defended, and others have rejected, without anyone having settled the matter.", "The lesson for the sympathetic outsider is therefore double. The easy refutation fails, because it attacks a claim the teaching does not make. But the easy defence fails too, because the teaching is not merely a technique; it is a technique whose authority rests on a claim about the self that may be true or false, and that deserves to be argued about on its merits rather than admired from a respectful distance."]
difficulty_reason: The author rejects both a refutation and a defence of the doctrine, so the stance is two-sided; the correct answer distinctions (exercise versus thesis, stream versus owner, therapy versus truth) are abstract.

subtopic: Seeing is an active, inferential interpretation of ambiguous sensory evidence, but this does not make the senses untrustworthy.
paragraphs: ["It is natural to think of seeing as a kind of recording. Light enters the eye, an image forms on the retina, and the brain, like a careful clerk, reads off what is there. The picture is attractive because it matches how perception feels: effortless, immediate, and apparently free of any contribution from the perceiver. Yet the retinal image is a poor document: it is upside down, flat, constantly jittering with the movements of the eye, and interrupted by a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina. Above all, it is ambiguous, in the sense that a small image on the retina could be a small object nearby or a large one far away; a patch of dim grey could be a dark surface in bright light or a pale surface in shadow. The eye, in short, delivers considerably less information than we ordinarily experience ourselves as seeing.", "For this reason many students of vision have preferred to describe perception as a form of inference. The brain, on this account, treats the incoming signal as evidence and settles on the interpretation that best explains it, given what it has learned about how the world usually is. Light tends to come from above, so a disc shaded darker at the bottom is seen as a bump and the same disc turned over as a dent. Objects tend to keep their size, so a person walking away is seen as receding rather than shrinking. These are not conclusions we reach; they are conclusions reached on our behalf, before anything is presented to awareness.", "The word 'inference' invites an obvious objection: if perception is a guess shaped by expectation, why do we not simply see whatever we expect? The answer is that the guess is tightly disciplined by the evidence, and that the expectations doing the work are of a peculiar kind. They are not the beliefs we hold and can revise in conversation, but assumptions built up over a lifetime of looking, and perhaps over the history of the species. This is why many visual illusions survive full knowledge of the trick. A viewer who has measured two lines and found them equal will still see one as longer; what she knows and what she sees have been settled by different processes.", "It would be a mistake, then, to conclude that perception is unreliable because it is inferential. The assumptions it relies on are mostly true of the environments in which they were formed, which is why they so rarely mislead us outside the laboratory, where illusions are carefully built to exploit them. What the inferential view really overturns is not our trust in the senses but the idea that seeing is passive. Every glance is a small act of interpretation, and its seeming effortlessness is the mark of how well the work is done, not evidence that no work is being done."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract argument that raises and answers an objection, then guards against an overreading; vocabulary is moderate.

subtopic: Inattentional blindness shows that we are poor judges of what we would notice, so where misses are costly we should design for attention that is already occupied.
paragraphs: ["Most people believe that anything sufficiently striking will catch their eye. If a person in a gorilla suit walked through a game of catch we were watching, we assume we would notice. A well-known series of experiments suggests otherwise. When viewers are asked to count the passes made by one team in a short video, a large share of them fail to see an unexpected figure stroll through the middle of the scene, even when it pauses to face the camera. Asked afterwards, many insist that nothing unusual happened, and some are indignant when the recording is replayed.", "The phenomenon, usually called inattentional blindness, is easy to misread as a failure of the eyes. It is not, or at least not in any sense that an optician could detect: the light from the unexpected figure reaches the retina as surely as the light from the ball. What fails is the selection that decides which parts of the scene will be built into conscious experience. Attention is not a spotlight that merely brightens what we are looking at; it is closer to a gate, and what does not pass through the gate is not dimly seen but, for practical purposes, not seen at all.", "The finding matters less because of its surprise value than because of the confidence it exposes. We are poor judges of what we would notice, because the things we miss leave no trace in experience from which we could learn that we missed them. Ordinary experience, which might be expected to correct our overconfidence, cannot do so, because an occasion on which we failed to notice something is, from the inside, indistinguishable from an occasion on which there was nothing to notice. A driver who looks at a junction while thinking about something else may have no sense that a cyclist was in view. Afterwards he will report, quite sincerely, that the cyclist came from nowhere. His honesty is not in question; his access to his own lapse is.", "This should not be taken to mean that attention is simply defective. A mind that admitted everything in the visual field to awareness would be overwhelmed, unable to follow the ball, read a page or hold a conversation in a crowded room. Selectivity is the price of focus, and on most days, when little that we fail to notice turns out to matter, the price is low. The lesson is narrower and more practical: where the cost of missing something is high, we should not rely on the conviction that we would have seen it, and should instead design tasks, roads and warning signals on the assumption that attention is already spoken for."]
difficulty_reason: Concrete examples and a clearly signposted argument; the stance is stated directly.

subtopic: Vivid memories of shocking public events are held with great confidence but change as much as ordinary memories, so vividness and certainty are weak guides to accuracy.
paragraphs: ["Ask people where they were when they heard of some great public shock, an assassination, a disaster broadcast live, the sudden death of a famous figure, and many will answer at once and in detail. They remember the room, who told them, what they were holding, the first thing they said. Such recollections have been called flashbulb memories, the name suggesting that a moment of intense feeling exposes the scene, as a flash exposes film, and fixes it for good. The people who hold them are rarely in doubt. Of all their memories, these seem the least likely to be wrong.", "The difficulty is that when such memories have been checked, they have often turned out to be wrong in exactly the ways ordinary memories are. Researchers have questioned people within a day or two of a widely reported event and then again months or years later. The later accounts frequently differ from the earlier ones, sometimes in small particulars and sometimes wholesale: a person who first wrote that she heard the news from a colleague at work later describes, with complete assurance, watching it on television at home. Confronted with her own earlier account, she may concede that she wrote it while continuing to feel that her present memory is the true one.", "What sets these memories apart, then, is not their accuracy but the confidence and vividness with which they are held; in these memories, conviction and correctness have come apart. One explanation is that the events are rehearsed endlessly. They are discussed with friends, revisited in anniversary broadcasts and retold until the story has a familiar shape. Each retelling is less a replay than a reconstruction, and the most recent reconstruction is the one that feels like the original. Emotion contributes too, but perhaps less to the record than to the sense of its importance: a moment that mattered seems as though it must have been remembered faithfully.", "None of this means that strong feeling has no effect on memory. People rarely forget that the event happened, and there is reason to think that emotion sharpens memory for whatever is central to an experience while letting the periphery blur. The trouble is that the details we are proudest of recalling, the room, the messenger, the coffee cup, are precisely the peripheral ones. The practical lesson extends well beyond public events. Wherever memory is used as evidence, the vividness of a recollection and the certainty of the person reporting it are weaker guides to its truth than we are inclined to believe."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief with an explanation and a concession; the final distinction between central and peripheral detail needs care.

subtopic: Forgetting is largely an editing function that keeps useful memories accessible, though not all forgetting is benign.
paragraphs: ["We tend to speak of forgetting as a failure, the mind's equivalent of a leaking roof: students blame it for poor marks, older people fear it as a sign of decline, and whole industries promise to reduce it. Behind these attitudes lies an assumption that an ideal memory would keep everything. Even our vocabulary betrays the attitude, since we speak of 'losing' a memory as though it were a possession that had slipped out of a pocket. It is worth asking whether the assumption behind such talk is true.", "Consider what such a memory would be like to live with. Every time you parked your car, you would recall not only today's space but every space you had ever used, each with equal force. Every time you met a friend, you would be confronted with each version of her face across the years. The problem would not be a shortage of information but a surplus of it, because the memory you needed would be buried among the memories you did not. Some people who report unusually complete recall of their own lives describe the gift less as a pleasure than as a burden, a past that will not stay in the past.", "Seen in this light, much forgetting looks less like decay than like editing. Memories that are rarely used become harder to reach, while those that are used often stay accessible, and the effect is less a loss than a reordering of priorities. This is roughly what a sensible filing system would do: it would keep the files you consult near at hand and move the rest to the back, on the reasonable bet that the past use of a memory predicts its future use. Some evidence even suggests that recalling one memory actively suppresses its competitors, so that using your new phone number makes the old one fade faster.", "This argument has limits, and it is easy to push it too far, for not all forgetting is useful: the losses caused by brain injury or dementia are not editing but damage, and nothing said here makes them less painful. Nor does a system that is well designed on average serve every individual case: the name you cannot recall at an important meeting is a real cost, even if it is the price of a sensible policy. The point is only that the capacity to forget is part of what makes memory useful, not simply a flaw in it. A memory that never let go would be a worse memory, not a better one."]
difficulty_reason: Everyday examples, a clear thesis and an explicit list of limits.

subtopic: Much expertise is trained perception rather than superior memory or reasoning, which makes it fast and usually right but brittle outside the cases that trained it.
paragraphs: ["A familiar demonstration from the study of chess runs as follows. A position from a real game is shown for a few seconds and then removed, and players are asked to reconstruct it on an empty board. Strong players replace most of the pieces correctly, while novices manage only a handful, and the obvious conclusion is that strong players simply have better memories. The less obvious and more instructive part of the demonstration comes next. When the same pieces are scattered at random, in arrangements that could never arise in play, the masters' advantage largely disappears, and they do little better than beginners.", "What the masters possess, then, is not a larger store for holding pieces but a different way of seeing them. Years of play have given them a vocabulary of familiar configurations, a castled king with its pawns in front, a bishop aimed down a long diagonal, and they take in a position as a few such units rather than as two dozen separate pieces. A novice looking at the same board sees wood on squares. The master sees a situation, and often, before any conscious calculation has begun, a sense of what the situation calls for.", "Similar observations have been made in fields as different as radiology, birdwatching and the reading of geological maps, where experienced specialists frequently report knowing that something is wrong with an image within a second or two, before they can say what it is. The birdwatcher who names a distant species from the way it flies, long before any marking can be made out, is drawing on the same resource. It is tempting to describe this as intuition, as though it were a mysterious faculty standing apart from knowledge. It is better described as knowledge that has been absorbed into perception, so that it no longer needs to be consulted, because it shapes what is seen in the first place.", "This view has practical consequences, though they are easily overstated. If expertise lies partly in the eye, it cannot be fully transmitted by rules and explanations; the learner has to look at a great many cases, with feedback, until the patterns become visible. But perception is not the whole of expertise. Masters still calculate, and careful specialists still check their first impressions, because a pattern that is recognised instantly can also be misrecognised instantly. The trained eye is fast and usually right within the territory that trained it, and that qualification matters: presented with a case unlike those it has learned from, its speed becomes a liability rather than an asset."]
difficulty_reason: A case study generalised across fields, with a concession that limits the thesis; the argument is clear but the final qualification must be tracked.

subtopic: We judge duration in two ways, by attention while it passes and by memory afterwards, so there is no single answer to how long something felt.
paragraphs: ["There is a small puzzle about time that most people have noticed without ever stating it. A week spent travelling somewhere new seems to vanish while it is happening, so that there is never enough of it; yet once the traveller is home, the same week looks enormous, crowded with places and faces, as if it had lasted a month. A week at a familiar desk behaves in the opposite way. It drags while it is lived, each afternoon longer than the last, and then collapses in memory into a single grey item that seems to have taken no time at all.", "The puzzle dissolves once we accept that we judge duration in two quite different ways. While an interval is passing, our sense of its length depends largely on how much attention we pay to time itself: boredom draws attention to the clock and stretches the hour, while absorption draws it away and the hour shrinks. Looking back, however, we have no clock to consult. We estimate how long a period lasted from what it left behind, and a period that left many distinct memories is judged to have been long. Novelty therefore works in opposite directions on the two judgements, shortening the interval as experienced and lengthening it as remembered.", "This distinction sheds light on a complaint that becomes common in middle age, that the years go faster than they used to. The complaint is almost always retrospective. Few people find that a particular afternoon passes faster at fifty than at fifteen; what they find is that last year, viewed as a whole, seems to have been brief. If remembered duration tracks the number of distinct memories, the explanation is not far to seek, since adult life is more routine than youth, with fewer firsts, and a year of repeated weeks leaves less behind to measure it by.", "The account is persuasive, but it should be held loosely. It is unlikely that a single factor explains how time seems at every age, and other changes, in health, in responsibility, in how far ahead people habitually plan, probably play a part. Still less does it follow, as some cheerful advice suggests, that one can lengthen a life simply by filling it with novelty. A crowded year may indeed look longer in retrospect, but it will feel shorter while it is lived, and there is no obvious reason to prefer one of these measures over the other. What the distinction teaches is not a technique for buying time but a caution against speaking of how long something 'really' felt, as though there were only one answer."]
difficulty_reason: A puzzle resolved by a distinction, applied to a familiar complaint and then hedged; the two kinds of judgement must be kept apart throughout.

subtopic: The rival verdicts that mind wandering is a costly lapse or a useful activity come from studying different occasions; its value depends on context and on the wanderer's awareness.
paragraphs: ["For much of its short history as a subject of research, the wandering mind was treated as noise. Participants in experiments were supposed to attend to the task in front of them, and the moments when their thoughts drifted to lunch or to an argument with a sibling were lapses to be minimised or averaged away. When researchers began to study these lapses directly, by interrupting people at random moments in their day and asking what they had been thinking about, the first surprise was how common the lapses were. The method had the merit of catching thought in the act, before the thinker had time to tidy it into a more respectable account of where her attention had been. A considerable part of waking thought, it turned out, is about something other than what the thinker is doing.", "Two quite different interpretations of this finding have since competed. On the first, mind wandering is a failure of control: it is associated with errors in reading and driving, with poorer performance on tests of sustained attention and, in some studies, with lower reported mood at the moment of wandering. The mind that drifts is the mind that has lost its grip, and the remedy is training in attention. On the second interpretation, these costs are real but partial, and they ignore what the drifting mind is actually doing. Much wandering thought is directed at the future, at plans, rehearsals of conversations and the weighing of unfinished business, and some of the solutions that arrive unbidden in the shower or on a walk may owe something to the same process. On this view the mind that drifts is not idle but working on a different problem, one it has judged, so to speak, more pressing than the task at hand.", "Each interpretation, I think, makes the same mistake, which is to speak of mind wandering as though it were one thing with one value. The evidence for costs comes largely from tasks that demand continuous attention, where any lapse is damaging by design, while the evidence for benefits comes largely from situations in which the external task is undemanding, so that little is lost by leaving it. Tasks of the first kind are chosen precisely because they make lapses easy to count, and situations of the second kind because they leave room for thought. It is hardly surprising that the two literatures reach different verdicts, since they are, for the most part, looking at different occasions. Nor does the link with low mood settle the matter. A person who is worried is likely both to feel worse and to find his thoughts pulled towards his worries, so that wandering may be as much a symptom of unhappiness as its cause.", "A more useful question is not whether the mind should wander but when, and with what awareness. Drifting during a lecture one has chosen to attend is a cost; drifting while washing dishes may be a free opportunity to think. There also seems to be a real difference between thought that slips away unnoticed and thought that is allowed to roam, as when a person deliberately sets a problem aside and lets her attention go where it will. The second kind is under a loose but genuine control, since the person can notice it and call it back. If this is right, the goal of training attention should not be to abolish wandering, an aim that is probably unachievable and possibly harmful, but to make wandering more visible to the wanderer, so that she can tell which kind of occasion she is in."]
difficulty_reason: Two rival views are reported at length before the author's own position, which rejects a shared assumption of both; the stance must be kept apart from the views reported.

subtopic: Retrieving material strengthens memory more than restudying it, though learners misjudge this, and the benefit lies in low-stakes recall with feedback rather than in more examinations.
paragraphs: ["In most schools a test is understood as a thermometer. It is applied at the end of a period of learning to find out how much has been learned, and like a thermometer it is supposed to leave the thing it measures unchanged. The understanding is so familiar that it seldom occurs to anyone that it might be false. Yet one of the more robust findings in the psychology of memory is that the act of retrieving something from memory is not a neutral reading: it changes the memory, and generally strengthens it, so that material which has been recalled once is more likely to be recalled again than material which has merely been seen again.", "The contrast is clearest when the two activities are set against each other. Suppose two groups of students study the same passage, after which one group rereads it while the other closes the book and writes down whatever it can remember. The design holds constant both the material and the time spent on it, so that the only difference between the groups is whether they looked at the passage again or tried to bring it back unaided. Tested a few minutes later, the rereaders often do as well or better; tested a week later, the group that practised recall tends to remember considerably more. The advantage of retrieval, in other words, is easily hidden by the timing of the measurement, which may be one reason why it was overlooked for so long by teachers and students alike.", "What is more striking is how little the students themselves sense any of this. Asked to predict their own performance, rereaders tend to be the more confident group. Rereading produces a feeling of fluency, in which the sentences are familiar and slide past easily, and ease of processing is readily mistaken for mastery. Attempting recall produces the opposite feeling, since it is effortful, it exposes gaps and it is often unpleasant, which is presumably why students left to themselves so rarely choose it. Teachers are not immune to the same illusion, since a class that has just reread its notes looks, and feels, better prepared than one that has just struggled to recall them. The method that feels like learning and the method that produces it are, at least here, not the same, and the lesson generalises uncomfortably: a learner's own sense of how well a session went is an unreliable guide to how much it achieved.", "It would be easy to draw from all this a crude conclusion, that schools should simply test more, but the finding does not support it. What strengthens memory is the effort of retrieval, not the apparatus of examination, and the apparatus can work against the effort. A high-stakes test that provokes anxiety, or that is followed by no feedback, may teach students little except to fear tests, and a wrong answer recalled confidently and never corrected may itself be strengthened. The useful practice is humbler than the word 'test' suggests: it consists of frequent, low-stakes attempts to recall, each followed by a chance to check, built into ordinary study. None of this requires abolishing examinations, which serve purposes of certification that have little to do with memory; it requires only that they not be mistaken for the whole of what testing can do. Understood in this way, the thermometer turns out to be one of the more effective means of raising the temperature it was meant only to record."]
difficulty_reason: Dense argument that overturns a common belief, adds a finding about self-assessment and then blocks a crude policy conclusion; several fine distinctions are tested.

subtopic: Public dread of rare, imposed or catastrophic risks partly reflects defensible values that counts of expected deaths omit, though it is not a reliable guide on its own.
paragraphs: ["Experts who manage risk often speak of the public with weary patience. People, they observe, fear the wrong things. They worry about a nuclear plant that has never harmed anyone in the district while driving, without a second thought, along a road that kills several of their neighbours every year. They demand inquiries after a single dramatic accident and shrug at the steady toll of falls in the home. On this account the task of policy is to correct a problem of perception: to replace vivid fears with sober numbers, so that resources follow expected deaths rather than headlines.", "There is something to this, but less than its confidence suggests. When people are asked to describe what makes a hazard frightening, their answers are not random. Risks feel worse when they are imposed rather than chosen, when they could kill many people at once rather than a few at a time, when their effects are delayed or invisible, and when those who create them are not those who bear them. None of these features is captured by a count of expected fatalities, yet none of them is obviously foolish. A person who accepts the dangers of rock climbing but objects to a factory releasing an untested chemical into the river is not confused about arithmetic. She is drawing a distinction between a risk she has consented to and one that has been placed on her by others, and that distinction is a moral one that most legal systems also recognise.", "Seen this way, the gap between expert and lay rankings of hazards is partly a disagreement about what the question is. The expert asks how many people will die; the citizen asks, in addition, whether the arrangement that produces those deaths is fair, controllable and worthy of trust. To call the second question irrational is to settle a dispute about values by redescribing it as a dispute about facts.", "None of this makes dread a reliable guide. The features that make a hazard feel threatening can be manufactured by vivid reporting, and fear can drive choices that increase the very danger it is meant to avoid. If travellers abandon aircraft for cars after a well-publicised crash, they may exchange a small risk for a larger one without noticing the trade. The sensible response is neither to dismiss public fear as noise nor to treat it as a verdict. It is to take it apart: to ask which of its components reflect values that deserve a hearing in policy, and which reflect only the salience of a recent and alarming image."]
difficulty_reason: A clear claim, reply and qualification in plain vocabulary; the stance is stated openly in paragraphs 3 and 4.

subtopic: The idea that too much choice harms people has been oversold; large assortments burden choosers only under specific conditions, so the usual remedy is better structure rather than fewer options.
paragraphs: ["Few findings from the psychology of decision-making have travelled as far as the idea that too much choice is bad for us. The claim has a satisfying shape. It flatters the suspicion that modern abundance has not made people happier, and it offers a tidy remedy: fewer options, simpler shelves, shorter menus. Retailers have trimmed product lines in its name, and essayists have used it to diagnose a whole culture of anxious shoppers frozen before walls of nearly identical goods. Its appeal, in short, owes at least as much to its moral resonance as to the strength of the evidence on which it was originally built.", "The evidence, however, is less tidy than the slogan. A handful of striking early experiments suggested that people offered many options were less likely to choose at all, and less satisfied when they did. Later attempts to reproduce such effects produced a far more mixed picture: sometimes the effect appeared, sometimes it vanished, and sometimes larger assortments made people more likely to buy. A finding that reverses under slightly different conditions is not a law of human nature. It is a clue that the conditions themselves are doing the work.", "What might those conditions be? The more careful research points to a few. Large sets seem to burden people when they lack settled preferences in the domain, when the options differ along many dimensions that are hard to compare, when no option is marked as a sensible default, and when the decision feels consequential enough to invite later regret. A wine enthusiast choosing among forty bottles is browsing; a novice choosing among forty pension funds is drowning. The number of options is the same. What differs is whether the chooser has a way of sorting them, and therefore whether the abundance in front of him registers as an opportunity or as an accumulation of possible mistakes for which he alone will be answerable.", "This reframing matters because it changes the remedy. If abundance itself were the problem, the answer would be to cut. If the problem is the absence of structure, the answer is often to organise: to group options by the features people care about, to supply defaults that can be overridden, to let people narrow the field in stages. Cutting still has its place, particularly when most of the options are poor or nearly identical. But a policy of reduction applied everywhere would deprive the enthusiast of what she values in order to rescue the novice from a difficulty that better design could have removed."]
difficulty_reason: Short, concrete paragraphs with an explicit thesis and one clear concession; the wine and pension contrast makes the argument easy to follow.

subtopic: Anchoring on numbers supplied by others is better explained by selective search for confirming evidence than by insufficient adjustment, so the remedy is to argue against the anchor, not to think harder.
paragraphs: ["Ask people to estimate a quantity they do not know, after first asking whether it is higher or lower than some number, and their estimates will drift toward that number. The effect survives when participants have watched the number being produced at random, when they are told it is meaningless, and when they are paid for accuracy. It appears among amateurs and professionals alike, in guesses about the age of a building, the price of a house or a reasonable figure with which to open a negotiation. That arbitrary numbers can move consequential judgements is now one of the least disputed findings in the study of decision-making. Why they do so is more disputed, and the answer matters more than it first appears.", "The older explanation treats the anchor as a starting point. People begin at the number they are given and adjust away from it toward what seems plausible, but they stop too soon, at the first value that falls within a range they can accept. On this view anchoring is a failure of effort: the mind is a reluctant traveller who halts at the nearest acceptable station. The remedy follows naturally. Slow people down, ask them to think harder, give them reasons to care, and they will travel further from the anchor.", "A second explanation locates the problem earlier. When we are asked whether a building is older than, say, two hundred years, we do not merely note the number; we test it, and testing a hypothesis tends to mean searching for evidence that would make it true. We recall the building's worn stone and its old-fashioned windows, and these recollections, now freshly available, shape the estimate that follows. The anchor does not set a starting point so much as select the evidence. If this account is right, effort is no cure, because a more diligent search conducted in the same direction only gathers more of the same evidence.", "The two accounts are not exclusive. When people produce an anchor themselves, as when they start from a figure they already know and correct it for some difference, something like insufficient adjustment seems to occur, and in those cases encouraging effort does help. But for anchors supplied by others, which are the ones that negotiators, sellers and advocates supply deliberately, the evidence favours the selective account, and with it a different remedy: not to think harder about the number one has been handed but to think deliberately against it, by asking what would make it wrong."]
difficulty_reason: Two competing mechanisms must be kept apart, and the conclusion depends on a distinction between self-produced and supplied anchors.

subtopic: 'Overconfidence' names three distinct tendencies that behave differently; overprecision is the most robust and damaging, and each form needs its own diagnosis and remedy.
paragraphs: ["It is often said that overconfidence is the most pervasive of the biases, the one from which many of the others draw their strength. The claim is repeated so often that it is easy to miss how much it conceals. 'Overconfidence' names at least three different things, and they do not always travel together. Treating them as one has made the phenomenon seem both more universal and more mysterious than it is.", "The first is overestimation: believing that one has performed, or will perform, better than one actually does. The second is overplacement: believing that one is better than other people. The third, which receives less public attention, is overprecision: excessive certainty that one's beliefs are accurate, shown when people asked for a range they are ninety per cent sure contains some true value give ranges that contain it far less often than that. These sound like variations on a single vanity, but they come apart in revealing ways. On tasks that are easy, people tend to underestimate how well they have done, even as they place themselves above others; on tasks that are very hard, the pattern reverses, and many people will rate themselves below average at, say, juggling or composing verse while still overestimating their own scores.", "What explains such reversals is less a desire to think well of oneself than the way information is distributed. People usually know more about their own performance than about other people's, so their judgements of others are pulled toward a vague middle. When a task is hard, they sense that they did poorly, if not quite how poorly, but assume that others did less badly; when it is easy, the opposite. A good deal of what looks like ego, in other words, is a predictable consequence of reasoning from imperfect information about the people with whom one is being compared.", "Overprecision is different. It shows no comparable tendency to reverse, appearing on easy and hard questions, among novices and among specialists, and it is the form that does most harm in planning, where projects are budgeted against ranges too narrow to include what actually happens. It is also the form that most resists exhortation: telling forecasters to be humble rarely widens their intervals much. More promising are procedures that change the question, such as asking people to assign probabilities to several ranges in turn, so that the possibility of an outcome far from their best guess must be considered explicitly rather than waved away. The lesson is not that confidence is good or bad but that a single word has been doing the work of three, and that each of the three needs its own diagnosis."]
difficulty_reason: Three closely related technical terms must be kept distinct, and the reversal pattern in paragraph 2 is easy to scramble.

subtopic: Teaching people about biases rarely changes how they reason on new problems; redesigning decision procedures fits the evidence better because it does not rely on individual self-correction.
paragraphs: ["If biases are errors, it seems natural to suppose that teaching people about them should reduce them. Hence the many workshops in which managers, doctors and analysts are taken through a catalogue of the mind's failings, from anchoring to the sunk-cost fallacy, in the hope that knowing the names will help them avoid the traps. The hope is reasonable, and it is mostly disappointed. Participants usually leave such sessions able to define the biases and to spot them in descriptions of other people's reasoning. What they far less often do is reason differently when a fresh problem, dressed in unfamiliar clothes, arrives in their own work.", "Part of the difficulty is that biases rarely announce themselves. A textbook problem about sunk costs is labelled, at least implicitly, by the chapter in which it appears; a real decision about whether to keep funding a struggling project comes with no such label, and with colleagues, budgets and reputations attached. Recognising a pattern in a tidy example is a different skill from noticing it in a messy situation, and teaching the first does not automatically produce the second. There is also a subtler obstacle. People readily accept that biases exist and readily see them at work in others, while judging their own conclusions to be the products of careful thought. Instruction can even sharpen this asymmetry, supplying a vocabulary for diagnosing colleagues without unsettling one's own sense of seeing clearly.", "None of this shows that debiasing is hopeless. A few interventions built around repeated practice, varied examples and immediate feedback on one's own errors have produced improvements that outlasted the session, though how far they reach beyond the kinds of problem used in training remains uncertain. And there is a quieter strategy that sidesteps the question of individual reform altogether: changing the procedures within which decisions are made. A committee that collects independent estimates before discussion, or a review that requires someone to argue the case against a favoured plan, does not need its members to have become wiser. It builds the correction into the routine.", "The contrast is instructive. Approaches that rely on informing the individual treat bias as a kind of ignorance, curable by knowledge. Approaches that redesign procedures treat it as a standing feature of minds working under ordinary conditions, to be managed rather than eliminated. The second view is less flattering, but it fits the evidence better, and it has the practical merit of not depending on each person's ability to catch themselves in the act."]
difficulty_reason: The argument turns on a contrast between two conceptions of bias, with a concession in paragraph 3 that must be weighed against the conclusion.

subtopic: Expert intuition deserves trust only where the environment in which it was learned had regular cues and quick feedback, and the expert's own confidence is no guide to whether it did.
paragraphs: ["Debates about intuition tend to fall into two camps that talk past each other. One camp collects cases in which experienced professionals, asked to explain a snap judgement, cannot say how they knew, and yet were right: the nurse who senses that a patient is deteriorating before the monitors register anything, the engineer who distrusts a design at a glance. The other camp collects cases in which confident experts did no better than simple formulas, or than chance, at predicting outcomes in their own fields. Each camp treats its own cases as the typical ones and the other camp's as curiosities.", "A way through the impasse begins by asking what intuition is. On the most plausible account it is recognition: the rapid matching of a present situation to patterns stored from earlier ones, which brings with it a sense of what is likely to happen next and of what to do. Recognition of this kind can be only as good as the patterns it has learned, and patterns can be learned only where two conditions hold. The environment must contain regularities that link cues to outcomes, and the person must have had extensive practice with feedback quick and clear enough to reveal whether a judgement was right. A ward where patients either recover or worsen within hours satisfies both conditions. A market in which prices reflect the guesses of many other participants, and in which the consequences of a choice emerge slowly and mixed with luck, satisfies neither very well.", "This account explains why both camps can find their cases. It also yields a less comfortable conclusion. The feeling of knowing that accompanies intuition is produced in the same way whether or not the underlying patterns are valid. A forecaster who has spent years in an environment with little regularity can feel as sure as a nurse, because confidence grows with familiarity and with the coherence of the story one can tell, not with accuracy. Subjective certainty therefore tells us almost nothing about whether to trust a judgement. What tells us something is the environment in which the judgement was learned.", "The practical upshot is not that intuition should be confined to a list of approved professions. The same expert may work in a high-validity environment for some tasks and a low-validity one for others. A clinician may become very good at judging, within minutes, whether a patient needs urgent attention, while long-range predictions about the same patient's recovery, whose outcomes arrive years later and are shaped by many intervening events, remain little better than guesses. The question to ask of any intuition, then, is not who holds it or how firmly, but whether the conditions for learning it were ever present."]
difficulty_reason: The passage resolves a debate with a two-condition account and then draws a counter-intuitive consequence about confidence; the stance is explicit but abstract.

subtopic: Many framing effects are reasonable responses to the information a speaker's choice of frame conveys, though a residue remains, so whether responding to a frame is an error depends on whether the frame was a signal.
paragraphs: ["The demonstration is by now familiar. Two groups are offered the same treatment, described in two ways: to one group as leaving ninety in a hundred patients alive after a year, to the other as seeing ten in a hundred die. The numbers are identical, yet the first description reliably attracts more support than the second. Since the treatment does not differ, the argument runs, a rational agent should not respond to the difference in wording, and the fact that people do respond is evidence that their preferences are shaped by presentation rather than substance. The principle appealed to, that logically equivalent descriptions should produce the same choice, has seemed so obvious that few have thought it needed defending.", "Yet the principle is less obvious than it looks once we remember that descriptions do not fall from the sky. Somebody chooses them, and the choice is rarely arbitrary. A doctor who believes a treatment is worth trying tends, without any intent to manipulate, to speak of the patients it saves; a doctor with doubts more naturally mentions those it fails. Speakers also tend to describe a quantity in terms of the reference point from which it has moved: a glass that was full and has been partly drunk is more often called half empty than half full. If such regularities hold, then the frame carries information that the bare numbers do not, and a listener who draws an inference from it is not being swayed by mere wording. She is reading what the speaker's choice of words reveals, much as she would read an emphasis or a pause.", "On this view, many framing effects are better described as sensitivity to implicit information than as failures of logic, and the experimenter who insists on equivalence has mistaken the logic of sentences for the logic of conversation. The equivalence holds between the propositions; it does not hold between the acts of uttering them, because those acts tell the hearer different things about the speaker. Participants who bring their ordinary conversational competence into the laboratory are, in a sense, being too reasonable for the experiment's purposes.", "This rehabilitation should not be pushed too far. When experiments go to some lengths to make the frame visibly arbitrary, for example by assigning descriptions by an evident coin toss or by presenting both descriptions together, the inference from frame to speaker has nothing to work on, and a rational participant should set it aside. Effects in such conditions are often smaller, which is what the information account predicts, but they do not always vanish. Some residue seems to reflect the plain pull of words such as 'die' and 'lose', a reaction that would survive any amount of reflection about speakers. The information account explains a good deal of the phenomenon; it does not explain all of it.", "What follows is a more discriminating verdict than either side usually offers. Whether responsiveness to a frame is a lapse depends on whether, in the situation at hand, the frame was a signal. Outside the laboratory it usually is, which is why habits formed in conversation are worth having. The danger lies precisely in that usefulness. A listener who reasonably treats frames as informative can be exploited by a speaker who knows the convention and chooses a frame to suggest a recommendation he would not dare to state outright. The fault in such cases lies less with the listener's inference than with the speaker's abuse of a norm that ordinarily makes the inference sound."]
difficulty_reason: The argument moves through a received view, a rehabilitation, a limit on that rehabilitation and a conditional verdict; the distinction between propositions and acts of utterance is abstract.

subtopic: The ecological critique of bias research is right that errors depend on norms and environments, but it overreaches in assuming people match heuristics to environments, which is an open empirical question.
paragraphs: ["For several decades one research tradition in psychology has proceeded by a simple method. Set people a problem whose correct answer is fixed by logic or probability theory, record the ways in which their answers depart from it, and infer from the pattern of departures the shortcuts the mind must be using. The method has been extraordinarily productive. It has yielded a catalogue of systematic errors, and with it a picture of human judgement as a set of serviceable but crude rules of thumb that fail predictably whenever a problem is constructed to expose them. That picture has travelled well beyond psychology, into economics, law and medicine, where it is now invoked to justify the design of forms, defaults and warnings meant to protect people from their own shortcuts.", "A rival tradition objects not to the findings but to the frame. A rule of thumb, it argues, can be judged only against the environment in which it is used, and the problems of the laboratory are often unlike the environments in which human judgement developed and in which it is mostly exercised. More provocatively, it points out that simple rules can outperform elaborate ones. When a decision must be made from a small sample in a noisy world, a model that weighs many cues carefully will fit the data at hand closely, including its accidents, and will then predict new cases worse than a rule that attends to one or two strong cues and ignores the rest. Ignoring information, which the first tradition tends to read as a symptom of limited capacity, can on this account be a source of accuracy.", "The point is sound, and it is worth seeing why it does not abandon the idea of a norm. The advantage of the simple rule is itself a result of statistical theory: it accepts a little systematic error in exchange for a large reduction in sensitivity to noise, and in small, noisy samples that exchange is often a good one. To praise frugal heuristics on these grounds is not to reject normative standards but to replace one standard, agreement with a probabilistic calculation on a fully specified problem, with another, accuracy in predicting cases one has not yet seen. That second standard is arguably the one that matters for creatures who must act on incomplete information.", "Where the rival tradition overreaches is in moving from what heuristics can do to what people actually do. To show that a rule performs well in some environments is not to show that people use it in those environments and abandon it in others. That further claim, that minds select their tools to suit the structure of the task, is an empirical hypothesis, and the evidence for it is uneven. People sometimes apply a rule where it serves them and sometimes carry it into settings where it misleads, and modern life supplies many settings, from the interpretation of medical test results to the assessment of financial risk, that resemble the laboratory more than the forest or the village market.", "The disagreement, then, is narrower than its polemics suggest. Both traditions accept that judgement relies on shortcuts, and both, when pressed, accept that a shortcut can be good or bad depending on where it is used. What separates them is a question that neither has fully answered: how well people match their methods to their circumstances. Answering it requires studying environments as carefully as minds, which neither tradition, in its more confident moments, has been much inclined to do."]
difficulty_reason: A debate between two research programmes is adjudicated through abstract points about norms, sampling noise and the gap between capacity and use; the author sides partly with each.

subtopic: Boredom is not an empty absence of feeling but a functional signal that an activity fails to engage us, which constant distraction muffles rather than answers.
paragraphs: ["Boredom is usually described as a kind of emptiness, the feeling of having nothing to feel. On this view it is a residue, what remains when interest drains away, and the natural response is to fill the space with whatever is at hand, much as one might fill an awkward silence with remarks about the weather. The description is understandable, since boredom rarely announces any object of its own, but it gets the state almost exactly backwards. Boredom is not an absence. It is an active and often insistent signal that the activity in front of us is failing to engage the capacities we have available, and it exists to make us do something about that.", "The comparison with other unpleasant states is instructive. Hunger is disagreeable, but nobody concludes from this that hunger is a defect; its discomfort is the means by which it gets us to eat. Boredom works in a similar way. A person bored by a repetitive clerical task does not merely register that the task is dull; she feels restless, glances at the clock, begins to imagine alternatives. The unpleasantness is doing work. It pushes attention away from a situation that offers too little and towards a search for one that offers more, whether that means a harder problem, a different companion or simply a walk.", "None of this implies that boredom is always benign. A signal is useful only when there is some way to act on it, and many situations offer none. The patient in a waiting room, the passenger on a delayed train and the worker who cannot leave a monotonous post all receive the message without being able to respond, and in such cases boredom curdles into frustration or something close to despair. There are also signs that people will sometimes reach for almost any stimulation rather than endure an unoccupied mind, even stimulation they would otherwise find unpleasant. The signal, in other words, can be loud enough to drive choices that serve no one, and a theory of boredom that celebrated it without reservation would be as misleading as one that dismissed it.", "What follows is a reason to be wary of the most popular remedy. If boredom is a message about the fit between a person and an activity, then an endless supply of small distractions does not answer the message; it merely muffles it. Someone who reaches for a screen at every lull may never feel bored for long, but may also never learn what the boredom was pointing at: a job that has stopped stretching them, a routine that has outlived its purpose, a curiosity that has gone unfed. The more useful question, when boredom arrives, is not how to make it stop but what it is about."]
difficulty_reason: Clear thesis stated early, one familiar analogy, an explicit concession and a practical conclusion; vocabulary is plain.

subtopic: Habits are responses attached to contexts rather than strong desires, so they are better changed by altering cues than by strengthening resolve, though with limits.
paragraphs: ["Popular advice about habits tends to treat them as a contest of will. Bad habits persist, on this account, because people lack the resolve to stop, and good ones fail to form because people give up too soon. The remedy is accordingly motivational: set firmer goals, remind yourself why they matter, and try harder. This view has the appeal of moral simplicity, since it locates every failure in a lack of character and every success in effort, and it is repeated in a great deal of well-meant advice. The trouble with this picture is that it misdescribes what a habit is. A habit is not a desire that has grown strong but a response that has become attached to a context, so that the context itself, rather than any present intention, sets the behaviour going.", "Consider someone who checks her phone each time she sits down on the morning train. At first the action may have been chosen, perhaps as a way of passing an otherwise idle part of the trip, but after hundreds of repetitions it no longer needs choosing. The seat, the motion of the carriage and the familiar stretch of the journey are enough to bring the hand to the pocket, and she may find the phone in her hand before she has formed any wish to look at it. Asking her to resolve more firmly misses the point, since resolve is not what produces the act. The cue is.", "If this is right, the most effective way to change a habit is often to change the circumstances that trigger it, not to strengthen the will that opposes it. Putting the phone in a bag rather than a pocket, sitting in a different carriage, or giving the first minutes of the journey to some specific task all interrupt the link between cue and response. Each of these requires a single decision rather than a renewed act of resistance every morning, which is precisely why such changes tend to outlast good intentions. It is often observed that people find it easier to alter their routines after moving house or changing jobs, and the account explains why: the old cues have simply disappeared, and with them much of the pressure to repeat old behaviour.", "Two cautions are in order, however, if the argument is not to be pushed further than it can go. First, not every repeated behaviour is a habit in this sense; some acts are repeated because the person goes on wanting the result each time, and for these, motivation does matter. Second, the power of context cuts both ways. The same disruption that frees someone from an unwanted routine can dissolve a welcome one, which is why a regular exercise habit so often lapses after a move. Willpower is not irrelevant, then, but it is a poor tool for a job that the environment, suitably arranged, performs more cheaply and more reliably."]
difficulty_reason: Single clear thesis developed through one extended example, with two explicit cautions; concrete language throughout.

subtopic: Hedonic adaptation is real but uneven and is overstated by group averages, so it does not show that circumstances make no lasting difference to wellbeing.
paragraphs: ["Few findings in happiness research have travelled further than the idea of hedonic adaptation. People who experience a good or bad change in their circumstances, the finding goes, tend over time to drift back towards their earlier level of wellbeing, as though each of us were tethered to a personal set point from which events can pull us only temporarily. In its popular form the idea has hardened into something like a philosophy: since we adapt to everything, the pursuit of better circumstances is futile, and contentment is a matter of temperament rather than of how one lives. The research, read with any care, gives considerably less support to this conclusion than its popularity would suggest.", "To begin with, adaptation is uneven. People appear to adjust quite quickly to many gains, such as a higher salary or a larger house, which soon become the new normal against which further comparisons are made. But some conditions resist adaptation stubbornly. Persistent noise, a long and unpredictable commute and chronic pain seem to remain unpleasant year after year, perhaps because they keep demanding attention and never settle into the background of experience. The lesson is not that circumstances do not matter but that they matter selectively: what we stop noticing stops affecting us, and what keeps intruding does not.", "A second problem lies in how the evidence is summarised. Many studies report that, on average, a group's wellbeing returns towards its earlier level some time after an event such as marriage or the loss of a job. An average, however, can conceal very different individual paths. A group in which some people end up much happier and others much less happy can show almost no change overall, and the reassuring flat line then describes almost nobody in it. When researchers have examined individuals rather than averages, they have tended to find that a substantial minority do not return to where they began, which is precisely the information that a headline about set points discards.", "None of this means that the original insight was mistaken. People do adapt to a great deal, and the observation usefully corrects the belief that one more purchase or promotion will produce lasting delight. The error lies in the step from 'we adapt to much' to 'nothing we do makes a lasting difference'. That step is no more justified than its opposite, and it carries a practical cost, since it can discourage people from changing the very conditions, the noisy flat or the gruelling journey, that are most likely to keep wearing them down."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a popular reading of research with two separate objections and a concession; the statistical point about averages needs care.

subtopic: The information gap account explains targeted curiosity well but not exploratory curiosity, so curiosity should be treated as at least two kinds, with consequences for teaching.
paragraphs: ["One influential account of curiosity holds that it arises from a gap between what a person already knows and what that person would like to know. On this view curiosity is not a general appetite for novelty but a response to a specific, noticed absence: the missing end of a story, the answer to a riddle, the identity of the person who has just telephoned. The account has much to recommend it. It explains why we are rarely curious about subjects of which we know nothing, since we cannot notice a gap in a field we cannot see, and why a little knowledge is often more stimulating than none. It also explains why curiosity so frequently vanishes the moment the answer arrives, leaving behind a satisfaction that is oddly short-lived.", "Yet the information gap account fits some cases far better than others. It is at its strongest when the gap is well defined, as in a puzzle with a single solution or a mystery with a culprit. It is weaker when applied to the kind of curiosity that drifts without a target, the impulse that leads someone to wander along the shelves of a library, to turn over stones on a beach or to follow a footnote simply to see where it leads. In these cases there is no specific question waiting to be answered. If anything, the person seeks out situations in which questions might arise, and the pleasure lies as much in the searching as in any particular discovery.", "Defenders of the account sometimes reply that the wanderer is simply responding to many small gaps in quick succession. The reply preserves the theory, but at a cost. If any movement of attention whatever can be redescribed after the fact as the closing of a gap, the account no longer explains anything in particular; it becomes a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis. It seems more accurate to say that there are at least two kinds of curiosity, one that seeks to close a specific gap and one that seeks to encounter the unfamiliar, and that the influential account is a good theory of the first.", "The distinction matters for anyone who wishes to cultivate curiosity, and for teachers above all. A lesson built on the first kind poses a sharp question and withholds the answer just long enough to make it wanted. A lesson built on the second provides a rich environment and the time to wander in it, without specifying in advance what ought to be found. Both have their place, but a classroom organised entirely around the first may produce students who are excellent at finishing puzzles and rather less inclined to go looking for them."]
difficulty_reason: Assesses a theory's scope, rebuts a defensive reply on methodological grounds and draws a practical consequence; moderately abstract.

subtopic: The stage model of grief is poorly supported and harmful when treated as a norm, though its popularity reflects a genuine service it once performed.
paragraphs: ["Ask people what grief involves and many will describe a sequence: denial, then anger, then bargaining, then depression, and at last acceptance. The sequence has become so familiar that it can seem like a discovery about human nature, as settled as the stages of a fever. It began, however, as a description of how some terminally ill patients responded to the news of their own approaching death, drawn from clinical conversations rather than from any systematic study of the bereaved. Its migration from the dying to the grieving, and from a set of observations to something closer to a timetable, happened largely outside the kind of research that might have tested it.", "When grief has been studied directly, the tidy sequence has not fared well.
