A theory that predicted the fading of faith and got that prediction wrong in much of the world cannot be rescued by pointing to the part that survived, and some of its proponents did expect the strands to move together. The more modest conclusion is that the debate has been conducted at the wrong level of generality. To ask whether the world is becoming secular is to ask a question with no single answer; to ask which institutions have slipped free of religious authority, and on what terms religion now competes for influence within them, is to ask questions that the evidence can actually settle."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract conceptual analysis with three technical distinctions, an indirect stance and a concession that blocks the obvious conclusion.

topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
subtopic: Festivals of inversion have no fixed political meaning: they dramatise hierarchy in a way that can confirm or expose it, and circumstances decide which, so the safety valve image should be dropped.
paragraphs: ["Many societies have set aside days on which the ordinary order is turned upside down. In the Roman Saturnalia, masters are said to have waited on their slaves at table; in parts of medieval Europe, junior clergy elected a mock bishop and parodied the liturgy; in countless village festivals men dress as women, children give orders to adults, and the powerful are mocked in songs that would be punished at any other time of year. Such festivals of inversion have long puzzled those who study them, because they seem to put the most fundamental arrangements of a society at risk for the sake of a few days of licence.", "Two explanations have dominated. The first, often called the safety valve theory, holds that inversion protects the order it mocks. Resentments that accumulate under hierarchy are released in a bounded, harmless form, and when the festival ends everyone returns to their place, relieved and more willing to stay there. The second reverses the judgement. On this view, the festival gives people a glimpse of a world arranged otherwise, keeps alive the memory that rank is not natural, and so contains the seed of real defiance. Supporters of each view can point to cases. Rulers have tolerated and even funded such festivals, which suggests they found them useful; they have also banned them, which suggests they found them dangerous, and on a few occasions a carnival has indeed turned into a riot.", "What both explanations share is the assumption that the meaning of inversion is fixed by its form, so that one need only decide, once and for all, whether turning the world upside down conserves it or threatens it. The historical record does not support so tidy a choice, since the same festival, with the same masks and the same songs, has been a harmless frolic in one decade and the occasion of an uprising in the next. The difference lay not in the ritual but in its circumstances: a bad harvest, a disputed tax, a quarrel between factions of the elite that made the mockery of one of them useful to the other. Inversion, in other words, does not carry its own political charge; it takes one from the situation into which it is performed.", "The safety valve theory has a further weakness that is easy to overlook because its central image is so vivid. It pictures discontent as a kind of pressure that builds up in a closed vessel and can be let off in measured bursts. There is little reason to think that resentment, which is attached to particular injuries and particular persons, behaves like steam that can be vented without residue; people who have mocked their masters for a day do not obviously feel less aggrieved afterwards, and they may feel more entitled to their grievance for having heard it voiced aloud by a crowd. The image persuades because it is mechanical, not because anyone has observed the mechanism.", "A more promising account starts from a simpler observation. To turn a world upside down, one must first show which way up it is. The mock bishop presupposes a real one; the servant who gives orders for a day makes plain who gives them on every other day. Inversion is thus a vivid lesson in hierarchy, and in that sense it does teach the order it reverses. But the lesson cuts both ways, since a ranking that can be so easily reversed in play is shown to be a convention rather than a fact of nature. Which of these lessons is learned depends, again, on what else is happening. That is an unsatisfying conclusion only for those who wanted the festival to have a single meaning."]
difficulty_reason: Five paragraphs that reject two theories on different grounds and then build a third; the reader must keep the objections and their targets distinct.

topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
subtopic: The costly signalling account of demanding ritual is illuminating but incomplete, because it ignores ritual form, rites imposed on children and the way cost helps to create the commitment it displays.
paragraphs: ["Why do so many religious and quasi-religious groups ask their members to do things that are difficult, uncomfortable or expensive? Long fasts, pre-dawn prayers, restrictive diets, distinctive dress that invites ridicule, vows that forgo income or marriage: from a narrowly economic point of view these look like pure loss. An influential answer, borrowed from the study of animal behaviour, is that the costs are the point. A signal that is cheap to send can be sent by anyone, and so tells an observer little. A signal that is costly to send, and costlier still for someone who does not mean it, is credible precisely because it is hard to fake.", "Applied to ritual, the idea runs as follows. Groups that depend on mutual aid, sharing harvests, lending money or protecting one another, are vulnerable to people who take the benefits of membership without bearing its burdens. Demanding rituals screen such people out. Someone who is willing to rise before dawn for years, or to give up foods that everyone else enjoys, is unlikely to be only nominally attached, and the others can extend trust accordingly. The theory also explains a pattern that has often been remarked upon: groups that lower their demands in the hope of attracting members sometimes find that they lose them instead, as the value of belonging falls along with its cost.", "This is a genuinely illuminating account, and it captures something that purely symbolic interpretations of ritual tend to miss: that rituals are not only statements of meaning but also transactions with consequences for who can rely on whom, and that their cost is part of how they work rather than an unfortunate by-product. But it is incomplete in at least three ways. First, it explains why a ritual should be costly, not why it should take the particular form it does. Any sufficiently burdensome act would serve as a signal, yet communities care intensely about the precise words, gestures and times of their observances, and would not accept a different hardship of equal cost as a substitute. Second, many of the most demanding practices are imposed on children long before they could choose them. A rite performed on an infant may say something about the commitment of the parents, but it cannot be a signal of the child's own.", "The third gap is the most important. The signalling theory treats ritual as a message addressed to observers, as though the performer were already fully committed and merely needed to prove it. Yet people who undertake demanding practices commonly report that the practice changes them: that the fast or the vigil produces the conviction it was supposed to display. If that is so, cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it. A person who has sacrificed much for a group has reasons to value it that did not exist before the sacrifice, and the observer who reads his devotion as a signal is reading something that the ritual itself helped to create.", "None of these objections overturns the signalling account. They suggest instead that it describes one function among several, the one most visible to an outsider calculating whom to trust. A fuller theory would ask what ritual does to the people who perform it as well as what it tells the people who watch, and would treat the form of a rite as something that matters in its own right rather than as an arbitrary carrier of cost."]
difficulty_reason: Exposition of a theory followed by three numbered objections; the structure is signposted but the third objection is conceptually subtle.

subtopic: Rising degree requirements for many jobs reflect a competition for position rather than a rise in the skill the work demands, and the costs fall hardest on those who cannot pay for extra years of study.
paragraphs: ["When a job that was once filled by school leavers begins to advertise for graduates, the usual explanation is that the work has become more demanding. Machines have taken over the routine tasks, the story goes, and what remains calls for the analytical habits that only a university can supply. There is something to this. Some occupations really have changed beyond recognition, and an office clerk today handles systems that would have baffled a clerk of fifty years ago. But the explanation is offered far more often than it is checked, and when one looks at what people in many of these jobs actually do, the change in the work is often modest beside the change in the paperwork required to get it.", "A more economical account treats the degree less as a certificate of skill than as a ticket in a queue. When few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one was selecting a small group who were, on average, more persistent and better connected than the rest. As degrees became common, the same requirement no longer separated anyone, and employers who wanted to keep selecting raised the bar again, asking for a master's where a bachelor's had once sufficed. Each employer is behaving sensibly; it is merely using the cheapest filter available. Yet the sum of these sensible choices resembles a crowd at a parade in which everyone stands on tiptoe: no one sees better than before, and everyone is more tired.", "The costs of this arrangement are not evenly spread. Students from families that can afford several years of fees and forgone earnings keep pace with the rising bar; those who cannot are shut out of work they could perfectly well perform. A requirement introduced in the name of competence thus ends up rewarding the capacity to pay for time. Meanwhile the graduates themselves often discover that much of what they studied is barely used in the job, and that what the employer valued was the signal rather than the substance.", "None of this is an argument against education, which has goods that no labour market can measure. It is an argument against confusing two things that the word 'qualification' runs together: what a person can do, and how long a person has been able to stay in school. Some employers have begun to test applicants directly on the tasks the job involves. Where this is done, an awkward question comes into view, namely whether the degree requirement it replaces was ever a guarantee of quality or merely a habit that nobody had thought to examine."]
difficulty_reason: One clear thesis, a vivid analogy and a plainly signalled concession at the start and end; little abstraction.

subtopic: The weekend was a negotiated compromise that traded irregular, self-chosen rest for guaranteed but standardised free time, which in turn changed leisure into something scheduled and sold.
paragraphs: ["We tend to think of the weekend as a natural feature of the calendar, as if two days of rest had always followed five of work. In fact the arrangement is fairly recent, and its history suggests that free time is not simply the absence of work but something that has to be made, defended and shaped. Before the factory, many artisans worked in bursts, labouring late into the night to finish an order and then taking a day or two off whenever it suited them; in parts of England the habit of stretching Sunday's rest into Monday was common enough to be given a mock saint's name, 'Saint Monday'.", "Factory production could not tolerate this irregularity. Machines were expensive and had to run whenever the hands were present, and an employer could not plan production around workers who might drift in on Tuesday, so the long struggle over hours was therefore also a struggle over the shape of time. Workers wanted fewer hours; employers wanted predictable ones. The compromise that eventually emerged, first a half-day on Saturday and later the whole of it, gave each side part of what it sought. Workers won rest that was guaranteed rather than snatched, and employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning.", "It would be wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory. For most working people, guaranteed free time was a real gain, and it was won against resistance. But the weekend also changed what free time was. Leisure that had once been taken at the worker's discretion became a fixed block, the same for everyone, and a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to. Football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday, and leisure came increasingly to mean something one went out and paid for at a scheduled time.", "The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better; it was often tied to poverty, to insecurity and to binges of overwork that left people exhausted. It is that arguments about working hours are never only about quantity. When people today argue over flexible schedules or a four-day week, they are reopening a question that the industrial age settled in one particular way: not merely how much time should be free, but who decides when it falls and what it is for."]
difficulty_reason: Chronological narrative with an explicit moral; the stance and its qualification are stated directly.

subtopic: The concealment of domestic servants helped produce the appearance of effortless gentility, and the wish to receive service without meeting the server survives in the modern service economy despite real gains for workers.
paragraphs: ["In the large households of the nineteenth century, the best servant was the one who was least noticed. Grand houses were built with back staircases so that maids carrying coal or slops need never meet the family on the main stairs, and bells rang in a basement corridor so that a summons could be issued without anyone having to see who answered it. In some houses servants were expected to turn aside, even to face the wall, when a member of the family passed. It is tempting to read all this as snobbery, a taste for keeping inferiors out of sight, but snobbery explains less than it seems to. The invisibility of servants was not a by-product of the genteel household; it was one of the things the household was for.", "What a gentleman's house displayed, above all, was ease: meals that appeared, fires that were lit, linen that was clean, all without visible effort. The ease was manufactured by a great deal of labour, and the labour had to be hidden for the ease to be believed. A servant glimpsed scrubbing a step was a reminder that comfort had a cost and a source; a servant unseen allowed the family to experience comfort as a natural condition of their kind of life. In this sense the architecture of concealment did not merely reflect a social hierarchy but helped to produce one, by allowing one class to appear exempt from necessity.", "Large-scale domestic service of this kind has largely disappeared, and it is easy to assume that its logic went with it. Yet much of the modern service economy seems designed to recreate the same experience by other means. Food arrives at the door from a kitchen the customer never sees, carried by a courier who is a first name on a screen. Offices are cleaned at night, after the staff have gone home. Apps promise that groceries, laundry and repairs will simply happen, and their designers speak, revealingly, of removing friction, as though the friction in question were not, very often, the encounter with another person who is doing the work.", "The comparison must not be pressed too far. The modern courier or cleaner is not bound to a single household, keeps hours that end, and has legal protections that a Victorian scullery maid lacked; to call such workers servants is to erase real gains. But the aspiration that the old houses expressed in brick and bells, the wish to receive service without meeting the server, has proved remarkably durable. What has changed is less the wish than the means of satisfying it, and the means are now available to far more people than ever owned a back staircase."]
difficulty_reason: The thesis turns on a functional claim (concealment produced hierarchy) and a qualified historical comparison; moderate abstraction.

subtopic: The concept of emotional labour survives the objection that all work involves emotion, because it concerns who controls and profits from the display of feeling, not whether feeling is present.
paragraphs: ["The idea that some jobs require workers to manage their own feelings, and not merely their hands or their minds, has travelled a long way from its origins in the study of flight attendants and debt collectors. It now turns up in discussions of nursing, teaching, retail and call centres, and even of the unpaid work of keeping a family cheerful. This expansion has drawn a predictable objection: if every job involves some management of emotion, the critics say, then the concept marks out nothing in particular. A surgeon must stay calm, a lawyer must appear confident, and a builder who loses his temper with clients will not keep them; are these, too, emotional labourers?", "The objection is fair against the loose use of the term, but it misses what the original idea was pointing at. The distinction was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not. It was between feeling that a worker manages according to her own judgement and feeling whose display is specified, monitored and sold by someone else. The surgeon's calm serves the operation and is left to her; nobody scripts it. The call-centre agent, by contrast, may be told how often to use the customer's name, scored on the warmth of her voice, and disciplined for a sigh. The emotion is part of the product, and the employer, not the worker, sets its terms.", "Seen this way, the concept is narrower than its popular use suggests, but also sharper. It directs attention not to the presence of emotion at work but to its ownership, and it suggests where the cost of such work lies. Most people can smile at a stranger without harm; the difficulty arises when the smile must be produced on demand, for hours, regardless of how the worker is treated, and when failing to produce it is a disciplinary matter. One would expect work of this kind to produce a fatigue unlike ordinary tiredness, and perhaps an uncertainty about which friendly feelings are one's own.", "None of this implies that friendliness in service is a sham, or that customers who enjoy it are dupes. Many workers take pride in easing a stranger's day, and a scripted greeting can be delivered with real goodwill. The point is that goodwill freely given and goodwill required by contract are different things, even when they look identical from the other side of the counter, and a concept that cannot tell them apart has lost the very thing that made it worth having."]
difficulty_reason: Objection and reply structure with a redefinition; the key distinction is abstract but illustrated by a clear contrast.

subtopic: The rise of omnivorous taste among elites has not ended cultural distinction but moved it, since breadth, a knowing manner of liking and selective dislikes now mark class as refusal once did.
paragraphs: ["For a long time the sociology of taste worked with a simple map. At the top of the social order sat a refined culture of opera, poetry and the old masters, at the bottom sat popular entertainments, and a person's place in society could be read, with fair accuracy, from the position of their preferences on this ladder. Elites, on this picture, distinguished themselves by what they refused. Liking the wrong music was not merely a private failing but a mark of origin.", "Surveys of cultural consumption in a number of wealthy countries have since complicated the map. The most educated and affluent groups, it turns out, are no longer best described as snobs who like only high culture. They are more often omnivores: they go to the opera and to the cinema, read literary fiction and crime novels, and are happy to discuss both a string quartet and a pop album. Some observers have greeted this as the end of cultural hierarchy, a sign that the old boundaries between high and low have dissolved and that taste has become a matter of individual preference rather than of class.", "That conclusion is premature. Breadth of taste is itself unevenly distributed, because it requires money, time, travel and, above all, the confidence to move between worlds without feeling out of place. The person who can talk knowledgeably about both a symphony and a street-food stall has accumulated a cultural range that is far harder to acquire than a liking for either alone. Moreover, omnivores rarely consume popular forms in the same way as their usual audiences. They tend to approach them with a knowing, curatorial attitude, prizing a song for its place in the history of a genre or enjoying a film with a touch of irony, and this manner of liking can mark distance as effectively as refusal once did.", "Nor is the omnivore's appetite unlimited. Research on what people say they dislike has suggested that the forms most often rejected by the highly educated tend to be those most associated with the least educated, so that the boundary has moved rather than vanished. None of this means that the loosening of old hierarchies is an illusion; it is a genuine change that the opera house must now compete for prestige with a well-chosen food truck. But distinction has not disappeared with the decline of snobbery. It has learned to express itself through openness, and openness is harder to criticise than exclusion because it looks so much like a virtue."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common interpretation, with two separate counter-arguments and a concession; ideas are abstract but clearly signposted.

subtopic: Professions are better understood as rivals contesting jurisdiction over problems than as either guarantors of competence or cartels, so their fortunes depend on claiming problems more than on skill.
paragraphs: ["Two accounts of the professions have long competed for our assent, and each is right about something. The first, which professionals themselves favour, holds that a profession is defined by esoteric knowledge put at the service of clients who cannot judge it. Because a patient cannot assess a diagnosis or a litigant a legal argument, the state licenses practitioners, and the licence is a guarantee of competence that protects the public from charlatans. The second account, favoured by economists of a sceptical turn, treats the same licence as a barrier to entry: by limiting the number who may practise, a profession raises its fees, and its talk of public protection is simply the language in which a cartel describes itself.", "What the two accounts share is more interesting than what divides them. Both look at one profession at a time, as if each stood alone facing its clients, and both assume that the work a profession does is simply given: there are diseases, so there are doctors; there are disputes, so there are lawyers. Yet the boundaries of professional work are anything but given. Whether persistent unhappiness is a medical condition, a psychological difficulty, a spiritual crisis or a social problem is not settled by the nature of unhappiness. It is settled, provisionally and repeatedly, by contests among psychiatrists, psychologists, clergy and social workers, each of whom claims that the problem properly belongs to it.", "Seen from this angle, a profession is less a guild guarding a fixed territory than one party in a system of rival claims, and its history is a history of conquests and retreats. Licensing remains important, but as a weapon in a jurisdictional struggle rather than as either a certificate or a mere device for fixing prices. Knowledge, too, matters in a different way. What wins a contested problem is often not superior skill in treating it but a more abstract body of theory, one that allows a profession to redefine the problem in its own terms and so to argue that its rivals were treating the symptoms rather than the thing itself. A profession whose knowledge is purely practical can be displaced by one that can explain why that practice works.", "This does not mean that competence is irrelevant or that the cartel theorist is merely cynical. Clients are protected by licensing, and fees are raised by it. But neither effect explains why some professions grow while others shrink, or why a body of practitioners who are perfectly good at their work can find that work quietly reassigned to others. The fate of a profession, on this view, depends less on how well it does what it does than on its ability to persuade others, including the state and the public, that the problems of the moment are its problems."]
difficulty_reason: Compares two views, identifies their shared assumption and replaces both with a third, abstract model; the stance is reached only through the whole argument.

subtopic: Affluent households have shifted from conspicuous display to hard-to-see spending on schooling, health and time, which transmits advantage more effectively and shields it from criticism by presenting it as virtue.
paragraphs: ["The phrase 'conspicuous consumption', coined by Thorstein Veblen in the 1890s, named a habit of the wealthy of his day: the purchase of goods whose chief use was to show that one could afford them. The mansion, the carriage and the idle household were, on this account, less comforts than advertisements. The idea proved so useful that it outlived the society that prompted it, and it still shapes how we picture status spending: the logo on the handbag, the oversized car, the watch that costs more than a year's rent.", "The picture now misleads more than it reveals, at least at the top. As mass production and global supply chains have made once-rare goods cheap, the handbag and the car have become available, in passable imitations, to almost anyone with a credit card. Display of this kind has lost much of its power to separate, and many of the most advantaged households have turned away from it. Their spending flows instead into things that are hard to see and harder to copy: private tuition and a house in the right school catchment, retirement savings, organic groceries, exercise classes, domestic help that frees time for reading, and clothing whose quality is recognised only by those who know what to look for. The signal, where there is one, is addressed to a narrow audience of peers rather than to the street. The pattern has come to be called inconspicuous consumption.", "It would be easy to treat the change as an improvement in taste, a retreat from vulgar display into quieter and more sensible habits. In part it is. Much of this spending yields real benefits in health, in learning and in security, and few would wish the rich to return to buying gold-plated taps. But the shift has two consequences that the language of good taste conceals. The first is that inconspicuous goods are more effective at reproducing advantage than conspicuous ones ever were. A diamond can be sold; a childhood spent in good schools, with books at home and parents who have time, becomes part of a person and can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later. Spending of this kind does not merely display a position; it passes it on.", "The second consequence is moral. Conspicuous consumption invited criticism precisely because it was conspicuous. The flashy car was an obvious target for the satirist and the moralist, and its owner could be accused of vanity. Inconspicuous consumption is much harder to criticise, because it presents itself not as display but as virtue: one is not showing off, one is merely eating well, looking after one's health and investing in one's children. The vocabulary that surrounds it, of wellness, sensible choices and doing the best for one's family, offers the satirist nothing obviously vulgar to mock. Those who cannot afford to do the same are not envied so much as quietly judged, as though their diets and their children's results were failures of character rather than of income.", "None of this is an accusation of bad faith. It does not require us to think the affluent hypocritical, or the parent paying for tuition secretly bent on buying status; most such choices are made sincerely, for the reasons people give. The point is structural rather than personal. A society in which advantage is transmitted through the visible accumulation of objects at least makes its inequalities legible. One in which advantage flows through habits, schooling and time has made them harder to see, and inequalities that are hard to see are also harder to argue about."]
difficulty_reason: A familiar concept is updated and critiqued through two named consequences, a concession and a disclaimer about motives; argument is clearly signposted.

subtopic: Public debate confuses absolute mobility, which can rise for all, with relative mobility, which is zero-sum, and so misreads economic slowdowns as closure and hides the cost that greater fairness imposes.
paragraphs: ["Few political promises are as widely shared as the promise of social mobility. Parties that agree on little else agree that a child's prospects should not be fixed by the circumstances of her birth, and the claim that mobility has stalled is one of the most damaging charges that can be laid against a government. Yet the word covers two quite different things, and much public argument about it goes astray because the two are run together.", "The first is absolute mobility: the share of people who end up better off than their parents, whether by income or by the kind of work they do. The second is relative mobility: the extent to which a person's position in the distribution, as opposed to their standard of living, differs from their parents' position. The two can move independently. In a period of rapid growth and expanding professional employment, most children may outearn their parents and many may enter occupations their parents never held, even if the chance of a child born near the bottom reaching the top, compared with that of a child born near the top, has not changed at all. Everyone rides the escalator up, but the order of people on it stays the same.", "This distinction explains a puzzle. When growth slows and the expansion of professional jobs levels off, absolute mobility falls, and people who do no better than their parents feel, reasonably enough, that something has closed. They often conclude that society has become less fair. Imagine a town where a mill employed one generation and new offices employed the next. The children did better than their parents without anyone being pushed aside, and the town experienced this as openness. When the offices stop hiring, the grandchildren find that the climb has ended. Yet on the measures that track their position against the children of the office managers, the chances may be much as they were: what has disappeared is not openness but the rising tide that once let a whole generation move up without anyone having to move down. The sense of closure is real; its diagnosis is frequently mistaken.", "The distinction also exposes an awkwardness that politicians prefer to leave unspoken. Absolute mobility can, in principle, be enjoyed by everyone at once. Relative mobility cannot. If positions are ranked, then for one family to climb another must fall, and a serious commitment to relative mobility is therefore a commitment to downward mobility for some children of the comfortable. It is not surprising that the comfortable resist it, often without any sense of doing so, through the ordinary devices of private tuition, a well-placed word, or the purchase of a house near the right school. Each of these looks like ordinary care for one's own children; together they amount to a defence of position.", "None of this makes one kind of mobility the real one. Absolute mobility answers a question about material progress: are people living better than their parents did? Relative mobility answers a question about fairness: does birth still decide where one ends up? Both questions matter, and neither is easy to answer with confidence, since incomes fluctuate and occupations change their meaning across generations. But a society that wants more of the second kind should be honest that it cannot be had at no one's expense, and a society that mourns the loss of the first should not mistake a slower economy for a more rigid one."]
difficulty_reason: Rests on an abstract conceptual distinction whose consequences are drawn out in two directions, with an even-handed conclusion; requires tracking which measure each claim concerns.

subtopic: The passion for completing a series is not in itself a manufactured compulsion; what commercial collecting takes from the collector is the power to define the series.
paragraphs: ["Ask a collector why she keeps buying stamps, coins or toy cars long after there is any room left to display them, and the answer is rarely about the objects themselves. More often it concerns a gap: the one issue missing from a run, the single variant that would finish a set. Collecting, on this view, is less a love of things than a love of completion. The individual stamp matters because of the place it occupies in a series, and its value to the collector rises sharply as the series nears its end, often far beyond anything a buyer outside the hobby would think of paying.", "Manufacturers learned long ago to exploit this. A cereal box that contains one of twelve plastic figures, a sticker album with a few deliberately scarce pages, a line of trading cards issued in waves: each turns an ordinary purchase into a step towards a whole that the buyer did not know he wanted until he was shown its outline. The empty album is the real product. Once its spaces are printed, every blank becomes a small reproach, and the purchase that fills it brings a satisfaction out of all proportion to what was bought.", "It would be easy to conclude that collecting is simply a manufactured compulsion, a weakness that the market has learned to farm. That conclusion goes too far. Many of the most devoted collectors pursue series that no company ever designed: the railway timetables of a vanished line, the matchboxes of hotels that have since closed, the scattered editions of a minor poet. Here it is the collector who defines the set, deciding what counts as belonging to it and therefore what counts as missing. Such collecting is a way of ordering the world, of drawing a boundary around a scattered field and making it intelligible. Many museums began, in part, as exactly this kind of private project.", "The difference between the two kinds of collecting is not the passion involved, which can be equally intense, but who holds the map. When the series is invented by a seller, completion is a target set by someone else, and the finish line is often moved just as it comes into view, with a new wave or a special edition. When the collector draws the map, completion is a judgement she makes for herself, and the pleasure lies as much in the defining as in the finding. The danger of the commercial version is not that it creates desire, since all collecting does that, but that it quietly takes the act of definition away from the person doing the collecting."]
difficulty_reason: Clear contrast between two kinds of collecting, signposted by the concession in paragraph 3; concrete examples and moderate vocabulary.

subtopic: Retro goods sell not a remembered past but an edited token of dissatisfaction with the present, which is worth understanding rather than scorning.
paragraphs: ["A curious feature of the market for retro goods is how many of their buyers are too young to remember the originals. Record players styled like those of the nineteen-sixties, cameras that imitate the look of early film models, soft drinks reissued in the bottles of half a century ago: these sell briskly to people for whom the period they evoke is something seen in old films rather than lived. Whatever such buyers are nostalgic for, it cannot be their own past, and any explanation of the trade has to begin from that awkward fact.", "The usual explanation is that they are being fooled, that advertisers have invented a golden age and sold it back to a generation with no means of checking. There is something in this, but it misreads what the buyer is after. Nostalgia has always been less a memory than a mood, a way of expressing dissatisfaction with the present by furnishing it with an imagined contrast against which its deficiencies become visible. The retro object does not claim to restore the past; it offers a small, ownable piece of a world that seems slower, sturdier and easier to understand than the one its owner actually lives in. That such a world never quite existed matters less than the fact that the feeling it answers is real.", "What is striking is how carefully the past is edited in the process. The reissued record player has a socket for a phone; the vintage-look camera stores its pictures on a memory card and adds the scratches digitally. The inconveniences that made the originals what they were, the waiting, the expense, the fragility, are removed, and only the surface is kept. Retro design is in this sense the opposite of preservation: it keeps the look of an earlier time while discarding the conditions that gave the look its meaning.", "None of this need be a cause for scorn. Some revived products are genuinely better made than the disposable goods they replaced, and a taste for the durable, in an economy organised around rapid obsolescence, is not foolish. But it is worth being clear about what is being bought. The buyer of a retro radio is not recovering a lost way of life; he is purchasing a token of his unease with his own, and the market is happy to supply as many such tokens as that unease will bear."]
difficulty_reason: Direct argument with concrete examples; the stance is stated plainly in paragraphs 2 and 4.

subtopic: Demands that immigrant restaurants serve 'authentic' food freeze one stage of a continuous adaptation; the better test is whether the cooks are free to cook what they judge good.
paragraphs: ["Few words are used more freely by restaurant reviewers than 'authentic', and few are applied more selectively. A dish is praised as authentic when it is served in a cramped room, by a cook who speaks the diner's language haltingly, at a price that suggests nobody is getting rich. The same dish, served with tablecloths and a wine list, is suspected of having been tamed. Authenticity, in this usage, is less a property of the food than of the scene around it, and the scene is one that the visiting diner has come to consume.", "Consider a hypothetical family that opens a restaurant serving the cooking of its home region in a city several thousand kilometres away. From the start, the cooks make changes. Some ingredients cannot be found and are replaced with local ones; some dishes are too laborious for a kitchen that must turn out fifty plates a night; others are sweetened or softened because the first customers sent them back. Within a generation the menu has become something that exists nowhere else: neither the food of the home region nor the food of the new city, but the food of the people who moved between them.", "Purists treat this history as a decline, and they reward the restaurants that seem to have resisted it, the ones with a second menu in the home language that outsiders must know to ask for. Yet even that second menu has passed through the same kitchen, the same suppliers and the same compromises. To call it the real food and the first menu a betrayal is to take one stage of a continuous adaptation and freeze it as the original. More troubling, the judgement is usually made by people with no stake in the tradition, who are in effect asking immigrant cooks to perform their own foreignness for an audience's satisfaction.", "None of this means that every adaptation is innocent. Cooks under commercial pressure sometimes strip a cuisine of everything difficult until it is recognisable only by name, and something real is lost when that happens. But the loss is better described as a narrowing of what the cooks themselves are free to make than as a departure from a fixed original. The more useful question to ask of a restaurant is not whether its food matches some imagined source, but whether the people cooking it have the room to cook what they think is good."]
difficulty_reason: The thesis emerges only in the last paragraph after a hypothetical case and a critique of purists; it includes a concession that must be distinguished from the main claim.

subtopic: The trickle-down theory of fashion is wrong about direction but right about its engine, the clash between belonging and distinction, which now operates through access rather than visible novelty.
paragraphs: ["An old explanation of fashion holds that it trickles down. Those at the top of a society adopt a new style to mark themselves off; those just below copy it, hoping to borrow some of the prestige; and once the style has spread far enough to lose its power to distinguish, the people at the top abandon it for something else. Fashion, on this account, is a chase that can never end, because the very success of imitation destroys the value of what is imitated.", "The obvious objection is that much of what is worn today did not begin at the top. Jeans were work clothes; the hooded sweatshirt was athletic gear; a great many styles that now appear on expensive runways were first worn by the young, the poor or the marginal, and were adopted by designers only later. If fashion so often bubbles up rather than trickling down, the old theory seems simply mistaken about the direction in which influence travels, and with it, one might suppose, about everything that followed from that direction.", "But direction was never the heart of the theory. Its real claim was that fashion is driven by a double motive, the wish to belong and the wish to stand apart, and that the two cannot both be satisfied for long. That claim survives the reversal untouched. When a luxury house borrows the clothing of a street subculture, it is not abandoning distinction but finding a new source of it: the style carries a borrowed credibility that a conventional luxury garment lacks, and wearing it signals a knowingness that cannot be acquired simply by paying more. The members of the subculture, for their part, frequently drop the style once it appears in expensive shops, for precisely the reason the old theory would predict.", "What has changed is the speed. When copies of a new look can reach inexpensive shops within weeks, visible novelty becomes a weak marker of status, since it is available to almost anyone almost at once. Increasingly, those who most wish to stand apart do so not by wearing what is new but by having had it first: by access to small releases that sell out in minutes, by acquaintance with designers before they are celebrated, by knowing what is coming rather than displaying what has arrived. The chase continues; it has simply moved to ground where the pursuers find it harder to follow."]
difficulty_reason: Classic objection-and-reply structure in which the reply redefines the theory's core claim; the final paragraph adds a further development that must be kept separate.

subtopic: Debates over whether global food chains erase or respect local identity wrongly focus on the menu, the least telling of three layers: a global format, local meanings, and a menu adjusted between them.
paragraphs: ["When a global fast-food chain enters a new country, the first thing commentators examine is its menu. If the chain serves the same burger it serves at home, critics see cultural flattening, the erosion of local tastes by a single corporate palate. If it introduces a spiced vegetable patty or a rice dish for the local market, its defenders announce that globalisation, far from erasing difference, accommodates it. Both sides agree, without ever saying so, that the menu is where the question of cultural influence will be settled.", "That assumption deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. A menu is the part of a chain that is easiest to change and, for that very reason, the part that tells us least. What the chain actually exports is a format: a way of organising food, labour and time. The counter at which one orders without a waiter, the fixed price displayed in advance, the promise that the meal will taste the same today as it did last month, the kitchen run like an assembly line by staff who can be trained in days: these travel intact, and they carry assumptions about efficiency and predictability that are far more foreign to many food cultures than any particular ingredient. A spiced patty served through such a system is a local flavour in a global grammar.", "Yet it would be wrong to infer that the format simply imposes its meanings wherever it goes, for customers bring meanings of their own. In some places a visit to a chain restaurant has been, at least for a time, a special occasion rather than a convenience: a clean, cool and respectable room in which a family can celebrate a birthday, or two young people can meet without attracting comment. The format was designed for speed, but the customers linger. They take a system built to minimise the time spent at the table and turn it into a place for spending time.", "The interesting story, then, has three layers rather than one. The format is global and changes slowly; the meanings attached to it are local and can diverge sharply from what its designers intended; the menu sits between them, adjusted constantly in response to both. To read cultural influence from the menu alone is like judging the spread of a language by the loanwords it has picked up, while ignoring both its grammar and the uses to which its new speakers put it."]
difficulty_reason: Critiques an assumption shared by two opposed camps and replaces it with a three-layer model; the closing analogy must be mapped onto that model.

subtopic: Owning little can function as a display of security whatever its practitioners intend, so reduced consumption is a move within the system of social display rather than an exit from it.
paragraphs: ["It has become common to describe the fashion for owning less, the bare room, the small wardrobe of good clothes, the ritual of discarding whatever does not earn its place, as a revolt against consumer society. Its advocates present it as a turn from having to being; its critics, when they bother, dismiss it as one more passing style. Both responses take the movement at its word, as a stance towards consumption. Neither asks what owning little communicates, which is a different question from what it intends.", "At the end of the nineteenth century the economist Thorstein Veblen described how the wealthy display their standing through conspicuous consumption, spending visibly on what serves display rather than use. The sparse interior seems at first to invert his picture. Yet emptiness has its own costs, and they are not evenly distributed. A bare floor in a crowded city is a quantity of expensive space left deliberately unfilled. A wardrobe of a dozen garments presupposes that each is durable enough, and the owner's life predictable enough, to require no more. Above all, the confident discarding of objects depends on the assurance that they can be replaced when needed. Households that live close to scarcity keep things, the spare part, the old jar, the coat a size too large, because they cannot count on being able to buy them again; for them, accumulation is a form of insurance. To throw away freely is to display that one has no need of such insurance.", "It does not follow that those who embrace minimalism are hypocrites whose real aim is to impress. That objection confuses motive with function. A practice can be sincerely chosen for its own reasons, calm, order, a dislike of waste, and still operate socially as a signal that its practitioners neither chose nor want. Many who pare down their possessions are doing exactly what they say. The point is rather that the meaning of a pattern of consumption is not fixed by the consumer's intention; it is fixed by what the pattern makes legible to others, and what restraint makes legible, in a society where most people cannot afford its preconditions, is security.", "The more consequential lesson concerns the hope of opting out. If even refusal can be read as a position within the system of display, then consuming less is not, by itself, an exit from that system; it is a move within it, and often one available only to those already well placed. This is not an argument for consuming more. It is an argument for suspicion towards any claim that a change in private taste can amount to a social critique, since the field of taste has repeatedly proved able to absorb its own refusals and return them as distinctions."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract argument that turns on the distinction between motive and function; the conclusion is a general claim about social critique that the reader must separate from a charge of hypocrisy.

subtopic: Brand communities are genuine collectives, but they are built on symbols owned by a firm, so the tribal analogy both captures and conceals their nature.
paragraphs: ["Marketers like to say that the strongest brands have communities rather than customers. They point to the owners of a particular make of motorcycle who ride together on weekends and have its emblem tattooed on their arms, to the users of a computer maker's products who queue overnight for a new model and argue online with the users of its rivals, and to the enthusiasts who restore and exhibit a discontinued car long after its manufacturer has stopped caring about it. Some commentators go further and call such groups tribes, or even congregations, complete with rituals, myths and heretics, as though buying a product were the first step in a conversion.", "The comparison is not empty. Members of these groups share a body of lore, the founding story, the legendary models, the right and wrong ways to use the product, and newcomers learn it much as initiates learn a tradition. They define themselves partly against outsiders, often the owners of a rival brand, and they police their own boundaries, distinguishing the real enthusiast from the person who has merely bought the thing. Most strikingly, they develop a sense of ownership over the brand that is not legal but moral. When a company alters a celebrated design or moves production to another country, its most loyal customers frequently respond not as disappointed consumers but as betrayed members, as though something that belonged to them had been taken without their consent.", "Yet the tribal analogy conceals as much as it reveals. Membership of a tribe is not usually something one buys, and leaving it is not usually as easy as buying something else. A brand community, by contrast, is entered through a purchase and can be abandoned at the price of another. More important, the symbols around which it gathers are the legal property of a firm whose interests are not the members' interests. The firm can redesign the emblem, discontinue the product or sell the brand to a competitor, and the members, however devoted, have no formal say in any of it. A tribe whose totem could be sold at auction would be a strange tribe indeed.", "It is tempting to resolve the tension by declaring one side the truth: either the community is an illusion manufactured by advertising, or the commercial setting is incidental and the solidarity is all that matters. Neither will do. The solidarity is real; people form friendships, give one another practical help and find meaning in these groups, and much of this happens without the company's involvement or even against its wishes. But the solidarity is organised around something its members do not control, and that fact shapes it. The anger that follows an unpopular redesign is the anger of people discovering, often for the first time, the limits of an ownership they had felt but never possessed.", "A brand community, then, is best understood neither as a tribe that happens to shop nor as a market that happens to feel warm, but as a peculiar hybrid: a genuine collective built on borrowed ground. Firms that grasp this tend to treat their communities with caution, consulting them, deferring to them on matters of heritage and sometimes ceding them real influence over decisions. Firms that do not, and that treat the community merely as a marketing asset to be managed, are apt to learn how quickly devotion can turn into grievance, and how little the language of community protects a firm once its members conclude that they have been treated as an audience rather than as partners."]
difficulty_reason: Five paragraphs moving from analogy to concession to critique to synthesis; the stance is explicit, but the synthesis must be held against two rejected one-sided views.

subtopic: Staged back regions in tourism rarely deceive knowing tourists; the real ethical cost is the shrinking private life of hosts, so tourism should be judged by what it leaves alone.
paragraphs: ["Tourists, it is often observed, are rarely content with what is shown to them. The monument, the parade, the dance performed on a stage in the hotel courtyard: all of these are understood to be presentations, arranged for visitors, and for that reason they seem to many travellers less real than whatever lies behind them. What the discerning visitor wants is the back region, the kitchen rather than the dining room, the village household rather than the folk show, the place where people are simply living rather than performing. Tourism, on this view, is a search for the unperformed, conducted by people whose very presence makes performance likely.", "The difficulty is that the search creates its object, for once visitors will pay to see behind the scenes, behind the scenes becomes a scene. Homestays are furnished to look lived in; working kitchens are tidied and lit for the guided tour; a weaving cooperative arranges its looms so that visitors can watch the ordinary work of the day at a convenient hour. Each of these presents itself as a glimpse of the back, and each is in fact another front, built in the shape of a back. Critics of tourism have made much of this, arguing that the visitor who congratulates himself on having escaped the tourist trail has merely been led down a more expensive branch of it.", "The criticism is accurate about the arrangements and, I think, mistaken about the tourists. It assumes that they are dupes who believe they have found the real thing and would be dismayed to learn otherwise. Many are nothing of the kind: asked directly, a good number will say that of course the homestay was prepared for them, that of course the cooperative works differently when no one is watching. What they value is not the illusion of having seen the unstaged but the experience of being admitted, of being received as a guest rather than seated as a spectator, and that experience is not falsified by the knowledge that it was arranged. A theatre audience is not deceived merely because it knows the actors are acting.", "If there is a cost in all this, it falls elsewhere. Every back region that is opened to visitors must be replaced by another, further back, where the hosts can live without being watched, and in places where tourism is the main source of income, that retreat can go a long way. The family that rents out its courtyard confines its own life to a back room; the village that stages its festival for visitors holds the version that matters to it in the off season, or not at all. The more successfully a community sells access to its private life, the less private life it has left to sell, and the less it has left to keep for itself.", "The usual question about staged authenticity is whether the tourist is being cheated. That question flatters the tourist by placing his experience at the centre of the moral picture, and it is in any case usually answered in his favour, since he generally receives what he knowingly pays for. The harder question concerns the hosts, and it is not whether they are deceiving anyone but how much of their lives they can afford to keep out of view. A tourism that respected its hosts would measure itself not by how much it manages to reveal but by how much it is content to leave alone."]
difficulty_reason: The author accepts the critics' description but rejects their moral conclusion, then relocates the ethical question; the stance shifts across five paragraphs and depends on the theatre analogy and a distinction between deception and cost.

subtopic: The obligation to return a gift is not a corruption of giving but the mechanism by which gifts create lasting ties, though it becomes oppressive when the receiver cannot reply.
paragraphs: ["Modern moral intuition tends to reserve its highest praise for the gift that expects nothing in return. A present given with an eye to what will come back seems to us slightly tarnished, closer to a trade dressed up in ribbon than to generosity. Anthropologists who have studied exchange in a wide range of societies have long found this intuition puzzling, not because people elsewhere are more calculating, but because in most places the obligation to return is understood as part of what a gift is. To receive is to accept a tie; to fail to reciprocate is not merely rude but a refusal of the relationship the gift proposed.", "Consider how carefully the timing and size of a return are managed in many communities. A neighbour who sends back a dish of sweets on the very evening she received one has not discharged a debt so much as declined a friendship; the speed of her reply announces that she wants the account closed. A return that matches the original exactly carries a similar message. What sustains the bond is a return that comes later and differs slightly in value, so that one party is always, for the moment, a little in the other's debt. On this view the imbalance is not a flaw to be corrected but the mechanism by which the relationship is kept running: an account that is never quite settled is an account that remains open.", "Seen in this light, the free gift is less an ideal than an anomaly. A gift that truly demanded nothing would create no tie, and a society composed only of such gifts would be a collection of strangers who happened to hand each other things. It is telling that the gifts we most often describe as free, such as anonymous donations, are precisely those designed to prevent any relationship between giver and receiver from forming.", "None of this means that the obligation to return is always benign. Where one party can give far more than the other could ever repay, the gift becomes an instrument of domination: the receiver is bound by a debt that cannot be cleared, and gratitude hardens into dependence. Patrons have long understood this, and so have recipients of charity, who sometimes refuse help precisely because they cannot answer it. The lesson, however, is not that we should aspire to gifts without strings. It is that the strings must be ones the receiver is able to hold. A generous act, properly understood, is calibrated to the other person's capacity to reply."]
difficulty_reason: A critique of a common belief with a concession in the last paragraph; the stance is clear but rests on an abstract claim about imbalance as a mechanism.

subtopic: The textbook story that money arose to solve the inconveniences of barter has little historical support, and its ordering of money before debt misleads us about what money is.
paragraphs: ["The story is told in so many introductory textbooks that it has come to seem like common sense. Once upon a time, it runs, people traded goods directly: a farmer with grain who wanted shoes had to find a shoemaker who happened to want grain. Because such a coincidence was rare, someone eventually hit on the idea of a commodity everyone would accept, such as shells, salt or metal, and money was born. Credit and debt, in this account, come last, a refinement that becomes possible only once coins are available to measure what is owed.", "The difficulty is that the story describes a world no one has found. Anthropologists who went looking for economies in which neighbours regularly exchanged goods by barter have, on the whole, come back empty-handed. What they found instead, in village after village, was something closer to running accounts. A woman who needs a pot from her neighbour simply takes it, and both understand that something will be owed; the debt may be repaid in grain at harvest, in labour at a wedding, or never precisely at all. Among people who expect to keep living beside one another, the problem of the double coincidence of wants scarcely arises, because no one needs the exchange to be completed on the spot.", "Barter does occur, but in revealing places. It appears between strangers who do not expect to meet again, between groups who distrust each other, and among people who were once used to money and have been cut off from it, such as prisoners trading cigarettes or townspeople whose currency has collapsed. In each case barter is a response to the absence of trust, not the primitive condition out of which trust and credit later grew.", "Defenders of the textbook story sometimes reply that it was never intended as history. It is, they say, a thought experiment showing why a medium of exchange is useful, and its value does not depend on whether any society actually passed through a barter stage. This is a fair point as far as it goes. But the thought experiment is not idle. By placing money first and debt last, it teaches us to see money as a neutral token that merely smooths trade between independent individuals, rather than as a way of recording obligations between people already bound to one another. If the record points the other way, the more natural conclusion is that money began as a method of keeping score."]
difficulty_reason: A clearly signposted critique of a familiar story, with concrete examples and a single concession; vocabulary is plain.

subtopic: Hospitality is an exercise of the host's authority as well as an act of generosity, and that authority is the condition that makes receiving strangers possible.
paragraphs: ["We tend to picture hospitality as the purest form of generosity: a door opened to someone who has no claim on us and nothing to give in return. The picture is not false, but it omits half of what the practice involves. In the many traditions in which welcoming strangers is held to be a sacred duty, the welcome is also a careful exercise of authority. The host decides where the guest will sit, what he will eat, when he will speak and, eventually, when he will leave. To accept hospitality is to accept, for a time, a place inside someone else's order.", "This asymmetry is not incidental. A stranger arriving at a settlement is, from the settlement's point of view, an unknown quantity: he may be a trader, a refugee, a spy or a raider. Hospitality converts this uncertain figure into a guest, someone whose position is defined and whose conduct is now governed by rules that the host administers. The rituals that so often accompany a welcome, such as the offering of water, the sharing of salt or bread and the formal exchange of names, can be read as stages in this conversion. The guest who eats at the host's table has implicitly agreed not to harm the household, and the host, in turn, has made himself responsible for the guest's safety against third parties.", "It is significant, too, that hospitality is so often limited in time. Many customs specify that a guest may stay a few days before his status must change; after that he becomes a dependant who works, a kinsman by adoption, or simply an unwelcome burden. The welcome is generous precisely because it is temporary. A guest who could stay forever on a guest's terms would gradually unsettle the household's order, and the host would cease to be master of his own house.", "Some philosophers have pressed for an ideal of unconditional hospitality, a welcome that asks no questions and sets no limits. As a corrective to the suspicion with which outsiders are often treated, the ideal has force. But taken literally it would dissolve the very relation it seeks to purify. Hospitality requires a host, someone who is at home and who can therefore offer a place; if every condition is removed, there is no longer anyone in a position to welcome. The authority that makes us uneasy is not a corruption of hospitality. It is the condition that allows a stranger to be received at all."]
difficulty_reason: Moves from a familiar picture to an analysis of power and then answers an objection; the final reversal requires following the whole argument.

subtopic: The parable of the ruined common pasture describes open access rather than a governed commons, and village commons managed by local rules show a third option beside private and state ownership.
paragraphs: ["A parable that became famous in the second half of the twentieth century asks us to imagine a pasture open to all. Each herder, reasoning that the benefit of an extra animal is his alone while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, adds another, and then another, until the grass is gone and all are ruined. The moral usually drawn is stark: resources held in common will be destroyed unless they are divided into private plots or placed under the control of the state.", "The parable is persuasive, but it describes something that most actual commons are not. In many villages, pastures, woodlots, fishing ponds and irrigation channels have been shared for generations without being exhausted, and not because the villagers were unusually selfless. They were governed by rules. A household might be allowed to graze only as many animals as it could feed through the winter from its own fields; grazing might move between sections of the hill in a fixed rotation; a watchman, paid in grain, might patrol the boundary, and offenders might face fines that rose with each repeated offence. The herders of the parable have no such rules, no means of watching one another and no way of punishing those who cheat. What the parable describes is not a commons but open access, a resource that belongs to no community at all.", "This does not mean that village commons always survive. They tend to fail in recognisable circumstances: when outsiders who are not bound by local rules can enter freely, when a distant authority overrides local arrangements with regulations that villagers neither understand nor respect, when migration thins the community so much that no one is left to keep watch, or when a sudden rise in the value of the resource makes cheating more tempting than it has ever been. These are real dangers. But they are dangers to particular institutions, not proof that shared ownership is doomed by human nature.", "The practical lesson is that the familiar choice between private property and state control is too narrow. To say so is not to romanticise village life; such arrangements can be strict, and some are unequal, giving larger shares to households that hold more land. Even so, a third possibility, communities managing their own resources by rules they have made and can enforce, has a long record of success, and policy that ignores it may destroy working arrangements in the name of preventing a tragedy that was never going to happen."]
difficulty_reason: A clearly structured rebuttal of a well-known parable, with concrete rules and a list of failure conditions.

subtopic: Oral traditions are shaped by present functions, so their distortions are patterned rather than random and can be partly read through, making them evidence of a distinctive kind.
paragraphs: ["For a long time the dominant attitude of academic history towards oral tradition was one of polite suspicion. A story passed from mouth to mouth over many generations, it was argued, must accumulate errors as surely as a manuscript copied by careless scribes, and in the absence of any original against which to check it, the historian had no way of telling the accurate parts from the embellishments. Against this, a more recent and more sympathetic current has insisted that societies without writing developed techniques of memorisation of extraordinary precision, and that their traditions deserve to be treated as archives in their own right. Each side, I want to suggest, misconceives the object it is arguing about.", "The error both share is to assume that an oral tradition is trying to do what a written chronicle does, namely preserve a record of past events for its own sake, and to differ only on how well it succeeds. Traditions are rarely maintained for that purpose. A genealogy recited at the installation of a chief exists to establish that he is entitled to the office; an account of the first settlers exists to explain why one lineage holds the best land and another serves as its ritual guardians. Because the tradition answers to present needs, it changes when those needs change, and its changes are not random. Lines that no longer matter drop out; ancestors who connect currently allied groups acquire importance; the long, uneventful middle of the past is compressed, so that the founders seem only a few generations removed from those who remember their grandparents.", "This is precisely why the sceptic's analogy with the copied manuscript is misleading. Random copying errors cannot be corrected without an original, but distortions that follow from a known function can, at least in part, be anticipated and read through. A historian who understands that a genealogy is a charter for office will be cautious about its middle generations and its convenient links, while attending closely to details that serve no present interest and are therefore unlikely to have been invented. Nor is all content equally fluid: formulaic songs, names of places and fixed ritual phrases are often transmitted with a fidelity that ordinary narrative never achieves, even when no one any longer understands what they mean.", "None of this licenses the opposite romanticism. A tradition that is reliable about the shape of an ancient migration may be quite wrong about who led it, and no technique of memorisation can protect a story from a community's interest in retelling it. Written sources, it should be added, are hardly exempt from the same pressures; charters and chronicles were also composed to justify claims, and historians learned long ago to read them against the grain. Oral tradition, approached in that spirit, is neither an archive nor a fiction. It is a record of what a community needed its past to be, and that is itself a kind of evidence about the past."]
difficulty_reason: Rejects two opposed positions by exposing a shared assumption; the argument turns on an abstract distinction between random and patterned distortion.

subtopic: Scientific validation of local ecological knowledge improves on dismissal but wrongly treats such knowledge as separable statements and lets authority run one way; mutual testing is better.
paragraphs: ["It has become common for conservation projects and agricultural agencies to announce that they have 'validated' some piece of local knowledge. Fishers' accounts of where a species gathers to spawn are checked against tagging data; herders' claims about which plants their animals avoid in a dry year are tested in feeding trials; farmers' weather signs are compared with rainfall records. When the local claim survives, it is welcomed into the scientific literature, and the project is praised for taking seriously people whose expertise was long ignored. This is an improvement on simple dismissal. Yet the language of validation carries assumptions that deserve more scrutiny than they usually receive.", "The first is that local knowledge is a set of separate statements, each of which can be lifted out and checked on its own. Much of what farmers and fishers know does not take this form. A farmer who decides when to sow may attend at once to the flowering of a particular tree, the behaviour of ants, the smell of the soil and the memory of the last three seasons, weighing them against one another in ways she could not easily put into words. Test any one of these signs in isolation and it may predict rainfall poorly; to conclude that the farmer's knowledge has failed would be to mistake a judgement for a list of rules. What is being evaluated is not what she knows but a fragment translated into a form the evaluator can handle.", "The second assumption is that the direction of authority runs one way. Science sets the standard, local knowledge applies for admission, and once admitted it belongs to the literature rather than to the people who held it. Communities have sometimes found that knowledge about medicinal plants or fishing grounds, once published, was used by outsiders in ways they had no say in. Validation, in other words, can be a means of transfer as much as of recognition.", "It would be wrong to conclude that local knowledge should be shielded from testing altogether. Some local beliefs are mistaken, as some scientific ones are, and the communities that hold them revise them in the light of experience more often than romantic accounts allow. The objection is not to checking but to a procedure in which only one side checks. Where farmers help decide which questions are asked and how the results will be used, and where scientific claims are also tested against their observations, the two bodies of knowledge can correct each other. That is a more demanding arrangement than validation, and a more honest one."]
difficulty_reason: Critiques a well-meant practice through two named assumptions and closes with a concession and an alternative; the stance is qualified rather than hostile.

subtopic: Households earmark money to make it carry social meanings, so fungibility is an arrangement that holds in impersonal settings rather than a natural property of money.
paragraphs: ["One of the first lessons of economics is that money is fungible. A rupee earned is the same as a rupee found, a rupee received as a gift or a rupee won at cards; since each can buy exactly what the others can, a rational person should be indifferent to where a sum came from and should spend it according to a single ranking of needs. This is what makes money so useful. It strips goods of their particular histories and renders them comparable, and it lets a stranger in one town trade with a stranger in another without either needing to know anything about the other's life.", "Ordinary households, however, behave as though they had never heard the lesson. Coins for the temple are kept in a separate tin; a grandmother's gift to a newborn goes into a savings account that no one will touch for rent even in a hard month; the money a woman earns from tailoring is spent on her children's schooling, while her husband's wages go to food and the loan; a windfall is spent on a celebration that the same sum, arriving as salary, would never have funded. Money that arrives in one way is marked, set aside and spent in another, as though each sum carried a label that its owners were bound to respect. Nor are such habits confined to poor households; in one form or another they appear in families at every level of income.", "The standard response is to call this mental accounting and to treat it as a lapse, a cognitive shortcut that serves people tolerably on the whole but leads them into avoidable errors. The errors are real. A family that keeps savings in a low-interest account reserved for a daughter's wedding while borrowing at a ruinous rate to repair the roof is paying heavily for a distinction that, in purely financial terms, does not exist. Yet to describe earmarking only as a mistake is to miss what it accomplishes. The grandmother's gift is set apart because it is a relationship as much as a sum: spending it on rent would feel like dissolving the bond it expressed. The tailor's earnings are spent on schooling because keeping them distinct allows her to claim, within the household, a sphere of decision that pooled money would not give her. Labels on money are the means by which people make it say something about who they are to one another.", "It may be objected that this shows only that people attach feelings to money, not that money itself ceases to be fungible. In the market, after all, the tailor's rupee buys exactly what her husband's does, and no shopkeeper asks about its origin. The objection is correct about the shopkeeper. But it concedes the point that matters. Fungibility holds where people have agreed to ignore the histories of sums, as in impersonal trade, and fails where they have not, as in the household, the family ceremony and the circle of friends who lend to one another.", "The single, featureless money of the textbook, then, is not a natural property of currency that social life afterwards distorts. It is an arrangement that holds in certain settings and that people are constantly unmaking elsewhere. To see this is not to deny that the arrangement is valuable, or that families sometimes pay dearly for their labels; it is to recognise that the indifference to origins which economics takes as its starting point is itself a social achievement, and a local one."]
difficulty_reason: A critique of a basic economic assumption with a concession about real costs and an objection answered; the examples keep the abstraction manageable.

subtopic: Rotating savings associations persist not as substitutes for missing banks but as tools that use a debt to the group to shelter money from other social claims.
paragraphs: ["In many parts of the world, groups of neighbours, co-workers or traders meet at regular intervals and each contributes a fixed sum to a common pot, which is then handed in its entirety to one member. At the next meeting the process is repeated and the pot goes to someone else, until every member has received it once and the cycle ends or begins again. The order may be fixed by lot, by agreement or, in some versions, by bidding, with the member who most urgently wants the money accepting a smaller pot and the difference shared among the rest. Such rotating associations go by dozens of local names, and for a long time development economists regarded them as makeshift substitutes for banks, ingenious but destined to disappear once formal credit reached the people who used them.", "That prediction has fared poorly. The associations persist among people who have bank accounts, and they have travelled with migrants into cities where banks are on every corner.
