It was the claim that a salaried, disciplined body of officers, visible on the street at all hours, could prevent offences from occurring at all. The patrol, rather than the arrest, was meant to be the core of the institution.", "This founding idea has an awkward property: its successes cannot be seen. A burglary that does not happen leaves no record, and a street that stays quiet because an officer passed through it twenty minutes earlier looks exactly like a street that would have stayed quiet anyway. The arrest, by contrast, is countable. It produces a name, a charge and a figure that can be reported upward and compared from one year to the next. Over time, institutions tend to drift toward what they can count, and police forces have been no exception. Officers come to be judged by how many people they detain, and the quiet beat, which was supposed to be the whole point, comes to look like idleness.", "It would be too simple to conclude that the preventive ideal was therefore an illusion. Critics sometimes point out that putting more officers on the street does not reliably reduce recorded crime, and they are right to be sceptical of large claims about deterrence. But the patrol was never only about deterrence. A visible and predictable presence tells residents that someone is responsible for the shared space of the street, and that sense of being looked after shapes whether people walk out at night, whether they report what they see, and whether they regard the police as theirs or as an occupying force. These effects are as hard to count as the burglary that did not happen, but they are not imaginary.", "The deeper lesson concerns what happens when a public institution is measured by its most legible output rather than by its purpose. A force that rewards arrests will produce arrests, and it may do so in ways that erode the trust on which prevention depends. Recovering the original idea does not mean abandoning measurement; it means admitting that some of the most important things a police force does will show up, if at all, only as an absence."]
difficulty_reason: A clear historical opening and a single line of argument; the one concession in paragraph 3 is signalled plainly.

subtopic: The passage argues that the passport began as a tool of selective state control rather than a key to travel, and that the protection it offers depends on the rank of the issuing state.
paragraphs: ["We tend to think of the passport as a document that lets people travel. It is the thing we pack and check twice before leaving for the airport, and losing it abroad feels like being stranded. Yet the history of the passport suggests that its first purpose was not to open borders but to give states a means of closing them selectively. A document that certifies who you are, and which state answers for you, is above all a tool for deciding who may enter, who may leave, and who may be turned back.", "For much of the nineteenth century, a traveller could cross many European frontiers without being asked for papers at all. Controls existed, but they were patchy, and in several countries they were relaxed as railways made movement faster and cheaper. The First World War changed this. Governments anxious about spies, deserters and the flight of men of fighting age began demanding documents at every crossing, and when the war ended the requirement was not withdrawn. What had been introduced as an emergency measure became the ordinary condition of international travel, and the expectation that every person should belong to exactly one state, and carry proof of it, hardened into common sense. Few people now remember that it was ever otherwise.", "None of this makes the passport simply an instrument of control. For the person who holds it, it is also a claim on protection: it entitles the bearer to return home and to seek help from the officials of the issuing state when abroad. The predicament of stateless people, who have no government willing to vouch for them, shows how much that claim is worth. Without it, a person can be refused entry everywhere and expelled from wherever he happens to be.", "The more uncomfortable point is that the protection is unevenly distributed. Two travellers standing in the same queue may carry documents of identical design and very different power, one admitting its holder to most of the world without a visa, the other inviting suspicion at every desk. What the passport records, then, is not only identity but rank in an order of states, an accident of birth that the individual did little to earn and can rarely change. Nor is that rank settled by anything the traveller does at the desk; it is negotiated between governments, through visa agreements and reciprocal arrangements, long before any individual reaches the frontier. To call the document a passport to freedom is to describe the experience of those whose papers happen to work."]
difficulty_reason: Concrete history and familiar experience; the stance and the concession in paragraph 3 are stated openly.

subtopic: Frontline officials cannot stop exercising judgement however detailed their rules, so reform should make that discretion visible and guided rather than try to abolish it.
paragraphs: ["Public debate about bureaucracy tends to oscillate between two complaints. One is that officials are rigid, applying rules mechanically to people whose circumstances the rules never anticipated. The other is that officials are arbitrary, treating similar applicants differently according to mood, prejudice or the length of the queue. The usual remedy for the second complaint is more rules: tighter eligibility criteria, standard forms, checklists that leave nothing to judgement. Each new scandal of favouritism produces another layer of instructions, and the layers accumulate. The remedy is seldom questioned, because it seems obvious that a rule applied uniformly is fairer than a person deciding as he pleases.", "What this remedy overlooks is that the officials who deal directly with the public, the benefits clerk, the housing inspector, the teacher deciding which pupil needs extra help, cannot stop exercising judgement however detailed their instructions become. A rule says that an applicant must provide proof of address; it does not say how hard the clerk should look for an acceptable document when the applicant has been living with relatives. Moreover, such officials almost always have more cases than time. They must decide whose file to open first, whose story to probe and whose to accept, and these decisions shape outcomes as surely as any formal ruling. When rules are tightened, judgement does not disappear. It retreats into these less visible choices, where it is harder to observe and correct.", "This is not to romanticise frontline discretion. The same latitude that allows a sympathetic clerk to find a way through for a desperate family allows an unsympathetic one to find reasons for delay, and there is ample reason to think that such latitude is not exercised evenly across applicants of different backgrounds. The case for discretion is not that officials can be trusted. It is that the choice is not between discretion and its absence, but between discretion that is acknowledged and discretion that is driven underground. Discretion of the first kind can be examined and improved; discretion of the second kind can only be suspected.", "Seen this way, the task of administrative reform changes. Instead of writing rules ever more finely in the hope of closing every gap, an agency might record the informal decisions its staff actually make, review samples of cases to see how similar applicants fare, and give officials explicit guidance on the purposes their judgement should serve. None of these steps would remove judgement from the counter; they would make it something an agency can see, discuss and, where necessary, correct. Such measures concede what the rule-writer prefers to deny: that every system of rules ends, at its edges, in someone deciding."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief with a concession; the key move (discretion relocates rather than disappears) must be followed across paragraphs 2 and 3.

subtopic: The contrast between citizenship by birthplace and by descent is a poor guide to how open a society is, since motives vary and naturalisation rules matter more.
paragraphs: ["Discussions of nationality law often begin from a tidy contrast. Under the principle of soil, a child born within the territory of a state becomes its citizen; under the principle of descent, citizenship passes from parent to child wherever the child is born. The first is commonly described as civic and open, since it admits anyone born on the land regardless of ancestry; the second as ethnic and closed, since it ties membership to bloodline. The contrast is useful as a first approximation, but as a guide to which societies are more welcoming it is close to misleading.", "Consider why states adopted the soil rule in the first place. Where governments needed to populate large territories and to secure soldiers and taxpayers, it was convenient to claim the children of newcomers automatically, whatever their parents' wishes or origins. The rule expressed less a generous conception of belonging than an interest in numbers. Conversely, the descent rule has served countries with large populations abroad, allowing the children of emigrants to retain a connection to a homeland they may visit only occasionally. Neither motive is obviously more liberal than the other, and the same rule can serve quite different ends depending on who adopts it and why.", "More importantly, the rule that governs birth is only one part of a citizenship regime, and often not the part that matters most. A state that follows the descent principle but allows long-term residents to naturalise after a few years, and extends citizenship to children who have grown up and been schooled in the country, may be far easier to join than a state that follows the soil principle but makes naturalisation slow, costly and uncertain for adults. The second state includes every child born on its territory and keeps their parents waiting at the door indefinitely. A single household may then contain citizens and foreigners under one roof, divided by nothing more than the place where each member happened to be born.", "None of this means the choice of birth rule is unimportant. The soil principle does guarantee something valuable: no one born in the territory can be left, by the mere fact of birth, a permanent outsider in the only country he has known, and states without it have sometimes produced generations of residents with no secure status. But that guarantee is better understood as one protection among several than as the defining mark of an open society. The question worth asking of any nationality law is not which principle it starts from, but how readily it turns people who have made their lives in a country into its members."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a familiar contrast that moves from motives to institutional design and ends with a concession; moderately abstract.

subtopic: The thesis that taxation breeds accountability while resource revenue erodes it survives only in a narrower form: accountability grows where rulers depend on the cooperation of the ruled.
paragraphs: ["There is an old argument, revived by students of public finance, that the way a state raises its money shapes the kind of state it becomes. A government that depends on taxing its own population must, to some degree, negotiate with that population. It needs to know who earns what and where they live; it needs officials who can assess, collect and keep accounts; and it needs taxpayers who will comply without being coerced at every turn. Each of these needs creates leverage for the governed. Those who pay can demand to know how their money is spent, and rulers who want a steady revenue have reason to listen.", "A government that draws most of its income from a single lucrative resource, such as oil or minerals sold abroad, faces no comparable pressure. Its revenue arrives through a handful of contracts with foreign buyers and requires little cooperation from ordinary citizens. It has no need to build an apparatus that knows the population in detail, and no need to trade services or a voice in decisions for compliance. Proponents of the argument suggest that such states can afford to be both unresponsive and administratively thin, buying acquiescence with subsidies and public employment rather than earning consent through bargaining.", "Stated baldly, the thesis is too mechanical. Taxation has often been extracted by force rather than negotiated, and many heavily taxed populations have obtained neither representation nor accountability in return. Nor are all resource-rich states alike: where competent institutions and habits of public scrutiny were established before a windfall arrived, the revenue has sometimes been managed with considerable openness. The sequence appears to matter as much as the source. A resource boom that lands on a weak state may keep it weak; one that lands on a state already accustomed to accounting for itself need not.", "What survives these qualifications is a narrower but sturdier claim. The point is not that taxes make governments good or that resource revenue makes them bad, but that accountability tends to grow where rulers need something from the ruled that cannot simply be seized. Taxation is one common source of that need, perhaps historically the most important, but it is the dependence, not the tax form as such, that does the work. A reform that raised more revenue from citizens without increasing what citizens could demand in return would therefore miss the point entirely, and might even entrench the habits of command it was meant to cure. Equally, a resource-rich government that chose to make itself dependent on its citizens, by funding services through broad taxes and setting its windfall aside, would be doing something more significant than balancing its books."]
difficulty_reason: Reports a thesis, qualifies it with counter-cases and restates a narrower version; the shift from 'tax form' to 'dependence' must be tracked.

subtopic: The main danger of constitutional emergency powers is quiet normalisation rather than dramatic seizure, so safeguards should make renewal progressively harder and publicly justified.
paragraphs: ["Almost every modern constitution makes room for its own partial suspension. In a war, an epidemic or a sudden collapse of public order, the executive may be permitted to rule by decree, restrict movement or detain people without the usual procedures, on the understanding that these powers serve to preserve the constitutional order rather than to replace it. The logic is respectable. A constitution that made no provision for emergencies would not prevent governments from acting in a crisis; it would simply ensure that they acted outside the law, improvising powers with no defined limits and no defined end.", "The danger that emergency provisions are usually designed to guard against is the dramatic one: a leader who declares a crisis in order to abolish the constitution altogether. That danger is real but comparatively rare. The more common pattern is quieter. An emergency is declared for a genuine reason, and then renewed, and renewed again, because the threat has not entirely disappeared and no official wants to be blamed if it returns. Measures adopted as exceptions are gradually written into ordinary statutes, where they no longer need renewal at all. And each emergency lowers the threshold for the next, since officials and citizens alike grow accustomed to powers that once seemed extraordinary.", "The standard remedy is the sunset clause, which makes emergency powers lapse after a fixed period unless they are renewed. Sunset clauses are better than nothing, but they tend to turn renewal into a formality, a vote taken under the shadow of the original fear by legislators who see little to gain from being the ones who let the powers lapse. What matters is not whether powers expire but how hard it is to extend them. A more demanding design would require larger majorities for each successive renewal, so that a measure which commanded a bare majority at the outset needed broad agreement to survive a year later, and it would oblige the government to state publicly, each time, why ordinary law is still inadequate to the threat.", "Such designs would not prevent a determined government from abusing emergency powers, and no constitutional text can do that alone; courts, a free press and an opposition willing to make itself unpopular all have parts to play. The purpose of the design is more modest: to make normalisation visible and expensive, so that an exception which has outlasted its reasons must be defended openly as a permanent change rather than slipping into permanence unnoticed. A government that genuinely needs lasting powers can still obtain them, but only by persuading a broad majority that the change should be lasting. The test of an emergency regime is less whether it can survive a coup than whether it can end."]
difficulty_reason: Problem and solution with an opening concession and a modest conclusion; the distinction between dramatic and quiet danger runs through the whole passage.

subtopic: The rule of law is best understood narrowly, as formal legality: a real but limited virtue that tends to obstruct injustice without guaranteeing against it, and that is obscured when made to stand for every political good.
paragraphs: ["Few political ideals are invoked as often, or defined as loosely, as the rule of law. In one usage it names a set of formal properties of a legal order: laws should be general rather than aimed at particular persons, public rather than secret, prospective rather than retroactive, clear enough to be followed, stable enough to be relied on, and applied by courts that are independent of those who hold power. In another usage the phrase stands for a much larger package. A state governed by the rule of law, on this richer view, is one that also protects fundamental rights, holds free elections and distributes its burdens fairly. Whatever is admirable in a constitutional democracy tends to be gathered under the same heading.", "The richer view has an obvious appeal. It seems perverse to praise a legal order for its clarity and consistency while it applies clear and consistent laws that strip a minority of its property or bar it from public life. Yet the inclusive definition carries a cost that its defenders seldom count. If the rule of law means everything good about a political system, the phrase ceases to pick out anything in particular. We lose the ability to say, of one regime, that its laws are cruel but at least public and predictable, or of another that it has excellent statutes on paper which officials ignore whenever it suits them. These are different failings, calling for different remedies, and a vocabulary that cannot separate them is a poorer instrument for judging governments, not a more generous one.", "The formal conception, moreover, is not as morally empty as its critics allege. A law that is public and prospective allows people to know in advance what will be required of them and to arrange their lives around it; a law applied by independent courts constrains the officials who administer it as well as the citizens who are subject to it. These are real goods even when the content of the law is objectionable, because they leave the governed some room to anticipate, avoid and contest what is done to them. It is also worth noticing that governments bent on oppression rarely find formal legality congenial. They tend to prefer secret directives, retroactive offences, vague charges that can be stretched to fit any critic, and enforcement that falls on enemies and spares friends. The formal requirements, in other words, get in the way of a great deal of injustice, even if they forbid none of it outright.", "This last point should not be pressed too far. The tendency of formality to obstruct oppression is a matter of experience, not of logic, and experience includes regimes that pursued grave injustice through meticulously drafted, publicly promulgated and impartially enforced laws. A defender of the thin conception must concede that legality of this kind is compatible with deep wrong, and that its tendency to discourage abuse is a probability rather than a guarantee. What can be claimed is narrower: that formal legality is one distinct virtue a legal order may have or lack, that its absence makes most other wrongs easier to commit, and that we see it most clearly when we refuse to let it stand for every other virtue at once. Questions about whether the laws are just, whether the rulers were chosen freely and whether the burdens are fairly shared remain, on this view, as urgent as ever; they are simply different questions, and they deserve to be asked in their own terms."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract comparison of two conceptions, with a defence, a counter-objection and a self-limiting concession; the author's stance is narrow and carefully hedged.

subtopic: The dead hand objection fails against entrenchment in general, because amendment rules arbitrate disagreements among the living, but it has real force against constitutions that are practically unamendable.
paragraphs: ["Every entrenched constitution invites an awkward question. If a majority of citizens today wishes to change some arrangement, why should it be prevented from doing so by rules that were drafted generations ago by people who are now dead, and who could not have imagined the conditions under which their successors live? A requirement that amendments win two-thirds of the legislature, or the approval of most regions, looks from this angle like a device for letting the past outvote the present. The objection has a democratic edge that is hard to dismiss: it asks by what right one generation sets the terms on which another must govern itself. Nor is it answered by praising the wisdom of the framers, since wisdom about one century is no warrant for authority over the next.", "The most familiar answer appeals to self-binding. Just as a sailor who knows he will be tempted by a dangerous song may order his crew to tie him to the mast and ignore his later pleas, a people may bind itself in a calm moment against the passions it expects to feel in an agitated one. Entrenchment, on this account, is not the past overruling the present but the present protecting itself from its own worst impulses. The image is attractive, but it does not fit the case. The sailor binds himself, and the man who later strains at the ropes is the same man who gave the order. A constitution binds people who were not present when it was adopted and who gave no order at all. To call this self-binding is to assume precisely the continuity of the collective self that the objection calls into question.", "A better defence starts from a different picture of what entrenchment does. Amendment rules do not, in practice, pit the living against the dead, because the dead cast no votes. What such rules do is set the terms on which living citizens must settle disagreements among themselves. When an amendment fails for want of a supermajority, it is defeated not by its framers but by a present minority large enough to block it. The requirement thus protects groups that might otherwise be outvoted on matters basic to their standing, and it encourages proposals that can attract support beyond a single faction. The protection is not merely theoretical: a group that knows it can block changes to its basic standing has less reason to fear the ordinary swings of electoral fortune, and more reason to accept defeat on everything else. Seen this way, the hand that restrains the majority is a living hand, and the real question is whether present minorities deserve such a veto, not whether the past deserves obedience.", "This reframing does not make the original worry vanish. It succeeds only where amendment is demanding but genuinely possible. A constitution whose amendment procedure is so onerous that no change has been achieved in living memory, or which declares certain provisions unamendable altogether, really does impose the judgement of its authors on everyone who comes after; there, no present coalition, however broad, can alter the text. The objection from the dead hand is therefore best understood not as a refutation of entrenchment as such but as a warning about its extremes. Between a constitution that any passing majority may rewrite and one that no one can, the useful argument concerns how much agreement change should require, and that is a question each generation is entitled to keep asking."]
difficulty_reason: Objection, a rejected reply, a better reply and a limiting concession; the author's position must be located between three views.

subtopic: Selection by lot has real democratic merits that elections lack, but because it cannot supply accountability it should supplement elected bodies rather than replace them.
paragraphs: ["Elections are so closely identified with democracy that it can seem perverse to ask whether they are democratic at all. Yet consider what an election rewards. To win, a candidate must stand out from the crowd: be better known, better funded, better connected or simply more persuasive on a platform than the people whose votes are sought. An election is, in this sense, a procedure for picking a distinguished few, and the chambers it fills tend to resemble the electorate less closely than a random sample of that electorate would. Many ancient Greek writers saw the point clearly; for them, filling offices by lot was the characteristically democratic method, and election was a device that favoured the prominent.", "The modern case for selection by lot builds on that old intuition. A body drawn at random from the adult population brings into the room the people who are usually spoken about rather than heard: the shift worker, the pensioner, the young parent who would never run for anything. Its members owe nothing to donors or to party managers, since nobody campaigned to put them there. Above all, they are free to change their minds. An elected representative who revises a position after hearing the evidence risks being called a turncoat; a citizen chosen by lot has no platform to betray, and so can treat a question as something to be worked out rather than a position to be defended.", "Critics usually reply that ordinary citizens lack the competence to legislate. This objection is weaker than it sounds. Few elected legislators are experts in more than a sliver of what they vote on; they rely on staff, committees and witnesses, and there is no reason a randomly chosen body could not do the same. A more serious difficulty concerns accountability. An elected member who disappoints can be removed at the next election, and the prospect of removal disciplines conduct in between. A member chosen by lot answers to no one, and the very independence that shields such a member from donors also shields him or her from voters. Those who propose replacing elected chambers with lotteries have not, to my mind, answered this objection.", "The sensible conclusion is not that lot should displace election but that it can do something election does badly. On some questions elected politicians have every incentive to avoid committing themselves, because any clear answer will cost them votes. A panel chosen at random, given time, evidence and a duty to hear opposing witnesses, can show what ordinary people conclude once they have actually thought the matter through, and its recommendations can then be put to the legislature or to the voters for decision. The lottery's virtue is that it reveals considered public judgement; its limit is that no one has authorised the people it selects to rule."]
difficulty_reason: A claim, objection and reply structure with a concession that changes the conclusion; abstract but clearly signposted.

subtopic: Compulsory voting imposes only a light duty and changes campaign incentives for the better, but it does not make voters better informed.
paragraphs: ["In a handful of democracies, adults who fail to vote without a good excuse are fined a small sum. To many people elsewhere this looks like a contradiction in terms: surely a free citizen is entitled to stay at home. The objection deserves a hearing, but it is less forceful than it first appears. What such laws typically require is attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular. Ballots remain secret, and a citizen who wishes to register indifference or protest can spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank. The duty imposed is closer to that of serving on a jury or completing a census form than to an order about what to believe. A subtler version of the objection holds that deliberate abstention is itself a political statement, a refusal to lend legitimacy to a contest one regards as empty. Yet a citizen who feels this way loses very little under compulsion, since the blank ballot preserves the statement and arguably sharpens it: a deliberately empty ballot can be counted, whereas a deliberate absence is indistinguishable from the absences of those who merely forgot.", "The more interesting question is what compulsion actually changes. Where voting is voluntary, turnout is usually lowest among the young, the poor and the recently arrived, so the electorate that politicians court is older and wealthier than the population as a whole. Campaigns respond rationally to this. A large share of their effort goes into persuading their own likely supporters to turn up, and one of the cheapest ways to do that is to make those supporters angry or afraid about the other side. When almost everyone votes, that strategy loses much of its point. There is little to be gained by stirring up people who will vote anyway, and the votes worth competing for belong to citizens who have not yet made up their minds.", "Supporters of compulsion sometimes go further and claim that it produces wiser decisions. Here caution is needed. Being required to attend a polling station does not make anyone better informed, and a citizen who resents the obligation may simply mark the first name on the list. Compulsion enlarges the electorate; it does not educate it. Its real contribution is quieter. It shifts the incentives of those who seek votes, away from rousing the faithful and towards addressing the undecided, and it allows the result to claim to speak for nearly everyone rather than for those who happened to feel strongly enough to come out. That is a modest achievement, but in an age of angry campaigning it is not a small one."]
difficulty_reason: Three clearly organised paragraphs with an explicit objection, reply and qualification; vocabulary is plain.

subtopic: The secret ballot protects voters chiefly by making intimidation and bribery unenforceable rather than by appealing to virtue, so it must be compulsory and must be actively maintained as voting methods change.
paragraphs: ["The secret ballot is now so taken for granted that it is easy to forget how recent it is and how fiercely it was once opposed. For much of the nineteenth century, in many countries, voters declared their choices aloud or on papers that others could see, and the reform that replaced this practice was resisted not only by those who profited from intimidation. A respectable strand of liberal opinion held that the vote was a public trust, exercised on behalf of the whole community, and that a trust ought to be discharged in public. A man who knew that his neighbours would see his vote, the argument ran, would be ashamed to cast it for a selfish reason.", "The argument has a certain nobility, and it rests on a real insight: people do behave differently when they are observed. Its error lies in assuming that the observer will be the voter's conscience. In practice the people most interested in how a tenant, a labourer or a clerk had voted were the landlord, the employer and the local party agent, and the pressure they applied had little to do with the public good. Publicity did not make votes more responsible; it made them more obedient.", "The less obvious virtue of secrecy is that it disarms bribery as well as intimidation. Buying a vote is a kind of contract, and a contract is worthless if one party cannot check whether the other has kept it. Once no one can verify how a ballot was marked, the buyer who pays in advance cannot know whether he has bought anything, and the seller can take the money and vote as he pleases. Secrecy, in other words, works less by appealing to the voter's virtue than by making a certain kind of corruption unenforceable. This also explains why secrecy has to be a duty and not merely a right. If voters could choose to reveal their ballots, those under pressure could be required to prove their compliance, and the protection would collapse for exactly the people who need it most.", "That point matters more now than it once did. A ballot marked at home, at a kitchen table, can be watched by a domineering relative; a ballot photographed in a booth with a telephone can be shown to whoever demands proof. Neither practice is sinister in itself, and both make voting easier for many people. But they reopen the gap that secrecy was designed to close, and they suggest that the privacy of the vote is not a natural condition of democratic life but an arrangement that has to be maintained, and occasionally rebuilt, as the means of voting change."]
difficulty_reason: A history of an idea that turns on a non-obvious mechanism (unverifiability) and applies it to the present; moderately abstract.

subtopic: Populism is best defined as a claim to represent exclusively a single authentic people, an anti-pluralist stance, but the definition must not be used to dismiss the grievances that draw people to populist movements.
paragraphs: ["Few political terms are used as loosely as populism. It is applied to movements of the left and of the right, to leaders who promise to spend lavishly and to those who promise to cut, to campaigns against banks and to campaigns against immigrants. A word that covers so much risks covering nothing, and some scholars have concluded that it is merely a label for whatever kind of politics the speaker happens to dislike. That conclusion is premature. The variety of populist programmes is real, but it may simply show that populism is not a programme at all.", "Consider the most common attempt at definition: populism as hostility to elites. This cannot be sufficient, since criticism of the powerful is the ordinary business of opposition in any democracy, and a definition that made every challenger a populist would be useless. What distinguishes the populist is a further claim, namely that there exists a single, authentic people whose will is already known, and that the movement or leader in question alone gives it voice. Opponents are therefore not merely mistaken; they are illegitimate, and citizens who vote for them are not quite part of the people. On this account the core of populism is not anti-elitism but anti-pluralism, a refusal to accept that the people may be divided in good faith.", "The value of this definition is that it explains a pattern which approaches based on policy tend to miss. A movement that claims to embody the whole people has difficulty accepting defeat, since a loss at the polls must then be explained as fraud, manipulation or the work of enemies; and once in office it is tempted to treat independent courts, a critical press or a neutral civil service as obstacles placed between the people and its rightful expression. None of this follows from hostility to elites alone. It follows from the claim to a moral monopoly of representation.", "Yet the definition carries a hazard of its own. Precisely because it locates the danger in a style of claim rather than in a set of grievances, it can tempt those who use it to dismiss the grievances along with the style. Many people drawn to populist movements have real complaints: about decisions taken far away from them, about parties that seem interchangeable, about institutions that consult them rarely. To treat such voters as a symptom to be managed, rather than as citizens with reasons, is to deny them the standing that pluralism promises, and to confirm the populist story that an elite has stopped listening. The definition is a tool for recognising a threat to democratic competition; it is not a licence to stop asking why the threat finds an audience."]
difficulty_reason: Conceptual argument about definition, with the stance carried by distinctions (anti-elitism versus anti-pluralism, style versus grievance) and a reflexive final twist.

subtopic: Although widely distrusted, political parties perform functions that democratic government needs, so weakening them tends to shift power to other organised interests; the remedy for bad parties is better parties.
paragraphs: ["Political parties have few admirers. It is a commonplace of political commentary that they are distrusted, and reformers of every persuasion have proposed ways of loosening their grip: independent candidates, direct votes on policy, primaries open to any voter who cares to take part. The suspicion is understandable. Parties reward loyalty over judgement, they paper over disagreements in order to win, and their leaders sometimes seem more interested in the survival of the organisation than in the purposes it was founded to serve.", "Yet much of what makes democratic government workable is done by parties, and done so routinely that it goes unnoticed. A modern electorate contains millions of people with conflicting interests. Someone has to assemble those interests into a programme coherent enough to be offered, defended and, if elected, attempted; someone has to recruit and test the people who will hold office; and someone has to give voters a simple way of knowing what a candidate broadly stands for without studying the record of each individual. Parties do all three. Most importantly, they make accountability possible. A government formed by a party can be judged as a team at the next election, whereas a legislature of independents, each with a private bargain to defend, offers voters no one in particular to reward or punish.", "This is why some reforms intended to democratise parties have had awkward consequences. When candidates are chosen in primaries open to anyone, the party organisation loses much of its ability to screen out those who would damage it, and the candidates who win are often those with the most intense supporters rather than those with the broadest appeal. When membership dwindles, the organisation does not disappear; it becomes a smaller circle of professionals and funders, less rooted in local life and more remote from the voters it claims to represent. Weakening the party, in other words, does not necessarily hand power to citizens. It may hand it instead to whoever is able to organise without one: wealthy individuals, single-issue lobbies, the personal following of a celebrity.", "None of this makes parties virtuous. A party that faces no serious competition will serve itself, and the defenders of party government have sometimes mistaken the indispensability of parties for their innocence. The argument here is a narrower one. It is that the familiar complaints about parties are complaints about particular parties behaving badly, and that the cure for bad parties is better ones, more open to their members and more seriously contested, rather than a politics that tries to do without them altogether."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief with a clear turn ('Yet') and a closing concession; concrete examples support abstract functions.

subtopic: Disruption is often essential to democratic protest, but it is legitimate when it seeks a hearing in proportion to its cause and not when it tries to prevent others from acting on their own decisions.
paragraphs: ["A common complaint about protest is that it inconveniences people who have done nothing wrong. Commuters are delayed, shops lose trade, ambulances must find another route. The complaint has some force, but it often hides an assumption that deserves to be questioned: that legitimate protest would cause no inconvenience at all. A march that nobody notices, held where nobody has to walk around it, is hardly a protest. Part of the point of gathering in public is to make a claim that others cannot easily ignore.", "This is why disruption has always been close to the centre of democratic protest rather than at its edge. Groups without money, office or access to the press have few ways of placing an issue on the public agenda, and a temporary cost imposed on the wider community is one of them. Many causes now regarded as plainly just were first brought to public notice by people who were considered a nuisance, and their critics complained, in much the same terms as are heard today, that they had chosen the wrong methods and the wrong moment.", "None of this means that any disruption is acceptable. The useful distinction is between disruption that seeks a hearing and disruption that seeks to impose an outcome. The first imposes a cost in order to make others pay attention; it accepts that, once they have paid attention, they may still disagree. The second tries to make it impossible for others to act on their own decision, for instance by preventing a lawful vote from taking place or by keeping people from a service they are entitled to use. Protest of the first kind is part of the argument on which democracy runs. Protest of the second kind substitutes pressure for persuasion, and a democracy can rightly limit it.", "Proportion matters as well. A blockade that delays traffic for an afternoon is different from one that prevents a hospital from receiving supplies, even if both are aimed only at securing attention. Those who protest have a responsibility to choose methods whose costs bear some relation to the importance of what they are saying, and those who govern have a responsibility not to treat every inconvenience as an emergency. Neither responsibility can be reduced to a simple rule, and particular cases will always be argued over; but the alternative to such argument is worse. A society that tolerates no disruption at all has, in effect, decided that only those who already have a hearing deserve one."]
difficulty_reason: A clearly signposted claim, distinction and qualification with everyday examples.

subtopic: What the decline of local newspapers chiefly costs democracy is routine observation of local government, a function that the internet does not replace and that must now be supported deliberately, whatever the flaws of the papers that once provided it.
paragraphs: ["When a town loses its newspaper, the loss is usually mourned in the language of community: the obituaries, the school sports results, the notices of births and marriages that no one else will print. These are real losses, but they are not the ones that matter most for self-government. What disappears with the local paper is something duller and more important, namely the habit of attendance. For decades, in many places, a reporter sat through the meetings of the council, the planning committee and the school board, read the budget documents that nobody else read, and noticed when a contract went to the same firm for the third time without a tender.", "Most of what such reporters wrote was unremarkable, and much of it was barely read. Its value lay less in any particular story than in the knowledge, shared by every official in the room, that someone was taking notes. Officials who know that a question may be asked in print tomorrow tend to ask it of themselves today. Monitoring of this kind works rather as a speed camera does: its effect is measured not by the fines it issues but by the careless driving it prevents. Remove it, and the immediate result is not a wave of scandal, since there is no longer anyone to report one, but a gradual loosening of the restraint that observation imposed. The absence of bad news, in a town without a reporter, is not evidence of good government.", "It is often said that the internet has more than made up the difference, since anyone can now publish and residents can share information instantly. This confuses the supply of commentary with the supply of attention. A neighbourhood forum can spread a rumour about the council in minutes, but it seldom has anyone willing to spend three evenings a month in council meetings, or the training to read a set of accounts. National outlets, for their part, cover local government only when it produces a story large enough to interest a national audience, which is usually to say only after the damage is done. What the internet has multiplied is reaction; what has thinned out is the patient, unglamorous observation on which informed reaction depends.", "None of this should be allowed to turn into nostalgia. Many local papers were timid with powerful advertisers, cosy with the town's leading figures and given to boosterism, celebrating every new development while asking few questions about who would profit from it. A press that depends on the goodwill of the people it covers is a weak watchdog, and some of the papers now lamented were weak in exactly this way, flattering the very people they ought to have been questioning. The case for local journalism does not rest on the virtue of the institutions that happened to provide it.", "It rests, rather, on the function those institutions performed, however imperfectly. If that function is to survive the collapse of the business model that once paid for it, it will have to be supported deliberately: by newsrooms funded as public goods, by universities that send students to cover meetings, perhaps by public records published in forms that a busy citizen can actually read. Each of these options carries hazards, and money from the very governments that journalists are meant to watch carries the most obvious one. But a democracy that leaves the observation of its local governments to chance should not be surprised when those governments begin to behave as if no one is looking."]
difficulty_reason: A case leading to a general point, with an objection answered and a concession against nostalgia; the central mechanism (deterrence by observation) is explained by analogy.

subtopic: Voters' rational ignorance is not cured by information shortcuts, whose reliability depends on the political environment, but that dependence argues for improving the cues rather than rationing the vote.
paragraphs: ["That most citizens know little about the policies they vote on is one of the most frequently confirmed observations about modern democracies, and one of the least surprising. A single vote almost never decides an election, and the hours needed to master the details of tax law or trade policy are hours taken from work, family and sleep. Ignorance, in these circumstances, is not a failure of character. It is what a sensible person would choose if he or she treated the vote as a decision with private costs and a vanishingly small chance of making a difference. Economists call this rational ignorance, and the label is apt: the problem is not that voters reason badly but that they have little reason to acquire what good reasoning would need.", "Two very different conclusions are drawn from this. The first, which has gained a certain academic following, is that the franchise should be weighted towards those who know more, since a decision made by the informed is likely to be better than one made by everyone. The second, more common among defenders of democracy, is that ignorance matters less than it seems, because voters rely on shortcuts. They need not study a programme if they know which party proposed it; they need not understand monetary policy to notice whether prices are rising; they can follow the advice of an organisation they trust. A voter equipped with such cues, the argument goes, can vote much as she would if she were fully informed.", "The second conclusion is more attractive than the first, but it claims too much. A shortcut is only as good as the connection between the cue and the thing the voter actually cares about, and that connection is not guaranteed. Party labels are informative when parties are stable and their programmes distinct; when parties fragment or converge, the label says little. Judging a government by how things are going is reasonable if the government controls how things are going, but voters who punish an incumbent for a drought, or for a downturn that began abroad, are using a cue that measures luck as much as competence. And an endorsement is valuable only if the endorser shares the voter's interests, which is precisely what a well-funded campaign may try to disguise. Shortcuts, in short, do not make ignorance harmless; they make its effects depend on the environment in which voters find themselves.", "That dependence, however, is also the strongest reply to those who would ration the vote. If the quality of popular judgement varies with the reliability of the cues available, then the natural remedy is to improve the cues rather than to disqualify the people who use them. Parties with clear and lasting identities, intermediaries whose interests are visible, a press that reports what governments actually control: each of these makes ordinary shortcuts more trustworthy. Weighting votes by knowledge, by contrast, would leave the environment of cues untouched while inviting a quarrel, unlikely ever to be settled impartially, about who should set the test and what it should contain.", "Neither side, then, has quite grasped the problem. The critics are right that an uninformed electorate can be misled, and the defenders are right that citizens need not be experts to judge well. What both overlook is that the competence of voters is not a fixed property of individuals but partly a product of institutions, and that a democracy can therefore make its citizens wiser as voters without making any of them more learned."]
difficulty_reason: Comparison of two opposed views, each partly rejected, with the author's position emerging only from a reversal in paragraph 4 and a synthesis in paragraph 5.

subtopic: Neutrality for small states is best understood not as moral evasion but as a demanding strategy for staying out of wars, though it guarantees nothing.
paragraphs: ["Neutrality has a poor reputation among people who think seriously about war. To its critics it looks like a refusal to choose, a way for a small state to sit out the great moral contests of its time while others pay the price of deciding them. On this view the neutral is a free rider at best and a quiet collaborator at worst, trading with whichever side is winning and calling its caution a principle. The charge is not baseless, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what neutrality has usually been for the states that practised it with any success.", "For a small country surrounded by larger ones, neutrality is less a moral posture than a strategy, and a demanding one. Its purpose is to remove the country from the calculations of its neighbours, to persuade each of them that the territory will never be used as a road or a base by the others. That persuasion does not come from declarations. It has to be earned through a long record of evenhanded conduct, through refusing favours that would look like alignment, and, above all, through an army strong enough to make occupation expensive. The neutral that cannot defend its borders is not neutral in any meaningful sense; it is simply unclaimed, and unclaimed ground in wartime is soon claimed.", "Seen this way, neutrality is not passivity but a continuous effort of a particular kind. The neutral state must be ready to resist whichever side violates its frontier first, which means it must arm against all of its neighbours at once rather than against one. It must also be disciplined in peacetime, since a single treaty of friendship, a preferential trade deal or a careless remark by a minister can be read abroad as a signal of where it would stand in a crisis. Few alliances ask as much of their members as this solitary commitment asks of a country that has chosen it.", "None of this guarantees success. Neutrality works only so long as the great powers judge that respecting it costs them less than violating it, and when a neutral's territory becomes essential to someone's war plans, even a well-armed and scrupulous record may count for little. Nor does the strategic defence settle every moral question; a neutral that profits handsomely from a war it claims to stand apart from invites the suspicion its critics voice. But the critics usually ask the wrong question. They ask whether neutrality is admirable, when the more useful question is whether, for a particular state in a particular place, it is the course most likely to keep that state's people out of a war they could not win."]
difficulty_reason: A clear claim-and-reply structure with concrete reasoning and a plainly marked concession in the last paragraph.

subtopic: Whether a peace settlement lasts depends less on its severity or generosity than on whether its terms match the balance of strength and are enforced.
paragraphs: ["Few historical lessons are repeated as confidently as the one drawn from the settlement that followed the First World War. A harsh peace, the lesson runs, breeds resentment, and resentment breeds the next war; a generous peace, by contrast, turns yesterday's enemy into tomorrow's partner. The lesson is attractive because it joins morality to prudence. It tells victors that magnanimity is not only noble but wise, and that they can secure the future simply by being kind. It also offers a single, memorable explanation for one of the great catastrophes of the last century, and explanations of that kind are hard to dislodge once they have settled into textbooks and speeches.", "The trouble is that the record does not sort so neatly. Some severe settlements have held for generations, because the defeated party was too weak to overturn them and the victors remained willing to enforce their terms. Some lenient ones have failed, because the loser read leniency as a sign that it had not really been beaten and that a second attempt might succeed. What such cases suggest is that severity and generosity are the wrong variables to watch. A settlement lasts when its terms match the actual balance of strength, and when the powers that wrote it remain prepared to uphold it.", "By this measure, the worst settlement is not the harshest but the one that combines harsh terms with a weak will to enforce them. Such a peace gives the defeated every reason to resent the order and no reason to fear challenging it. Its demands are heavy enough to humiliate, yet the victors, tired of war and divided among themselves, let them be evaded piece by piece, until the settlement has lost both its authority and its power to deter. Much of the interwar story can be told in this way, as a failure less of severity than of follow-through.", "This is not an argument for cruelty dressed up as realism. Generosity has a real role, but it works best after the defeat has been made unmistakable, when it can be read as the confidence of a winner rather than the hesitation of a power unsure of its victory. Offering a defeated state a path back into the community of nations, through trade, membership of institutions and the eventual lifting of restrictions, gives it a stake in the order that no amount of punishment can create. The point is only that kindness must rest on a settlement that is clear about who won and is backed by someone willing to say so."]
difficulty_reason: A familiar lesson is stated and then corrected in plain steps; the concession in the last paragraph is clearly signalled.

subtopic: Economic sanctions often strengthen the regimes they target because hardship does not turn into political pressure, so they should be judged by leverage rather than by the pain they cause.
paragraphs: ["Economic sanctions are usually defended with a simple theory of pressure: cut a country off from markets, credit and imported goods, and its people will suffer; suffering people will blame their rulers; and rulers who fear their own people will eventually change course. Each link in this chain sounds plausible, and the whole has the further appeal of offering governments something to do that is stronger than protest and safer than war, a way of being seen to act without asking anyone to fight. Yet the chain breaks more often than its defenders admit, and it tends to break in the same place.", "The weak link is the assumption that hardship flows upward as political pressure. In a country whose government controls the press and the police, scarcity is easier to explain than to resist. The regime can present the shortages as the work of hostile foreigners, and the explanation is the more convincing for being partly true. Scarcity also hands the state new powers, which it is seldom slow to use. When imported medicine, fuel or spare parts become rare, whoever controls their distribution acquires a means of rewarding loyalty and punishing dissent. Meanwhile the groups best placed to demand change, the educated and the commercially minded, are often the first to emigrate or to be impoverished into silence. Far from loosening the regime's grip, sanctions can tighten it.", "The usual response is to make sanctions smarter: to target the assets and travel of named officials rather than the economy as a whole. This is a genuine improvement, since it spares ordinary people some of the cost and aims the pain at those who actually decide. But targeted measures have limits of their own, and those limits are not trivial. Powerful individuals rarely hold their wealth in their own names, and a regime under pressure learns quickly to route its money through intermediaries. Targeting reduces the moral cost of sanctions more reliably than it increases their effect.", "What the record suggests is that sanctions are often judged by the wrong measure. Their defenders point to the damage done, the fall in output and the collapse of the currency, as if these were evidence of pressure. They are evidence only of pain, and pain is not the same as leverage. Sanctions change policy when they alter the calculations of the people who make it, which usually requires that they be paired with a clear and credible offer of what will be lifted in return for what. A measure that hurts but promises nothing gives a government little reason to move, and some reason to dig in."]
difficulty_reason: A causal chain is taken apart link by link, with a concession about targeted sanctions and an abstract distinction between pain and leverage.

subtopic: Stable mutual nuclear deterrence may make lower-level conflict safer to start, so deterrence secures the absence of one kind of war rather than peace in general.
paragraphs: ["Among the arguments made for nuclear deterrence, the strongest is also the simplest: when two states can each destroy the other, neither can hope to gain from a general war, and so neither starts one. Whatever its moral costs, a balance of terror of this kind has a claim to have kept the largest powers from fighting each other directly for a long time. But the logic that makes the largest war unthinkable may make smaller ones more thinkable, and this possibility, sometimes called the stability-instability paradox, deserves more attention than the reassuring half of the argument usually receives.", "The reasoning runs as follows. If both sides are confident that neither will ever risk a nuclear exchange, then each can assume that a limited clash, whether a border skirmish, a proxy war or a raid by irregular forces, will stay limited. The fear that once restrained such ventures, the fear that they might spiral into catastrophe, is weakened precisely by the confidence that catastrophe will be avoided. Stability at the top of the ladder of escalation thus loosens the rungs near the bottom. A state that would never dare a full invasion may feel free to probe, provoke and nibble, reasoning that its opponent will not answer with anything that could lead to the unthinkable.", "It is important to be precise about what this claims. It does not say that nuclear weapons cause small wars, which have many causes and were common long before such weapons existed. It says only that mutual deterrence can lower the perceived risk of low-level aggression and so remove one brake on it. Nor does the paradox operate automatically. Its force depends on how confident each side is that escalation can be controlled. Where leaders doubt that a skirmish can be kept small, the old fear returns, and with it some of the old caution.", "The implication is uncomfortable for those who credit deterrence with keeping the peace. What deterrence may secure is not peace in general but the absence of one particular kind of war, while the violence that remains is pushed downward and outward, into contested borderlands and into the hands of proxies. That is no small achievement, given what the alternative might be, and nothing in the paradox implies that the world would be safer if the largest powers could once again contemplate fighting each other directly. But the achievement should be described accurately. A system that prevents catastrophe partly by making lesser conflicts safer to start is not a system of peace; it is a way of choosing which wars will be fought."]
difficulty_reason: An abstract strategic argument with a careful statement of what the claim does and does not say; the stance is qualified.

subtopic: Critics are right that soldiers of an aggressor lack a true moral right to kill, but the legal equality of combatants is a justified convention because any rule tracking the justice of causes would make war more savage.
paragraphs: ["The laws of war rest on a premise that, stated baldly, can seem scandalous. A soldier who fights for an aggressor and a soldier who fights to repel him are held to have exactly the same rights on the battlefield: each may lawfully kill enemy combatants, each must spare civilians and prisoners, and neither commits a crime merely by taking part. Whether the war itself was just, a question settled, if at all, by the cause for which it was begun, is treated as irrelevant to how it may be fought. The justice of going to war and justice in the conduct of war are kept in separate compartments, and the ordinary soldier is answerable only for the second.", "Philosophical critics have pressed hard on this separation, and their central argument is difficult to resist. Outside war, we do not think that someone who attacks without justification acquires a right to kill those who resist him; a robber who is fired on by the guard he is trying to overpower may not shoot back and call it self-defence. Why should the matter change when the attacker wears a uniform and acts on orders? If the right to kill in war derives, as it must, from the right to defend against an unjust threat, then those who pose the unjust threat seem to have no such right at all. On this view, the soldier of an aggressor state who kills a defending soldier does wrong, however scrupulously he observes the rules of conduct.", "I think the critics are right about the underlying morality and wrong about what follows for the laws of war. Rules for the conduct of hostilities must be followed by people who are frightened, poorly informed and dependent on their own government's account of why they are fighting. Nearly every belligerent believes, or is told, that its cause is just. A rule that granted the right to kill only to soldiers on the just side would therefore be claimed by both sides, and would offer no restraint precisely where restraint is most needed; worse, it would invite each side to treat captured enemies as criminals rather than as prisoners. The symmetry of the laws of war is not a judgement that both sides are equally innocent. It is a convention adopted because the alternative would make war more savage without making it more just.", "Conceding this does not license the conclusion that soldiers bear no responsibility for the wars they fight. A convention that withholds legal blame is not a certificate of moral innocence, and there will be wars whose injustice is so plain that an ordinary soldier could see it and ought to refuse. The doctrine of equality is best understood not as a truth about the morality of killing but as a practical arrangement that we maintain, knowingly, because it does more to limit the horror of war than any rule that tracked the moral truth more closely could do."]
difficulty_reason: The author agrees with the critics on one level and disagrees on another; the stance depends on keeping moral truth and legal convention apart.

subtopic: Collective security and the balance of power each fail alone, the first because states will not bear its costs and the second because it ignores justice, so lasting orders combine them.
paragraphs: ["Collective security is one of those ideas that seem obviously right until one asks what they require. The principle is that an attack on any member of an international system is to be treated as an attack on all, so that every aggressor faces the combined strength of everyone else. Against this, the older practice of the balance of power looks cynical: states align against whichever power threatens to dominate, and they change sides as readily as the threat shifts, guided by interest rather than by any judgement about who is in the right.", "The appeal of collective security lies in its impartiality, and so does its weakness. For the scheme to work, states must be willing to fight an aggressor regardless of who it is, which means fighting, if necessary, a friend, a major trading partner or a power whose goodwill they need elsewhere. They must also be willing to fight over places where they have no interest at all, because the principle admits no distinction between an attack that matters to them and one that does not. This is a great deal to ask of governments that answer to their own citizens, and the interwar experience suggests that, when the moment came, many would not pay the price. An organisation founded on the principle found its members ready to condemn aggression and reluctant to resist it.", "The balance of power asks less and so delivers more reliably, at least within its narrower aims. It does not require states to care about aggression as such, only about the rise of a power that could threaten them, and so it draws on motives that governments actually have. But its reliability comes at a price. Because it attends only to the distribution of strength, it is indifferent to the fate of small states whose conquest does not upset the balance; it can tolerate, and has often arranged, the partition of a weak country as a way of keeping the strong ones satisfied. Stability is its aim, and justice enters only by accident.", "The lesson is not that one principle should replace the other, but that each supplies what the other lacks. A norm against aggression, however imperfectly enforced, gives resistance to an expanding power a public justification and makes it easier to assemble allies who would hesitate to act on calculation alone. Balancing, in turn, supplies the motive that the norm cannot generate by itself. Orders that have lasted have usually combined the two, borrowing their legitimacy from the first and their enforcement from the second, and the mistake of the reformers who championed collective security was to imagine that legitimacy could do the work of both."]
difficulty_reason: A comparison of two principles with criticism of each and a synthesis; abstract but clearly signposted.

subtopic: Recasting sovereignty as a forfeitable responsibility does not resolve the conflict with humanitarian intervention but relocates it to the question of who decides, leaving a choice between two kinds of failure.
paragraphs: ["For much of the modern period the doctrine of sovereignty was understood as a wall. Within its borders a state was answerable to no outside authority, and what it did to its own population, however terrible, was a matter of domestic jurisdiction. The rule had a defensible rationale. A world in which any power could enter another's territory whenever it disapproved of how that territory was governed would be a world of permanent intervention, in which the strong would always find reasons to correct the weak. Non-interference was less a tribute to the virtue of governments than a device for keeping their quarrels within bounds.", "The atrocities of the late twentieth century made the wall look like a shield for murderers, and a new formula emerged to reconcile the old principle with the demand to act. Sovereignty, it was argued, is not a privilege but a responsibility: a state holds it on condition that it protects its people, and a state that massacres them, or cannot stop others from doing so, forfeits its claim to be left alone. The formula is elegant, because it seems to dissolve the conflict rather than adjudicate it. Intervention to stop mass killing no longer violates sovereignty, since the sovereignty in question has already been forfeited.", "The elegance is partly an illusion. The formula does not remove the hard question but relocates it. Someone must still decide when a government has failed badly enough to forfeit its rights, and in practice that someone is usually the state or coalition proposing to intervene, which is to say a party with interests of its own in the outcome. The old doctrine at least gave a clear answer to the question of who may enter: nobody. The new one replaces that answer with a judgement, and judgements made by the powerful about the weak have a history that should make anyone cautious. It is not a cynical point that intervention has tended to occur where the interveners had strategic reasons to be and not elsewhere; it is an observation about how a discretionary rule will be used.", "None of this is an argument for returning to the wall. A principle that obliged the world to watch a massacre it could stop would purchase order at a price few would accept once they had seen what it meant. The question is not whether sovereignty may ever yield, but how the decision that it should yield is to be made credible. Here the procedure matters as much as the facts. An intervention authorised by a broad body of states, through rules that apply to friends as well as to enemies, carries a legitimacy that one undertaken by a single power on its own assessment cannot, even when the atrocities alleged are equally real.", "The difficulty is that procedure can fail in the other direction. The bodies most able to confer legitimacy are also those in which a single interested member can block action, and the insistence on proper authorisation can become a reason for doing nothing while the killing continues. There is no formula that escapes this. A world that refuses all unauthorised intervention will sometimes stand by when it should act, and a world that permits it will sometimes see intervention used as a pretext. The honest position is to admit that we are choosing which of these failures to risk, and to stop pretending that a change of vocabulary has spared us the choice."]
difficulty_reason: Five paragraphs that move through a doctrine, its reform, a critique of the reform, a concession and a counter-concession; the author's final stance is a tragic choice rather than a solution.

subtopic: Because measures that ease the fear of abandonment in an alliance worsen the fear of entrapment, deliberate ambiguity is a rational instrument, though one that carries a hidden risk of miscalculation.
paragraphs: ["Every alliance contains a quiet bargain between two fears. A state that joins an alliance worries, on the one hand, that its partner will fail it when it is attacked: this is the fear of abandonment. It worries, on the other, that its partner will drag it into a war it has no wish to fight, over interests that are not its own: this is the fear of entrapment. The two fears pull in opposite directions, and much of what passes for the routine management of alliances, the ministerial visits, the joint statements, the careful wording of guarantees, is an effort to keep them in tolerable balance.", "The difficulty is that almost anything done to ease one fear aggravates the other. A state that tightens its commitment, by stationing troops on its partner's soil or promising automatic assistance, reassures the partner that it will not be abandoned. But the same assurance may embolden the partner to take risks it would otherwise avoid, confident that its ally will be obliged to follow. Loosening the commitment has the opposite effect: it restrains the partner, but it also invites the partner to doubt the alliance and perhaps to look for other friends, or to arm in ways that alarm its neighbours. There is no setting of the dial at which both fears disappear, and governments that search for one tend to lurch between them, reassuring an anxious ally one year and reining in an emboldened one the next.", "For this reason, the ambiguity of many alliance commitments, often criticised as a failure of nerve, is better seen as a deliberate instrument. A guarantee that is firm enough to deter an adversary but vague about the circumstances in which it will be honoured leaves the protecting power room to judge whether its partner has provoked the crisis. The partner, uncertain whether reckless conduct will be supported, has reason to be careful; the adversary, uncertain whether aggression will be resisted, has reason to be careful too. Consider a hypothetical great power that promises to defend an island partner but declines to say whether the promise covers a dispute the partner itself might start. The silence is not an oversight. It is the policy.", "The balance between the two fears is rarely the same for both members. A small state facing a powerful neighbour usually fears abandonment far more than entrapment, since it has few other places to turn, while its larger protector, with interests elsewhere and wars it would prefer not to fight, tends to fear entrapment more. Much of the friction within alliances that look harmonious from outside comes from this asymmetry: the junior partner asks for firmer pledges, the senior partner resists giving them, and each suspects the other of bad faith when each is in fact responding sensibly to its own position.", "Ambiguity is not free, however. Its value depends on each party reading the uncertainty in the way the protecting power intends, and there is no guarantee that they will. An adversary may conclude that a vague commitment is a hollow one and test it, discovering too late that it was real. A partner may conclude that it will be supported whatever it does, because it cannot imagine its patron allowing it to fall. Deliberate vagueness thus trades the visible risks of a firm commitment for the hidden risk of miscalculation, which is the more dangerous for being invisible until a crisis reveals it. The strategy rewards a protecting power that understands both its partner and its adversary well, and punishes one that merely hopes it does."]
difficulty_reason: A clearly defined dilemma is developed into a defence of ambiguity and then qualified; the concepts are abstract but well signposted.

subtopic: The great periodic fairs mattered less as large markets for goods than as fixed occasions for settling credit and exchanging commercial information.
paragraphs: ["It is tempting to picture the great periodic fair of the pre-modern world as a market that happened to be very large. Merchants arrived with bales of cloth, casks and livestock; buyers came from the surrounding districts; for a few weeks a meadow outside a town became a crowded street of stalls, and then it emptied again until the following year. On this view the fair existed because trade was too thin to support permanent shops, and it faded once towns grew large enough to sustain them. The account is not wrong, but it describes the visible part of the fair and mistakes it for the whole.", "Much of what happened at a fair left no bales behind. Merchants who met there once or twice a year used the occasion to settle accounts that had been running since the previous meeting, cancelling what one owed another against what a third owed the first, so that relatively little coin had to change hands. Promises to pay at the next fair circulated as a kind of credit, and their value rested on the expectation that everyone would return. A fair, in this sense, was a calendar as much as a place: it fixed the dates on which obligations fell due and gave distant traders a reason to keep faith with one another. A merchant who failed to appear risked more than a season's sales; he risked his standing with every partner who had expected to meet him.", "It was also a clearing house for news. Prices in distant regions, the solvency of a trading house, a harvest failure, rumours of war: all of this travelled with the people who came, and a merchant who stayed at home was not only missing customers but trading blind. The gossip of the fair was not idle. It was the means by which a scattered commercial world kept a rough common picture of itself. A thinly attended fair was therefore a loss twice over, since the absence of buyers was also an absence of reports, and those who controlled the best information often profited more than those who carried the most goods.", "Seen this way, the decline of the great fairs looks different. Permanent shops certainly took over much of the retail business, but the deeper loss was of the fair's other functions, which passed to institutions that did not depend on bodily presence: banks that kept accounts all year round, regular postal services and, later, printed lists of prices. None of this means that fairs ceased to matter as markets; many survived for centuries as places to buy animals or household goods. What they lost was their role as the hinge on which a whole year of commerce turned, and that role had never been visible in the stalls."]
difficulty_reason: Clear claim-and-correction structure with concrete examples and an explicit concession; vocabulary is plain.

subtopic: Because the pre-industrial household was a workplace, laments about the decline of the family mistake a change in the household's functions for a loss of family feeling.
paragraphs: ["Few ideas feel more natural than the distinction between home and work. We leave one for the other in the morning and return in the evening, and much of our moral vocabulary depends on the contrast: home is where we are valued for who we are, work where we are valued for what we produce. Yet for most of recorded history, in most agrarian and artisan societies, the distinction would have puzzled the people who lived in households. The house was where the work was done.", "Consider a weaver's dwelling in a pre-industrial town, or a farmstead in the countryside. The looms or the dairy stood beside the hearth, and the people who ate at the table included not only parents and children but apprentices, servants and labourers who lived under the same roof and the same authority.
