The essay at its best is therefore not the opposite of argument but argument conducted in the open, where the reader can see each step taken and judge for herself whether it holds."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract argument comparing two forms, with an embedded concession in paragraph 2, a defence of the first person, and a final limit on the thesis; the stance must be traced across five paragraphs.

subtopic: Serial publication should not be treated only as an excuse for the faults of nineteenth-century novels; it also produced their virtues, and the unified-design standard used against it is anachronistic.
paragraphs: ["Many of the long novels of the nineteenth century first reached their readers not as books but in instalments, issued monthly or weekly over a year or more, in magazines or in separate parts. Modern criticism has tended to treat this fact as an extenuating circumstance. When such a novel sprawls, introduces a character it later forgets, or closes a chapter on a contrived moment of suspense, the serial is invoked as an excuse: the author was writing to deadline, paid by length, obliged to bring readers back next month. The implication is that the real novel, the one the author would have written in better conditions, lies somewhere beneath the one we have, and that serial publication is a kind of noise to be filtered out.", "The trouble with this view is that it treats the serial only as a set of pressures, when it was also a set of possibilities, and many of the qualities we now admire in these books grew from it. A novel read over eighteen months is lived with in a way that a novel read over a week is not. Its characters age alongside their readers; its crises arrive amid the readers' own. The large casts and interwoven plots that later critics found unwieldy were in part a response to this rhythm, since a reader returning after a month's absence needed several lines of interest to pick up, and recurring figures with distinctive habits of speech helped her find her place. What looks in a single volume like digression could, at the pace of first reading, serve as the texture of a world one returned to.", "Serial publication also made the novel unusually public while it was still unfinished. An instalment could be discussed before the next was written, and authors could, and sometimes did, adjust their plans in light of how readers responded. A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control. It can as easily be seen as a kind of conversation, in which a book took shape partly through its encounter with an audience rather than being delivered complete to readers whose only role was to receive it. For a time the novel became a shared event, followed by readers who knew that a great many others were reading the same pages in the same weeks.", "None of this is to deny the costs. Writing to fixed lengths did produce padding, and the demand for suspense at the end of each part did produce cliffhangers that the story did not need and that read awkwardly once the parts were bound together. A reader of the collected volume is entitled to notice these. What deserves suspicion is the standard against which they are judged as failures: the ideal of the novel as a single, unified design, conceived whole and executed according to plan. That ideal has a history of its own, and it gained much of its authority later, among writers and critics who worked for a different market and under different conditions. Applied backward, it does not so much reveal the faults of serial fiction as convert its differences into faults.", "There is, finally, an irony in the critical embarrassment. Long television dramas, released in episodes and discussed between them, are now often praised by critics for the very qualities, the slow accumulation, the large cast, the sense of a world lived alongside, that the instalment novel was once thought to need excusing for. Nothing about the newer form proves the older one right, and a slack episode is no better for belonging to a celebrated series. But the shift in judgement suggests that what critics of the instalment novel took for timeless standards of form were, at least in part, the habits of one particular way of reading."]
difficulty_reason: A history of a critical attitude, with a substantial concession and a claim about an anachronistic standard; the stance shifts from defence to critique of the standard itself.

subtopic: Lists of untranslatable words show only that languages package meanings differently; translation always loses something, but by degree, not by kind.
paragraphs: ["Few kinds of article travel as easily as the list of untranslatable words. A language is said to possess a single word for the particular light that falls through leaves, another for the guilty pleasure of buying books one will never read, a third for the melancholy of a Sunday evening, and the reader is invited to marvel that English, or whatever language the list happens to be written in, has nothing to match them. The lists are charming, and most of the words in them are real. What is doubtful is the conclusion they are usually taken to support: that the speakers of a language without such a word cannot quite have the experience it names, or that a vocabulary is a window onto a national soul.", "Look at what the lists actually demonstrate. Each entry pairs a foreign word with a sentence or two of English explaining it, and the explanation is usually clear enough that the reader recognises the experience at once, often with a small shock of familiarity. The list, in other words, translates every word it calls untranslatable. What it shows is not that a meaning cannot cross from one language to another but that one language packages in a single word what another expresses in a phrase. That is a fact about how vocabularies happen to be divided up, and it tells us very little about what their speakers are able to think or feel. Every language lacks single words for countless things its speakers understand perfectly well.", "This is not to say that nothing is lost when such a word is carried across. A single word is easy to reach for; a phrase is not. A word that ordinary speakers use daily carries the weight of all those uses, along with a register, a sound and a set of associations that no paraphrase reproduces. The very existence of the word suggests that a community has found the experience worth naming, and that fact is itself a small piece of cultural information. For a translator working on a poem, where sound and compression matter as much as sense, these losses are real and constant, and no amount of explanation in a footnote restores them.", "But the losses are of degree, not of kind, and they are not peculiar to exotic words. They occur whenever any word is rendered by another, and even within a single language, where no two synonyms carry quite the same associations. Seen this way, the romance of the untranslatable flatters the reader, who feels worldly for knowing the rare word, and it encourages a picture of cultures as sealed rooms whose inhabitants can only be gazed at, never understood. The more modest and more accurate lesson is that translation is always possible and never complete, and that its difficulties lie less in the dictionary than in everything a word drags along with it."]
difficulty_reason: A single clear thesis stated early, a signposted concession and a plain conclusion; vocabulary is everyday.

subtopic: Judging film adaptations by how few details they change is confused; fidelity means finding the film's own means to do what the book did.
paragraphs: ["Whenever a much-loved novel reaches the screen, a familiar verdict follows: the book was better. Behind the verdict there usually lies a checklist. Was the heroine's age changed, a subplot dropped, a minor character merged with another, the ending softened? Each departure is counted as a fault, and the best adaptation, on this view, is simply the one that departs least, as though the novel were a fixed list of facts and the film an attempt, more or less competent, to copy that list onto a different surface. The habit is understandable, since readers who love a book feel protective of it, but as a standard for judging films it rests on a confusion about what an adaptation is.", "A novel and a film do not tell stories in the same way. A novel can spend twenty pages inside a character's head; a film must find something for the camera to look at. A novel handles time loosely, lingering or summarising as it likes, while a film runs at a pace the viewer cannot slow. To reproduce a book's events faithfully is therefore no guarantee of reproducing what the book does. Imagine a novel narrated by a man whose account of himself the reader slowly learns to distrust. A film that simply stages the events he describes, shot plainly and from the outside, may keep every incident and still lose the book entirely, because the book was never really about the incidents but about the gap between what the narrator says and what the reader comes to see.", "Conversely, an adaptation that alters a good deal may be truer to its source. A director who invents a visual device to unsettle our trust in what we are shown, framing scenes so that the viewer begins to doubt them, has understood that novel better than one who preserves its plot to the letter. The right question is not how much was kept but whether the film has found its own means of doing what the book did.", "None of this means that every liberty is defensible. Some adaptations borrow a famous title for its prestige and its ready-made audience while discarding everything that made the book worth adapting, and the complaint against them is fair. But it is fair for a different reason than the checklist suggests. Such films fail not because they changed things but because they changed the wrong things, keeping the label and throwing away the substance. Fidelity, properly understood, is a matter of purpose rather than of inventory, and judging it requires the critic to say what a book was for before complaining about what a film has left out."]
difficulty_reason: Familiar subject, a clear thesis, one extended hypothetical example and an explicit concession.

subtopic: Negative criticism is worth its space because it makes standards public and gives praise meaning, though restraint suits obscure books.
paragraphs: ["A respectable argument holds that negative criticism of new books is a waste of everyone's time. So many books are published each year that no critic can notice more than a sliver of them; the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious, and to spend it explaining why a book is bad is to deny it to a book that deserves attention. On this view the most damning verdict a critic can deliver is silence. A poor book left unmentioned simply sinks, and nothing is lost except the pleasure that some critics take in wounding. The position has the further appeal of seeming kind, which is no small recommendation in a literary world where writers and critics are often the same people.", "The argument is tidy, but it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read. If that were so, the notice of a weak book would indeed be wasted, since a reader who is told merely to skip something has learned nothing that he could use elsewhere. But criticism has always done something besides sorting. A careful account of why a book fails is also an account of what success would have looked like, and in giving it the critic makes public a set of standards that readers can test, dispute and apply for themselves. The reader who follows a well-argued case against a novel he admired may end unconvinced, yet he will read the next novel more alertly.", "There is a further cost to silence. If critics write only about the books they admire, praise becomes the sole currency of criticism, and like any currency issued without limit it loses its value. A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way. Readers soon learn to discount it, as they discount the admiring phrases printed on the cover of every new book, and the critic whose praise is sincere is then heard no more clearly than the publicist. The possibility of dispraise is what gives praise its meaning.", "None of this licenses cruelty, and the case for restraint does have force in one kind of instance. A modest first novel from a small press, which few people will encounter anyway, gains nothing from a public demolition, and neither do its readers. The negative notice earns its space when the book in question is prominent: widely praised, heavily promoted, or likely to shape what others write. There the critic who dissents is not kicking someone who is down but contesting a reputation that is already shaping public taste, and that is among the most useful things criticism can do."]
difficulty_reason: Claim and objection structure with an exposed assumption, an economic metaphor and a closing qualification that limits the thesis.

subtopic: A canon is better understood as the record of which works later writers answered than as a ranking of quality, though that conversation had its own exclusions.
paragraphs: ["Arguments about the literary canon are usually conducted as arguments about a list. One side defends a set of books as the best that a tradition has produced; the other replies that the list was drawn up by a narrow group of readers and reflects their tastes and their blind spots. Both sides, for all their hostility, agree on what a canon is: a ranking, a roll of honour, a verdict on quality that can be revised by adding names or striking them out. It is worth asking whether that shared assumption is right.", "A different account fits the actual history of canons better. On this account a work becomes canonical not because readers judge it excellent but because later writers cannot leave it alone. They answer it, parody it, borrow its situations, quarrel with its conclusions and rewrite it from the point of view of a character it neglected. The canonical work is then the one you must have read in order to understand a great many others; its status is less a medal than a position in a network of replies. This explains something the list model cannot. Canons contain works that almost everyone agrees are clumsy, uneven or dull in long stretches, and they exclude works of great finish that simply provoked no answer. A ranking by quality would not look like that; a record of a conversation would.", "The account has a consequence for those who wish to change the canon. If canonical status is conferred by later writing rather than by verdict, then a syllabus committee cannot make a book canonical by placing it on a reading list, any more than a critic could remove one by declaring it overrated. What can be done is to put neglected works where future writers will meet them, in print, in translation and in the classroom, and then to wait and see whether they are taken up.", "Yet the conversational canon is not thereby cleared of the exclusions its critics describe. Who gets to join a conversation depends on who was taught to read, who could find a publisher and whose replies were preserved. A tradition in which most writers came from one class or one sex will have conducted its conversation largely among them, and the canon it produced will reflect that. The conversational account does not answer the critics of the canon; it relocates their complaint, from the judgements of tastemakers to the conditions under which people could write at all, and that is where the remedy, if there is one, must be sought."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of an assumption shared by two camps, an alternative model with an explanatory test, a practical consequence and a qualification.

subtopic: Translations of classics date because each must settle ambiguities the original leaves open, so retranslation is part of a classic's life, not a record of failure.
paragraphs: ["Translators of the great books of the past often remark on a puzzle. The original of an old epic or a classical tragedy does not seem to age; readers return to it century after century and find it as alive as ever. Yet translations of the same work date quickly. A version that seemed fresh to its first readers can sound stiff or quaint within a lifetime, and every generation or two a new one appears, prefaced by the claim that its predecessors have become unreadable. Why should the copy age when the original, which is older and in many ways stranger, does not? The question is worth more attention than it usually receives, because the answer says something about what a translation is.", "The usual answer is linguistic: a translation is written in the language of its own moment, with that moment's idioms and its notions of what sounds dignified and what sounds plain, and these change. The original, by contrast, has been absorbed into a tradition that reads it as a historical text and forgives its strangeness. There is truth in this, but it cannot be the whole story, since old translations are often perfectly intelligible and still feel inadequate.", "A deeper reason lies in what translation requires. A great work is full of places where its sense is undecided: a word that could mean anger or grief, a line whose tone could be mocking or tender, a scene whose moral weight is left to the reader. The original can leave such places open, and much of its power to sustain rereading comes from that openness; a translator has no such freedom, because writing in another language forces choices at every point, and each choice settles a question the original left unsettled. The choices are not arbitrary, but they are shaped by what the translator's own age finds plausible or important, and so the translation records one generation's reading of the work. When the concerns of that generation fade, its translation comes to look like what it always was: an interpretation.", "Seen in this light, retranslation is not a sign that earlier translators failed. It is one of the ways a classic stays alive, each version making a fresh set of decisions and so showing a new reader something the others concealed. There is even an occasional reversal. Some translations become works of literature in their own right, read not as windows onto the original but for their own sake, and these, curiously, stop ageing in the way translations usually do; they come to be read, like originals, as historical texts. Their choices no longer look like a period's reading of another book; they look like the permanent features of a book of their own."]
difficulty_reason: A puzzle, a partial answer, a deeper explanation and a reversal; the key distinction between linguistic and interpretive ageing must be held throughout.

subtopic: Intentionalists and anti-intentionalists share a mistaken picture of intention as a private event; the intentions criticism needs are public, embodied in the work's choices.
paragraphs: ["Few questions in criticism have been argued so long, or with so little sign of settlement, as whether the meaning of a work is what its author intended. The intentionalist says yes: a text is an utterance, utterances are made by someone for a purpose, and to ignore that purpose is to read not the work but a sequence of marks that happens to resemble it. The anti-intentionalist says no: the author's state of mind is usually unavailable, frequently confused and in any case beside the point, since a published work belongs to the public language in which it was written, and its meaning is whatever that language, competently read, makes of it.", "Each side wins its arguments by making the other's view look absurd, and each is right about what it denies. The intentionalist is right that we cannot read without attributing purposes. To notice that a sentence is ironic, that a repetition is deliberate or that a sudden plainness of style marks a turning point is already to treat the text as the product of choices; strip away every assumption about purpose and the irony vanishes along with the design. The anti-intentionalist is right that a letter to a newspaper or a diary entry in which the author explains what the book means has no special authority over the book. Authors misremember, revise their motives after the fact and sometimes simply misjudge what they have made.", "The mistake common to both is to picture intention as a private event lying behind the text, which the text either reports faithfully or conceals. Intention in writing is better understood the way we understand it in action. We do not usually discover what someone meant by watching them and then consulting their inner life; we read the purpose in the shape of what they did. In the same way the intentions that matter to criticism are those embodied in a work's choices, its emphases and omissions, the expectations it sets up and then disappoints. They are public because the work is.", "This view does not make the author irrelevant, nor does it make the author final. A writer's notebooks may help us see a pattern we had missed, as the testimony of a witness may help a court, but the evidence is then the pattern, not the testimony. And a work may carry implications its author never foresaw and would perhaps have disowned: a novel written to celebrate a way of life can, through the very details it lovingly records, reveal the costs that way of life imposed on those at its margins. To point this out is not to defy the author's intention but to take the work's design more seriously than its author's later account of it."]
difficulty_reason: Two reported positions, each partly endorsed, followed by a reframing that rejects their shared premise; the author's own view is abstract and must be kept distinct from both.

subtopic: Rereading, not first reading, is where a book's design and the reader's own change become visible, though the first reading has effects of its own.
paragraphs: ["It is often said that a book can be read for the first time only once, and the remark is usually meant as a lament. On a first reading we do not know what will happen; we are carried by suspense, surprised by turns we did not foresee, and moved in a way that, the argument goes, can never quite be recovered. Rereading, on this view, is a kind of nostalgia: a return to a place whose excitement has been used up, pleasant perhaps, but a lesser thing than the original encounter. Schools encourage the same view without meaning to, since a syllabus moves on once a book has been 'done', as though a single passage through it were the whole of the work. The lament has real feeling behind it, and anyone who remembers staying up late to finish a novel knows what it describes.", "There is a case for the opposite view, that in an important sense only rereading is reading. A first reading is dominated by one question, what happens next, and that question consumes most of our attention. We skim descriptions to reach events, miss the significance of details whose importance has not yet been revealed and form judgements of characters that the book later overturns. Only when we know the ending can we attend to how the book reaches it: the early scene that quietly prepares a later one, the image that returns with altered meaning, the minor character whose remark, seemingly idle at first, turns out to state the novel's theme. Knowing the outcome does not empty these details; it fills them. Consider a novel built around a concealed secret. Read a second time, its hints, which at first seemed part of the scenery, stand out as hints, and the reader can admire the skill with which they were hidden in plain sight, a pleasure that the first reader, hurrying towards the revelation, could not have had.", "Rereading also reveals a change in the reader. The novel read at fifteen and again at forty has not altered a word, yet it is a different book, because the person reading it has acquired experiences that let different passages speak. A story of a marriage that seemed, to the young reader, a tale of dull people becomes, to the older one, almost unbearably exact. Nothing on the page has moved; what has moved is the range of experience the reader can bring to it, and with it the passages that seem to matter. In this sense a book reread is a kind of instrument for measuring oneself, and the measurements are often humbling: we discover what we were once unable to see, and sometimes that the passages we admired most were the weakest.", "None of this means that the first reading is worthless. It has a quality nothing later can supply, an innocence about what is coming that the writer counted on, and some effects are designed for it alone: the twist that recasts everything before it can surprise only once. Moreover, without a first reading there is nothing to reread, and the second encounter depends on the first even when it corrects it. Some books, indeed, are exhausted by one passage through them, and this is perhaps the most useful test of all. A book that offers nothing on a second reading was a mechanism for producing suspense, admirable in its way, while a book that gives more each time was something else. The difference between the two kinds is not visible from inside a first reading, which is one more reason to distrust the verdicts we reach there."]
difficulty_reason: A common view, its reversal, a second line of argument and a concession that becomes a test; moderately abstract but well signposted.

subtopic: Distant reading cannot interpret by itself; its value lies in posing questions for close reading and in testing claims drawn from an unrepresentative canon.
paragraphs: ["Literary history has always been written from a remarkably small sample. Of the many thousands of novels published in a given century, a scholar can read a few hundred in a working life, and the histories of the form are built on a smaller set still, the books that later readers chose to keep in print. When such a history says that 'the novel' turned inward at a certain period, or abandoned the omniscient narrator, or grew preoccupied with the city, it is generalising from a selection that was never meant to be representative. Nobody chose the canon as a sample; it was assembled by generations of readers for reasons of taste, teaching and accident, and there is no reason to expect it to resemble the whole from which it was drawn. The advocates of computational or 'distant' reading start from this embarrassment. If machines can process an entire century's output, counting words, tracking the length of sentences or the frequency with which characters are named, then claims about the form as a whole can at last be tested against the whole.", "The objections are familiar, and some are serious. Counting is not reading. The meaning of a word depends on its context, on irony, on the dramatic situation in which it is spoken, none of which a frequency table records. Critics add that many of the patterns such studies report are either trivial or confirm what attentive readers already knew, so that a great deal of machinery produces a modest result dressed in charts. There is also a subtler worry: the features a computer can count are those that can be defined mechanically, and these are not obviously the features that matter. A discipline that adopts such tools risks drifting towards studying what can be measured simply because it can be measured. Defenders of the method reply that every discipline begins by measuring crude things, but the reply concedes more than it denies.", "Yet much of this debate rests on a false picture of the choice. Distant reading does not replace close reading so much as change what close reading is asked to do. Its most interesting results are rarely the patterns themselves; they are the anomalies, the decade in which a measure behaves unexpectedly or the obscure novels that cluster with canonical ones on some feature nobody had thought to examine. A measure that shows some habit of style rising steadily for decades and then collapsing within a few years explains nothing by itself, but it tells a scholar exactly where to look. Such a finding means little until someone goes back and reads the books in question, and it is that return which produces understanding. The count poses a question; it does not answer one.", "Where the method does make an independent contribution is in the matter of the sample. Even if a computer can say little about what any single novel means, it can show that a generalisation drawn from the canon fails to hold for the much larger body of books that the canon left out. That is not a trivial service. A claim about what 'the novel' did, which turns out to describe only the few hundred books that survived into the syllabus, was never a claim about the novel at all, but about the tastes of the readers who did the selecting. The modest promise of distant reading, then, is less to tell us what literature means than to tell us more accurately which literature our claims are about."]
difficulty_reason: Dense argument that grants serious objections, reframes the debate and then isolates a narrower independent contribution; the final claim turns on sampling, an abstract point.

subtopic: A museum label should be judged not by how much it says but by whether it sends the visitor back to look at the work.
paragraphs: ["Few things in a museum are read as often, or looked at as little, as the wall label. Visitors approaching a painting frequently read the small panel beside it first, glance at the picture to confirm what they have been told, and move on. Curators have noticed this pattern for a long time, and it has produced two opposite reactions. One camp argues that labels should be shortened or removed altogether, so that the visitor is thrown back onto the object. The other argues that labels should be expanded, written in friendlier language and supplemented with audio guides and screens, since a public that does not know what it is looking at cannot be expected to care.", "Both reactions treat the label as though its only variable were quantity. The purist assumes that less text means more looking, but a visitor confronted by an unexplained altarpiece does not usually begin to look harder; more often she feels excluded and walks faster. The expansionist assumes that more text means more understanding, yet a long label that rehearses the artist's biography, the patron's family and the painting's later owners gives the visitor a great deal to know and very little to see. In each case the label is imagined as a container of facts, and the only argument is over how full the container should be.", "A better question is what the label asks the visitor to do. A label can close a picture, by telling the viewer what it means, or it can open it, by directing attention to something that can be checked against the canvas itself. Compare two sentences about the same imagined portrait. The first says that the sitter was a wealthy merchant who commissioned the work to celebrate his marriage. The second says that the merchant's left hand rests on a ledger while his right holds his wife's glove, and invites the reader to decide which hand the painter has lit more brightly. The first sentence can be absorbed without raising one's eyes; the second cannot be finished without looking.", "None of this means that historical information is a distraction. A viewer who does not know that a certain blue, ground from a semi-precious stone, was once among the costliest materials a painter could buy will miss part of what a patron was displaying when he asked for a sky full of it, and no amount of attentive looking will supply that fact. The point is that information earns its place on the wall when it changes what the visitor notices. Facts that merely sit beside the object, however accurate, belong in the catalogue, where they can be read at leisure by those who want them. The wall is too valuable, and the visitor's attention too brief, to be spent on anything else."]
difficulty_reason: Clear contrast of two camps followed by the author's reframing and a concession; concrete example and plain vocabulary.

subtopic: Permanent monuments end public discussion and so turn later disagreement into crisis, while temporary public art keeps a habit of collective judgement alive, though not every memorial should be temporary.
paragraphs: ["When a town decides to honour someone or something in public, its first instinct is usually to reach for bronze and stone. Durability is treated as a measure of respect: a statue meant to last for centuries seems to say more than a banner meant to last for a week. Yet the history of public art suggests that permanence is less a virtue than a wager, and frequently a losing one. A monument fixes one generation's judgement in a material that will outlast the judgement itself. Within a few decades the figure on the plinth may be unrecognised by most passers-by, and within a century it may be the cause of a quarrel its makers could not have imagined.", "The problem is not that later generations are fickle. It is that a permanent work is designed to end discussion rather than to take part in it. Once installed, it asks only to be accepted; there is no procedure built into it for being reconsidered. When disagreement finally arrives, it therefore arrives as a crisis, with petitions, counter-petitions and arguments over whether removal amounts to erasing history. A city that had expected its public art to change would face no such crisis, because it would already possess a habit of revisiting what stands in its squares.", "Temporary works offer one way of building that habit. A plinth that hosts a different commission every year or two, a sculpture placed in a park for a single season, a mural painted on the understanding that it will be painted over: each of these makes public art an occasion rather than a verdict. People argue about the new piece, grow fond of it or feel relieved to see it go, and in doing so they practise exactly the kind of collective judgement that a permanent statue forecloses. The work matters less as an object than as the conversation it starts.", "This argument has limits, and they should be stated. Temporary art can slide into novelty for its own sake, a rotating series of spectacles chosen to attract visitors rather than to say anything. And some public works aim at permanence for good reason: a memorial to the dead of a war or a disaster is meant to resist the passing of time, because forgetting is precisely the danger it guards against. The case against bronze is not a case against all lasting memorials. It is a case against the assumption that whatever a public wishes to honour must be honoured in a form that can never be questioned without a fight."]
difficulty_reason: A single clear thesis developed in order, with the limits flagged openly in the last paragraph; everyday examples.

subtopic: Cleaning old paintings often recovers real information, but because pigments also age it cannot restore an original state, so restorers should describe their work as reversible, documented interpretation.
paragraphs: ["Arguments about the cleaning of old paintings tend to repeat themselves with remarkable fidelity. A famous canvas is cleaned; the removal of darkened varnish reveals colours far brighter than anyone living has seen on it; and two parties form at once. One celebrates the recovery of what the painter actually intended, a picture freed from centuries of grime. The other mourns the loss of a mellow harmony that generations had loved, and suspects that the cleaners, in their zeal, have removed not only dirt but the delicate final glazes with which the painter softened his effects.", "It is tempting to treat this as a contest between truth and sentiment, with the cleaners on the side of truth. There is something to this. Natural resin varnishes do yellow and darken with age, and a sky that now looks olive may well have been painted as a clear blue; to prefer the olive because one is used to it is to prefer an accident over a decision. Cleaning has repeatedly shown that painters long thought murky were in fact bold colourists, and no honest account of the debate can pretend otherwise.", "Yet the cleaners' strongest claim, that they return the painting to its original state, is harder to sustain than it sounds. Pigments themselves change: some blues fade, some greens turn brown, some reds lose their glazes to light long before any restorer arrives. Removing the varnish from such a picture does not take it back to the day it left the studio; it produces a new object, one in which unchanged passages and altered ones sit side by side in proportions the painter never saw. The bright painting revealed by cleaning may therefore be no closer to the original than the dark one it replaced, only differently distant from it.", "What follows is not that cleaning should stop, but that it should be described honestly. Every restoration is a judgement about which of a painting's many histories to favour, and judgements can be wrong. The responsible course is to make such judgements in ways that can be undone where possible, to record exactly what has been removed and why, and to abandon the language of revelation in favour of the language of interpretation. A restorer who says 'this is what the painter meant' claims more than any evidence can give; one who says 'this is our best reading, and here is how we reached it' claims only what the craft can support."]
difficulty_reason: The author grants one side's point before undercutting its central claim; the key idea (a cleaned painting as a new object) is abstract.

subtopic: The fear of manipulated photographs distracts from the larger problem that even unaltered images are silent about what lies outside the frame, so their evidential value depends on their context.
paragraphs: ["Discussion of whether photographs can be trusted has long been dominated by the fear of manipulation. Early critics worried about staged scenes and retouched negatives; later ones about software that can add a figure to a crowd or remove one from a podium without leaving a trace visible to the eye. These worries are reasonable, and the tools that prompt them have become more powerful. But they direct attention to the least interesting way in which a photograph can mislead, and in doing so they leave the more ordinary and more pervasive problem almost untouched.", "Consider an unaltered photograph of a crowded square taken during a demonstration. Every figure in it was really there, standing exactly where the picture shows. The image is, in the narrow sense, entirely truthful. Yet it cannot tell us whether the square was full or whether the photographer stood at the one corner where people had gathered; whether the moment captured was typical of the afternoon or its single tense minute; whether the raised fists at the front belonged to protesters or to the counter-demonstration across the road. A photograph is accurate about what falls inside its frame and wholly silent about what falls outside it, and the frame is chosen by someone.", "This is why the manipulation debate can produce a false sense of security. A viewer who has learned to check for doctored pixels may conclude that an image which passes the check is reliable, when the check has said nothing about selection, timing or framing. An honest photograph can support a dishonest story as easily as a forged one can, and often more easily, since it will survive the very scrutiny that exposes a forgery.", "None of this makes photographs worthless as evidence. It means that their evidential value lies less in the single image than in its surroundings: the caption that states when and where it was taken, the other frames from the same roll or memory card, the identity and record of the person who took it, the existence of independent pictures of the same event. A photograph considered alone is a fragment that can be fitted into many stories. A photograph considered with these supports begins to narrow the stories it can serve. The question to ask of an image, then, is not only whether it has been altered but what would have to be true of everything around it for it to mean what it is said to mean."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief with an extended hypothetical; the key distinction (truthful image, misleading story) needs care.

subtopic: An auction price is neither a verdict on artistic value nor meaningless; it measures the desire to own, which tracks critical esteem only indirectly and becomes harmful when mistaken for a judgement of worth.
paragraphs: ["When a painting sells at auction for a sum that would fund a hospital, two responses compete for the headlines. The first treats the price as a verdict: the market, pooling the judgements of many informed buyers, has declared this one of the most important works of its kind. The second treats it as a scandal: the sum has nothing to do with art and everything to do with vanity, speculation and the search for places to park wealth. Each response captures something, but both share a mistaken premise, which is that the price is either a measure of artistic value or a measure of nothing at all.", "A price measures what someone will pay to own a thing, and owning a painting is not the same as valuing it as a painting. The buyer acquires an object that is unique, that cannot be reproduced without losing the very property being purchased, and that carries a name capable of conferring distinction on whoever holds it. Each of these features has a market logic of its own. Scarcity helps explain why a minor work by a celebrated painter can outsell a masterpiece by an obscure one; the name explains why a newly accepted attribution can multiply a canvas's price overnight without a single brushstroke changing. In neither case has anyone's experience of looking at the picture altered.", "This does not mean that prices float free of critical judgement. Over long periods, the artists whom critics, historians and museums take seriously tend also to be the ones whose works command high prices, and it would be perverse to call this coincidence. But the connection runs largely through reputation rather than through the works themselves: esteem builds a name, the name creates demand, and demand sets the price. The market thus registers critical judgement at second hand, much as a credit rating registers a company's prospects without being the same thing as its earnings.", "The real danger lies in the return journey. Once prices are reported as verdicts, they begin to shape the judgements they supposedly reflect. Visitors crowd around the record-breaking canvas while the room beside it stands empty; institutions hesitate to show or lend works whose insurance values have become unmanageable; young artists learn which styles sell. A measure of ownership, mistaken for a measure of worth, ends by teaching people what to look at. Resisting that confusion requires nothing more radical than remembering what a price is the price of."]
difficulty_reason: Rejects a false dichotomy and builds a causal chain with an analogy; moderately abstract economic reasoning.

subtopic: The loss of value when a forgery is exposed is not mere snobbery or delayed perception but reflects the fact that paintings are valued partly as achievements, which the forger's copy is not.
paragraphs: ["Suppose a painting has hung for decades in a museum, admired by critics and loved by visitors, and is then shown beyond doubt to be a forgery. Nothing about the canvas has changed: its colours and its composition are exactly as they were, and the pleasure that thousands took in it was genuine pleasure, not a misunderstanding awaiting correction. Yet the picture is taken down, its value collapses, and the critics who praised it are embarrassed. If what matters in a painting is what can be seen in it, this reaction looks irrational, a triumph of the label over the eye.", "Two familiar explanations are offered, and neither is adequate. The first says the reaction is mere snobbery: we cared about the famous name, not the picture, and the forgery has simply exposed the fact. There is truth here, since much of the fall in price reflects nothing loftier than the loss of a signature that could be resold. But the explanation proves too much; it implies that anyone who minds about the difference is a snob, including the scrupulous historian with no money at stake. The second says that the forgery must differ visibly after all, and that trained eyes, once alerted, can see its deadness. Sometimes this is so; yet the deadness is usually perceived only after the verdict is known, and a theory that can detect a difference only once it has been told where to look is not much of a theory.", "A more promising account begins from the thought that we value paintings not only as arrangements of colour but also as achievements. To admire a picture fully is partly to admire what was done in making it: a problem of light or space confronted at a particular moment, with the means then available, by someone who did not know how it would turn out. The forger faces a different problem, that of producing something that will pass as the solution to the first. The two canvases may look alike, but they answer different questions, and the exposure tells us that the question we thought we were admiring an answer to was never asked by this canvas at all.", "This view has a cost, and it should be admitted. It makes part of a painting's value depend on facts that cannot be seen in it, and so concedes that looking alone can never be the whole of appreciation. It also allows that a forgery may be a considerable achievement of its own kind, as a feat of imitation, without ranking it beside what it imitates. But the cost seems worth paying, because the alternative is to hold that the history of art could be rewritten, without loss, by anyone with a sufficiently skilful hand."]
difficulty_reason: Philosophical puzzle with two rejected explanations, each partly conceded, and an abstract positive account whose cost is acknowledged.

subtopic: For much of its history the commissioned portrait aimed to establish the sitter's position rather than reveal a personality, so the modern demand for psychological insight is one historical form of the genre, not its essence.
paragraphs: ["We tend to judge a portrait by asking whether it captures the person. A good portrait, on this view, reveals something of the sitter's inner life: a habit of mind, a private sorrow, the particular way one face differs from all others. Measured against this standard, many older portraits seem stiff and oddly impersonal. Rows of nobles stand in nearly identical poses, their faces composed into the same calm, their individuality apparently buried beneath velvet and armour. It is easy to conclude that their painters were trying to capture the person and largely failing.", "That conclusion mistakes what such portraits were for. For much of the history of European portraiture, and of several other traditions, the purpose of a commissioned portrait was less to record a personality than to establish a position. The sitter appeared as a holder of office, an heir, a bride, the head of a house. Costume, setting and objects carried meanings that contemporaries could read: the chain of a civic office, a dog standing for fidelity, a column suggesting constancy, a distant estate glimpsed through a window. A portrait of this kind was closer to a document than to a confession. Its sameness was not a failure of observation but a deliberate placing of the individual within a recognisable type, since what the patron wished to have recorded was precisely the type he had come to occupy. A contemporary who knew the conventions could read an entire biography of rank in a single canvas, whereas a modern viewer expecting the revelation of a character finds only an inventory of possessions.", "Likeness was not irrelevant. Families wanted to know what an absent bride looked like, and painters could be criticised for flattering too much or too little. But likeness served the larger purpose rather than defining it. A face had to be recognisable enough to attach the role to the right person, and beyond that the painter's task was to make the person fit the role. The expectation that a portrait should instead expose the sitter, catching him off guard or revealing what he might prefer to hide, belongs to a later and narrower moment in the genre's history. Where an older portrait does strike modern eyes as startlingly intimate, it is worth asking whether it was made for a public hall or for a private room, since the obligations of display weighed very differently in the two settings.", "Several changes made that expectation possible. The growth of a buying public outside courts and great houses created sitters with no office to display. New ideas about the self encouraged the belief that a person's truth lay within rather than in his station. And when photography arrived in the nineteenth century, it soon took over much of the trade in cheap likenesses, leaving painters free, or obliged, to offer something a camera seemed unable to supply. The psychological portrait, in other words, is not the essence of the genre finally achieved but one of its historical forms.", "To say this is not to claim that the older portraits had no inner life, or that modern ones are free of display. A shrewd painter could let a sitter's character show through the conventions, and a present-day portrait of a company chairman, with its carefully chosen office and posture, documents a position as surely as any court painting did. The point is only that we should judge a portrait by the question it was asked to answer. Faulting a court painter for failing to reveal a soul is like faulting a map for failing to be a landscape painting."]
difficulty_reason: History of an idea that overturns a common standard; clear paragraph roles, with qualifications in paragraphs 3 and 5.

subtopic: Slow looking rightly resists hurried viewing but wrongly assumes that time alone produces perception; seeing needs questions, whose own blinding effect slow looking can correct, so the two should alternate.
paragraphs: ["Anyone who watches visitors in a busy gallery will notice how briefly most pictures are looked at. A few seconds for the image, a little longer for the label, and the visitor moves on. In response, many museums now promote what is sometimes called slow looking: sessions in which participants are invited to sit before a single work for a quarter of an hour or more, noting whatever comes to their attention. The premise is simple and attractive. We miss what is in paintings because we do not give them time, and if we gave them time, they would show us more.", "The practice has real merits, and its critics should concede them. It interrupts the habit, encouraged by crowded rooms and handheld screens, of treating a picture as something to be recognised and ticked off. It gives permission to stay, which many visitors seem to need. And it does sometimes yield discoveries: a figure in the background that had gone unnoticed, a repeated colour that ties distant parts of the canvas together. But the premise behind it, that duration by itself turns into perception, is weaker than it looks. Fifteen minutes in front of a canvas can be fifteen minutes of reverie, of thinking about lunch, or of staring with growing unease at a surface that refuses to become interesting. Time is a condition of seeing, not a cause of it.", "What turns time into seeing is a question. The art historian who notices in a moment that the light in a landscape falls from two directions does not see faster because her eyes are better; she sees because she has learned to ask where the light comes from, and the painting answers. Expertise, in this sense, is a stock of questions that direct the eye, questions that are not mysterious endowments but are acquired, often laboriously, through the comparison of many works, and that can therefore in principle be taught. This explains why experts often see in seconds what a patient beginner misses in an hour. The beginner is not looking less; he is looking without a question, and an unguided gaze tends to settle on whatever is largest, brightest or most familiar.", "Yet the expert's advantage carries a risk of its own, and here the advocates of slow looking have a point that their own premise obscures. A stock of questions is also a stock of expectations. The historian who knows what to look for in a painting of a certain school may stop looking once she has found it, filing the picture under its category and failing to notice what does not fit. Questions direct the eye, but they also tell it where it need not go. Some of the most valuable observations a viewer can make come from setting expertise aside long enough to be surprised, and slow looking at its best is precisely a technique for producing that suspension.", "The two halves of the matter therefore need each other. Time without questions drifts; questions without time confirm what they expected. Neither ingredient is dispensable, and neither, taken in isolation, is sufficient for the kind of perception that the advocates of slow looking rightly prize. The most useful practice is neither the patient blankness that slow looking sometimes encourages nor the quick classification that expertise permits, but an alternation between them: a period of asking, a period of letting the asking lapse, and a return to the picture to see whether it has said something the questions did not predict."]
difficulty_reason: A dialectical argument that concedes, critiques, then partly rehabilitates a practice; the final position is a synthesis that wrong options can easily tilt one way.

subtopic: Musical improvisation is not freedom from rules but a fluency in internalised conventions so complete that they can be bent meaningfully.
paragraphs: ["The word improvisation tends to conjure an image of pure spontaneity: a musician who sits down with nothing prepared and lets whatever arrives come out. Listeners who admire improvisers often praise them in exactly these terms, as if the value of the performance lay in its having come from nowhere. Yet the image badly misdescribes what improvising musicians actually do. In the classical traditions of the Indian subcontinent, a performer exploring a raga is bound by an intricate set of expectations: which notes may be used, how the scale is approached in ascent and in descent, which phrases characterise the raga and which would make it sound like a neighbouring one. A jazz soloist working through a familiar tune is likewise held by the sequence of chords beneath the melody, by the length of each chorus and by a large shared stock of phrases that players absorb over years of listening.", "What these traditions share is not an absence of rules but a particular relation to them. The improviser has internalised the constraints so thoroughly that they no longer need to be consulted; they shape choices in the way grammar shapes the sentences of a fluent speaker, who does not pause to recall the rules before talking. The comparison with language is useful because it removes an apparent paradox. Nobody thinks that a conversation is unoriginal because it obeys grammar, and nobody thinks that grammar prevents people from saying things that have never been said before. On the contrary, it is the shared structure that makes a new sentence intelligible as new.", "This has a practical consequence for how improvisation is learned. A student who is told simply to be free usually produces something shapeless, or falls back on a handful of habits picked up by accident. Teachers in both traditions instead begin with imitation: the student copies phrases, sometimes for years, until the vocabulary becomes second nature. To an outsider this can look like the opposite of creativity. But imitation here is the means by which the constraints are absorbed, and only once they have been absorbed can the student vary them with confidence.", "None of this is to say that improvisation is merely the recombination of stored parts, or that the best improvisers are simply those with the largest memories. What listeners value in a great performance is often a moment at which a convention is stretched or bent in a way that still makes sense within the tradition, so that the surprise is felt as a surprise. Such moments are possible only for someone who knows exactly where the boundaries lie. Freedom in improvisation, in other words, is not freedom from form but a fluency so complete that form can be played with."]
difficulty_reason: A single clear thesis stated early and restated at the end, with concrete examples and an accessible analogy to language.

subtopic: Dance is preserved chiefly through direct teaching from dancer to dancer, which records what notation and film cannot, and its drift is the price of a living archive.
paragraphs: ["Of all the performing arts, dance has the most fragile relation to its own past. A play survives in its script and a symphony in its score, so that later generations, whatever they make of these documents, at least have something to argue over. A dance, by contrast, has for most of its history existed only while it was being danced and in the memories of those who danced it. It is tempting to conclude that dance is therefore an art without a history, or one whose history is a long series of losses, and that the remedy is simply better documentation.", "There have been serious attempts at such documentation. Systems of dance notation have been devised that record the position of each part of the body over time, and film and video now capture performances that would once have vanished. These tools are valuable, but they have not displaced the older method of transmission, in which a dancer who has performed a role teaches it directly to a younger dancer, in a studio, by demonstration and correction. Many companies that hold detailed records of their repertoire still rely on such teaching when a work is revived, and they tend to treat the written record as an aid to memory rather than as the work itself.", "The reason is not mere conservatism. What passes from one body to another in the studio includes things that a notation or a recording captures poorly or not at all: the weight of a movement, the quality of attention behind it, the reasons a gesture is timed as it is. A film shows what a particular dancer did on a particular night, including her idiosyncrasies and her mistakes; it cannot say which of those features belong to the choreography and which belong to her. A teacher who has danced the role can make that distinction, or at least has a considered view about it, and passes the view on along with the steps.", "This method has an obvious cost. Each transmission is also an interpretation, and over several generations a dance may drift a long way from what its maker first set. Yet the drift is not simply a corruption. A dance kept alive in bodies is continually tested against the dancers who perform it, and the features that survive are usually those that dancers have found to matter. The archive of dance, on this view, is not mainly a shelf of documents but a lineage of people, and its gaps are the price of its being alive."]
difficulty_reason: Concrete subject, clear contrast between documents and studio teaching, and an explicit concession in the last paragraph.

subtopic: Recording did not merely extend access to performances; by making them endlessly repeatable it transformed what performers and listeners take a performance to be.
paragraphs: ["It is often said that the phonograph and its successors simply made music available, carrying performances that had been confined to concert halls into the homes of people who would never have heard them. The claim is true as far as it goes, and the gain it describes is enormous: a listener in a small town can now hear more music in a month than a devoted concertgoer of earlier centuries could hope to hear in years. But the image of recording as a window, through which the listener observes a performance that would have happened in much the same way anyway, conceals the way recording altered both the performance and the act of listening.", "Consider first what repetition does. A live performance is heard once; its slips pass and are forgotten, and its moments of risk are experienced as risk. A recording is heard again and again, and on the tenth hearing a wrong note or a wavering tone is no longer a passing accident but a permanent blemish. Performers who recorded learned that what was acceptable, even exciting, in a hall could become intolerable on disc. As editing techniques improved, it became possible to assemble a single flawless performance from many takes, and the flawless performance became the standard against which the live one was measured.", "Listeners, in turn, came to the concert hall carrying recordings in their heads. Many now know a work first, and sometimes only, through one recorded interpretation, and they hear a live performance as a departure from it. This is a curious inversion. The recording was meant to be a copy of the performance; it has become, for many listeners, the original, and the performance its imperfect copy. Some performers have responded by playing more cautiously, aiming at the clean surface that audiences have learned to expect, at the cost of the spontaneity that once distinguished the live event.", "It would be wrong to treat this as a simple story of decline. Recording has also allowed listeners to compare interpretations in a way no earlier audience could, and it has preserved musical traditions that might otherwise have vanished with their last practitioners. The point is rather that recording is not neutral. A technology that lets us hear the same performance indefinitely changes what we think a performance is for, and an account of modern musical life that leaves this out has mistaken a transformation for a mere extension."]
difficulty_reason: The argument turns on an abstract distinction (window versus transformation) and an inversion of copy and original, with a concession at the end.

subtopic: The pleasure of sad music is best explained not by denying the sadness or by a safe frame around it, but by the shape that music gives to the feeling over time.
paragraphs: ["Few facts about music are more familiar, or more puzzling on reflection, than the willingness of listeners to seek out music that makes them sad. People do not, on the whole, go looking for grief or disappointment in the rest of life, and they would think it odd to be offered a sorrowful afternoon as a treat. Yet slow laments, songs of loss and the darker movements of symphonies are among the most loved music in many traditions, and listeners return to them deliberately.", "One response dissolves the puzzle by denying its premise. On this view the listener does not really feel sad at all; she recognises sadness in the music, much as she might recognise a sorrowful expression on a carved mask, and what she enjoys is the beauty and skill with which the sadness is expressed. The view has the merit of explaining why sad music does not ruin anyone's day. But it fits poorly with what many listeners report, which is that they are moved, sometimes to tears, and not merely informed. A second response accepts that the feeling is real and explains the pleasure by the frame around it: the sadness arrives without a loss to cause it and without consequences to follow, so it can be savoured in a way that the sadness of life cannot.", "Both responses capture something, but both treat the emotion as a single state, present or absent, mild or intense. What music does with an emotion is closer to giving it a shape over time. A lament does not simply announce sorrow; it gathers, rises, breaks, returns to a phrase heard earlier and comes to rest. The listener who follows it is led through a version of sorrow that has a beginning, an end and a recognisable order, which is precisely what the sorrows of ordinary life usually lack. The pleasure, on this account, lies less in the feeling than in the form the feeling is given.", "This does not mean that sad music always pleases, or pleases everyone. Many people who are grieving find that they cannot listen to the music they loved before, at least for a time, and their experience is a useful check on any theory. A frame that keeps sadness at a safe distance should make such music easier to bear in grief, not harder. The account offered here does better: a shaped and completed sorrow may be unbearable to someone whose own sorrow has no shape yet, because the contrast is too sharp."]
difficulty_reason: Compares two reported views with the author's own and uses a test case against one of them; the reasoning is abstract but signposted.

subtopic: Period-instrument performance has produced vivid results, but its appeal to authenticity is a poor justification; its research is valuable as a provocation, not a rulebook.
paragraphs: ["During the twentieth century a movement grew up among performers of European music written before about 1800 that sought to recover how that music had sounded when it was new. Its adherents played on instruments built to older designs, or on surviving originals: harpsichords rather than modern pianos, gut strings rather than steel, wooden flutes without the elaborate keywork of later models. They studied treatises on performance written in the period and drew from them conclusions about tempo, ornamentation and the size of ensembles. Much of the result was a revelation. Textures that had sounded thick and heavy when played by large modern orchestras became transparent, and pieces long heard as dutiful exercises began to sound witty and alive.", "The difficulty lies in the word that the movement often attached to itself, authenticity. If authenticity means sounding as the music sounded to its first audiences, the goal is in one important respect unreachable. Even if every instrument and every tempo could be reconstructed exactly, the listeners could not be. An audience that has heard the music of the following two centuries hears an older piece against all of it; a dissonance that once startled may now pass unnoticed, and a small ensemble that once seemed ordinary may now sound austere and pointed. The same sounds, entering differently formed ears, do not produce the same experience.", "A second difficulty concerns the composers' own wishes. It is sometimes assumed that a composer who wrote for the instruments of his day would have wanted exactly those instruments, and that a performance on them is therefore more faithful to his intentions. But composers wrote for what was available, and some of them are known to have been dissatisfied with the instruments and players they had. To infer a preference from a circumstance is to confuse what a composer was given with what he would have chosen.", "None of this tells against the performances themselves, many of which are among the most vivid of the past century. It tells against a particular way of justifying them. The best of these performances persuade not because they are correct, in the sense of matching a lost original, but because the research behind them led performers to hear possibilities that habit had concealed. Historical evidence used in this way is less a rulebook than a provocation: a reason to try something, which must then succeed or fail as music."]
difficulty_reason: Two separate objections to a justification are distinguished from praise of the practice itself; the conclusion is a fine distinction between correctness and provocation.

subtopic: Early collectors wrongly treated variation in folk songs as decay from an original; variation is how such songs live, so records should preserve it.
paragraphs: ["When collectors began, in the nineteenth century, to travel through the countryside writing down the songs of rural singers, they often approached their task as an act of rescue. The songs, they believed, were ancient and dying, and each singer they encountered was a damaged witness to an original that had once existed in a purer and more complete form. Variation between versions was evidence of decay: a verse forgotten here, a line garbled there, a tune that had wandered from its proper shape. The collector's responsibility, accordingly, was to compare the surviving fragments and reconstruct, as far as the evidence permitted, the song as it had existed before the damage began.", "This picture borrowed its method from the editing of ancient manuscripts, where it makes good sense. A classical text was written once by a particular author, and later copies really are more or less faithful to it. A folk song is a fundamentally different kind of object. It was never fixed in a single authoritative form; it existed only in individual performances, each of which was shaped by the singer's memory, temperament and taste, and by the particular audience and occasion. A singer who shortened a ballad for a restless crowd, or changed the name of a town to one her listeners knew, was not corrupting a text. She was doing what singers of such songs had always done, and what had made the songs worth keeping.", "Seen this way, variation is not the symptom of a song's decline but the very mechanism of its survival. Songs that could be adapted to unfamiliar places and new purposes travelled widely; songs that resisted such adaptation were gradually forgotten. The very versions the collectors regarded as degraded were often the ones in which a song was most alive, because they showed it being fitted to the people who still sang it. There is an irony here. By printing a single standard text, often assembled from several singers, the collectors gave the songs the fixed form they had never had, and later performers sometimes learned from the printed page instead of from other singers.", "It would nevertheless be unfair to dismiss the collectors' work on this account. Without their notebooks a great many songs would be irrecoverably lost, and some of them took care to record variants and the names of the singers they heard. The lesson is narrower. A record of oral music is valuable precisely to the extent that it preserves the variety which the collectors' theory taught them to regard as noise."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a historical method by analogy and contrast, ending in an irony and a narrowed conclusion; vocabulary is plain.

subtopic: A musical work is neither its score alone nor whatever a performance makes of it, but the score as read through a shared performing practice, to which fidelity is owed.
paragraphs: ["A familiar way of thinking about Western art music divides the creative labour with reassuring neatness. The composer makes the work and records it in a score; the performer's task is to realise the score faithfully, adding as little of himself as the music allows. On this view the score is the work, or at least its complete specification, and a performance is good to the degree that it delivers what the notation contains. Its attractions are considerable. It accounts for our confidence that two strikingly different performances are nevertheless performances of the same composition, and it furnishes the critic with a standard: the performer who alters the notes has made a mistake, whatever the result sounds like.", "The difficulty is that notation specifies far less than the view requires. A score fixes pitches and their order with considerable precision, and durations rather less, but a great deal of what listeners hear as the character of a performance is left open or indicated only roughly. A marking that asks for a loud passage does not say how loud, and the right loudness in a small room is not the right loudness in a large hall. A word indicating a lively tempo admits a range of speeds wide enough to make one performance sound urgent and another relaxed. Nothing in the marks tells the player exactly how long to linger at the high point of a phrase, or how to weigh the notes of a chord against one another. These are not trivial details that a faithful performer can safely settle at random; they are much of what makes the music sound the way it does.", "One response is to swing to the opposite extreme and say that the work simply is the performance, the score being no more than a set of instructions that each performer completes as she pleases. This rescues the performer's creative contribution, but at a considerable theoretical price. It cannot explain why some performances strike informed listeners as wrong-headed even when every note is in place, or why a performer who takes a slow movement at double speed has done something worse than make an unusual choice. If the score were merely a recipe to be finished at will, there would be no ground for such judgements, and yet musicians make them constantly and with considerable agreement.", "That agreement points to what both positions conspicuously omit. Scores are never interpreted in isolation. They are read by musicians trained in a practice: a shared and largely unwritten understanding of what the marks mean in a given style, which conventions apply, what kinds of freedom are expected and where those freedoms stop. In music of one period a trill is understood to begin on the note above; in another it begins on the main note; the score is usually silent on the point, and the practice supplies the answer. The work, on this account, is neither the marks alone nor whatever a given performance makes of them, but the marks as a practice reads them. Fidelity is owed to that combination.", "It may be objected that practices evolve, so that the work would apparently evolve with them, which seems absurd. But the objection establishes considerably less than it appears to. Practices do change, slowly, and the identity of a work is correspondingly less fixed than the first view supposed; that is a cost worth accepting, since it matches how musicians actually argue about performances. What does not follow is that anything goes. A practice at any moment draws lines that its members can defend, and a performer who knowingly crosses them is making a claim that must be argued for, not exercising a right."]
difficulty_reason: Abstract argument about the identity of a work, steering between two rejected views and answering an objection; the conclusion depends on the whole structure.

subtopic: Live theatre is distinguished not by the mere presence of actors but by the capacity of performance and audience to affect one another, which places a demand on theatre itself.
paragraphs: ["Defenders of live theatre, when pressed to explain why anyone should purchase an expensive ticket to see what could be watched more cheaply and comfortably on a screen, usually appeal to presence. The actors are there, in the same room, breathing the same air; on screen they are only images. The answer is sincere, but considered as an argument it is considerably weaker than it sounds. A great many things are physically present to us without being valuable for that reason, and a lecture delivered in person is not obviously better than the same lecture recorded. If presence were all that distinguished the stage, the case for theatre would rest on something close to a superstition about physical proximity.", "A more promising answer begins from what presence makes possible. A filmed performance is complete before any viewer encounters it; nothing the viewer does, however attentive or distracted, can reach back and alter it. A stage performance is still being made while the audience watches, and the audience is among the conditions under which it is made. Actors in a comedy learn to hold a line until the laughter at the previous one has crested and begun to fall, and the length of that pause differs from night to night because the laughter does. In a tense scene, a silence of a particular quality in the house tells the performers that they have the room, and they may let a moment stretch further than they would before a restless audience. These adjustments are individually small, but cumulatively they mean that a stage performance can be, in part, a response to the particular people assembled to witness it.", "The audience, moreover, is conscious of this reciprocity. Spectators in a theatre are aware that they can be heard and, in an intimate space, seen; they are also aware of one another, and a laugh that spreads along a row, or fails to, shapes what each person feels. The experience is less that of watching an object than of taking part, in a minor and mostly silent way, in an event whose outcome is not wholly settled. That is why a performance can fail in the theatre in a way that a film cannot: not through a flaw in its making, which a film may also have, but through a breakdown between stage and house.", "It may be objected that this account flatters most actual theatre, which is rarely so delicately attuned to its spectators. Many productions are drilled to such precision that they vary little from night to night, and in a large commercial house the performers can barely see past the first rows. That is true, and it calls for a qualification rather than a retraction. The responsiveness described here is a capacity of the live form, not a guarantee; a production can choose to use it or to suppress it, and one that suppresses it entirely has given up the main thing that the stage offers and the screen does not. Film, meanwhile, has resources of its own, the close-up and the edit among them, and nothing here implies that it is a lesser art.", "The case for live theatre, then, is not that the actors are physically near but that the performance and its audience remain capable of affecting one another. It follows, perhaps uncomfortably for some institutions, that the strongest argument for theatre is simultaneously a demand upon it. A theatre that wishes to justify its prices by appealing to liveness owes its audience a performance in which liveness actually does some work."]
difficulty_reason: Rejects a familiar argument, replaces it with a subtler one, concedes a strong objection and turns the conclusion into a demand; several distinctions must be held at once.

subtopic: When many people make the same mistake with an everyday object, the fault usually lies in the object's design rather than in the people, and blaming them hides the cure.
paragraphs: ["When a person pushes a door that should have been pulled, the usual verdict is that the person was careless, and the verdict is so automatic that we rarely notice how strange it is. A door has one job that involves its user, which is to tell an approaching hand what to do, and a door that sends the wrong message has failed at that job as surely as a door that sticks in its frame. Yet the failure is booked to the person, who apologises and blushes, while the door goes on misleading everyone who comes after.", "The habit of blaming users has a simple source, which is that designers judge their objects from the inside. They know which way the door swings because they drew it, and they know which button on the oven sets the timer because they chose its position.
