A serious dictionary does not decide what words mean; it reports, as carefully and as comprehensively as it can, what speakers and writers have been observed to mean by them.", "The method is easiest to see in the large historical dictionaries begun in the nineteenth century. Their editors did not sit down and define words from their own sense of correctness. They gathered evidence: slips of paper, many of them sent in by volunteer readers, on each of which a sentence containing a word had been copied out with its source and date. A definition was written only after the slips for a word had been sorted into piles according to the senses they seemed to show. Where the evidence was thin, the entry was thin; where a sense appeared in the slips before anyone had thought to approve of it, it went in regardless. The definition, on this model, is a summary of a body of quotations, and the quotations printed beneath it are not decoration but the grounds on which it rests.", "It does not follow that a dictionary is a neutral mirror. The evidence has to be collected by someone, and collectors read some kinds of text more than others; for a long time published literary prose was heavily over-represented, while the speech of the street and the workshop barely appeared. Someone must also decide where one sense ends and another begins, a judgment the slips cannot make for themselves. And the labels a dictionary attaches, such as 'informal', 'nonstandard' or 'archaic', are themselves verdicts, even when they are offered as descriptions. A dictionary that claimed to have no point of view would simply be concealing the one it has.", "The honest position lies between the court and the mirror. A good dictionary is an argument from evidence: its claims can be checked against the citations, and they can be revised when new evidence arrives, which is why the best dictionaries are never finished. To read one well is to notice the quotations as well as the definitions, and to treat its authority as that of a careful witness rather than a judge. That is a more modest authority than the one we usually grant it, but it is a sturdier one, since it does not collapse the first time usage moves on."]
difficulty_reason: Comparison of two rejected views (court, mirror) leading to a middle position; abstract but well signposted.

subtopic: Poorer comprehension on screens owes more to skimming habits that devices train than to the screen itself, though paper does offer some real advantages.
paragraphs: ["Each new medium of reading arrives with a lament attached. The prevailing anxiety is that screens are making us worse readers: that a generation raised on phones can no longer follow a sustained argument, and that anything read on a device is necessarily read badly. Some of this anxiety is supported by evidence. A number of studies have reported that people tend to understand long and demanding texts somewhat less well on screens than on paper, especially when they are working against the clock. But the usual interpretation of such findings, that the screen itself damages comprehension, is too quick.", "Consider what readers characteristically do on screens. Most of what they encounter there is brief, and much of it is read in order to decide whether to read it at all: headlines, messages, feeds, search results. Over years, this produces a thoroughly practised habit of skimming, in which the eye hunts for familiar key words and moves on, and when the same reader is later handed a dense essay on a tablet, the habit accompanies the device. The reader skims because skimming is what that screen has always been for, and comprehension suffers accordingly. On this account the difficulty lies less in the glass than in the expectations that the glass has gradually trained.", "This explanation carries a more encouraging implication. Habits, unlike physiological limitations, can be changed, and some of the gaps reported in the research seem to narrow when readers are given more time, or are asked to slow down and summarise what they have read. A reader who approaches a screen with the deliberate intentions he would bring to a printed book may perform nearly as well as he would with the book itself. The underlying capacity for sustained attention is not lost; it is simply not being called upon.", "Yet none of this shows that the medium makes no difference at all. Paper offers a reader a sense of place that a scrolling screen does not: the thickness of the pages already read, the position of a passage on the left or right page, the feel of a chapter's length in the hand. These cues help some readers remember where an idea appeared and how a long argument is organised, and a screen supplies them only weakly. The sensible conclusion is therefore a qualified one. Screens are not destroying our capacity to read deeply, but they make it easier not to, and readers and teachers who want deep reading on screens will have to ask for it deliberately rather than expect it by default."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief with an explicit alternative explanation and a clearly marked concession; accessible vocabulary.

subtopic: Editors shape books more than the picture of solitary authorship admits, but the right lesson concerns how credit is assigned, not a claim that editors are hidden authors.
paragraphs: ["The picture of the author that most readers carry is a picture of solitude: one person, one desk, one manuscript that emerges complete and is then merely printed. Publishing reinforces the picture at every step. The author's name alone goes on the cover, the author gives the interviews and accepts the prizes, and the acknowledgements page, where the other contributors are thanked, is the page readers most reliably skip. Yet anyone who has watched a book being made knows that the finished text is rarely the text the author first submitted.", "Between those two texts stands, among others, the editor. At the broadest level, an editor may tell an author that the book begins in the wrong place, that a character is doing no work, or that the argument of a long middle section has already been made in its first ten pages. At the finest level, an editor queries a word, a comma, the order of two clauses. Much of this advice is accepted, some of it is fought over and some is refused; but the book that reaches the reader has been shaped by all three outcomes, since even a rejected suggestion can force an author to articulate why a passage must stay. The work is deliberately invisible. A good edit, like good stage lighting, is meant to pass unnoticed, and editors who want their contribution celebrated are generally thought to have misunderstood the job.", "One tempting response is to declare that editors are secret co-authors and that the solitary author is a fraud. This overcorrects. In most cases the author supplies the material, the voice and the governing intention, and the editor works on what the author has made rather than making it; the relation resembles that between a performer and an exacting coach more than that between two composers. There are exceptions, cases in which an editor's cuts and rewritings have been so extensive that the question of whose book it is becomes genuinely difficult to answer, but they are exceptions precisely because they unsettle us.", "The real lesson concerns how we assign credit rather than who deserves the most of it. Our habits treat authorship as an all-or-nothing property, possessed entirely by one person, when the making of most books is a graded collaboration in which contributions differ in kind as well as in size. Recognising this would not diminish authors. It would make it easier to see what they actually do, which is not to produce text from nothing but to direct a process that others help to carry out, and to bear responsibility for the result."]
difficulty_reason: Claim, tempting overcorrection and reply, ending in a reframing; the distinction between who deserves credit and how it is assigned is abstract.

subtopic: Print did not by itself fix texts; textual stability was a slow social achievement built around the press, which has implications for digital texts.
paragraphs: ["It has become a commonplace that printing fixed the text. Before the press, the argument goes, every copy of a work was made by hand, and every copyist introduced errors of his own, so that texts drifted further from their originals with each generation of transcription. The press ended the drift: it produced hundreds of identical copies at once, and it was this identity, more than mere abundance, that allowed scholars across a continent to cite the same page and to dispute the same words. The thesis is powerful, and in its broad outline it is not wrong. But it credits the machine with an achievement that took centuries and required far more than machinery.", "Look closely at the books of the hand-press period and the identical copies begin to dissolve. Printers corrected errors while a sheet was being run, stopping the press to change a letter or a line and then carrying on; the sheets already printed were too costly to waste and were bound up alongside the corrected ones. Two copies of the same edition may therefore differ on any number of pages, and it is possible that no surviving copy matches any other exactly. Reprints, authorised or not, introduced fresh errors and silent improvements of their own. To a reader of the period, a printed book was a more dependable object than a manuscript, but it was not the guaranteed replica that the commonplace imagines.", "What made print seem fixed, then, was less the press than a slowly assembled set of expectations and institutions around it. Legal rights over copies gave publishers a motive to suppress unauthorised versions. Scholarly editors developed procedures for collating copies and establishing a single authoritative text. Readers learned to expect that a citation to page and line would lead others to the same words, and that expectation, once widespread, pressed printers toward the consistency it presupposed. Fixity was in this sense a social achievement that the technology made possible but did not by itself deliver.", "The distinction matters because the same commonplace is now being run in reverse. Digital texts, we are told, are inherently unstable: they can be altered silently, updated without notice, made to differ from one reader's screen to the next. That is true of the technology, but the history of print suggests that it is not the whole story. Whether digital texts become stable will depend on whether comparable institutions grow up around them: archives that preserve versions, conventions for citing them, and readers who expect, and demand, that a text once published remains what it was. The machine sets limits; it does not settle the outcome."]
difficulty_reason: Qualifies a widely held thesis rather than rejecting it, separates enabling from delivering, and then reverses the argument onto a new case; the stance is indirect.

subtopic: Library classification schemes embed contestable judgments about knowledge, but the remedy is to keep them revisable and visible, not to abandon order.
paragraphs: ["A library catalogue looks like the least ideological of documents. Its function, apparently, is merely to inform a reader where a particular book is located, and the call number on a spine seems as neutral as a street address. But a classification scheme does more than locate. To place a book, it must first decide what the book is about, and to do that it must divide the whole of knowledge into classes, arrange the classes in an order, and decide which subjects deserve broad territory and which can be squeezed into a corner. Every call number is, in compressed form, a small theory of what its book is about. These are not merely technical decisions. They are judgments about how the world is organised, made by particular people at a particular time, and then built, quite literally, into buildings.", "The judgments show most clearly where a scheme meets subjects its makers did not think central. One widely used decimal scheme, devised in the nineteenth century, gave most of the numbers in its religion class to varieties of Christianity, leaving the rest of the world's traditions to share a small remainder. Nobody needs to suppose malice to explain this; the scheme reflected the collections and the assumptions of the libraries its maker knew. But the consequence outlived the assumptions. A library using such a scheme in a city of many faiths must either cram large collections into long, unwieldy numbers or improvise local fixes that make its shelves harder to share with other libraries.", "The effect is not confined to how much space a subject receives. Classification also governs adjacency, and adjacency governs discovery. A reader who goes to the shelf for one book finds its neighbours, and much of what people learn in libraries they learn through this kind of sideways encounter. Suppose a hypothetical study of household labour is shelved among works on economics; its browsers will meet it as an argument about production and value. Shelved instead among works on the family, it will be met as an argument about domestic life. The book is the same, but the conversation it is placed in is not, and the scheme, rather than the author, has chosen the conversation.", "From this one might conclude that classification is a kind of censorship which libraries should abandon in favour of keyword search, which appears to impose no order at all. The conclusion does not follow. Search systems rank their results, and ranking embodies choices just as surely as shelving does; the choices are merely harder to see. Moreover, a collection with no arrangement is not neutral but unusable, since a reader can then find only what she already knows to ask for, whereas the browser of a well-ordered shelf may stumble on books she never knew existed. Some order is the price of a library's being useful, and every order has a point of view.", "The more defensible lesson is that classification should be treated as revisable and should be visible as a choice. Schemes have in fact been revised many times, often after communities pointed out how they were misdescribed, and catalogues increasingly allow a book to carry several subject headings even though it can stand in only one place. Revision is not a confession of failure but the ordinary condition of any scheme that tries to describe a body of knowledge which keeps changing beneath it. No scheme will ever be neutral. What can reasonably be asked of one is that it knows it is not, and that it leaves room for readers to cross the boundaries it draws."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief followed by an objection (abandon classification) and reply; examples are concrete, the stance is explicit.

subtopic: The ladder that ranked scripts from pictures to the alphabet fails descriptively, historically and in its standard of judgment, though scripts can still be compared relative to purposes.
paragraphs: ["For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, scholars who wrote about the history of writing liked to arrange the world's scripts on a ladder. At the bottom stood picture-writing, in which signs resembled the things they named; above it came scripts in which signs stood for whole words; above those, scripts whose signs stood for syllables; and at the summit, the alphabet, in which a few dozen letters represented the individual sounds of speech. The ladder told a story of progress toward economy and abstraction, and it rarely escaped notice that the peoples occupying the topmost rung were, in most such accounts, the authors' own.", "The ladder has not survived scrutiny well. Its first difficulty is descriptive. The scripts it consigned to the lower rungs were seldom what it said they were: the characters of Chinese, often presented as pictures of things, are in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another indicates, however loosely, sound. Such a script is not a halting step toward phonetic writing but a different and highly developed answer to the problem of recording a language. Its second difficulty is historical. The sequence it describes is, at best, the history of one lineage of scripts in one region, and to present it as the path that all writing must follow is to mistake a family tree for a law of nature.", "The deeper difficulty concerns the standard of judgment. The ladder assumed that a script should be ranked by how few signs it needs, so that fewer signs meant a better system. Economy of inventory is a real virtue; a child learning an alphabet with regular spelling can sound out unfamiliar words within a few years, and few would deny that this is an advantage. But it is one criterion among several. A script that represents meaning directly can be read across spoken varieties that differ so much in pronunciation that their speakers cannot follow one another in conversation. A mixed system, such as the one used for Japanese, can show at a glance which parts of a sentence carry lexical content and which carry grammar, an aid to rapid reading once the system is mastered. And an alphabet is only as economical as its spelling permits; a language whose spelling has drifted far from its pronunciation, as English has, can oblige its learners to memorise many words almost as wholes.", "None of this implies that scripts are equal in every respect or that the choice of script is unimportant. The costs of learning differ, and some of them fall heavily on those with the least schooling. A script deliberately devised in fifteenth-century Korea, whose letter shapes reflect how the sounds they represent are produced, was designed with exactly such learners in mind, and its designers evidently believed that some ways of writing were better than others for certain ends. That belief is a ranking of a kind, but it is a ranking relative to a purpose, which is precisely what the ladder lacked.", "It is also worth noticing what the ladder's critics should not claim. To deny that the alphabet is the summit of writing is not to say that literacy rates owe nothing to scripts; they plainly owe something. It is to say that they owe much more to schools, to the availability of reading matter and to whether reading pays, and that societies with very different scripts have reached near-universal literacy once those conditions were in place. The ladder told us that the script was destiny. The record suggests it is closer to terrain: it shapes the route, but it does not decide who arrives."]
difficulty_reason: Three-part critique followed by two concessions that limit the critique itself; requires tracking the difference between an absolute ranking and a purpose-relative one.

subtopic: The gloomy skew of the news comes less from a taste for bad tidings than from a definition of news as the sudden and unusual, and is best corrected by supplying context.
paragraphs: ["Complaints that the news is too gloomy are as old as newspapers themselves, and they usually take the form of an accusation: editors, it is said, prefer misery because misery sells, and they feed their readers a steady diet of disaster in the knowledge that calm and contentment do not move copies. The accusation is not exactly false, but it misplaces the problem. Most of the skew in what reaches the public does not come from a taste for bad tidings. It comes from a definition of news itself, which privileges what is sudden, unusual and attributable to a single moment. A factory that closes on a Tuesday is news; a thousand small firms that open over a decade are not, because no single day contains their story.", "This definition has consequences that no individual editor intends. Events that are rare are reported precisely because they are rare, and the reporting makes them feel common. A reader who encounters three stories about aircraft accidents in a month may come away more afraid of flying than of driving, although for most travellers the ordinary hazards of the road, which seldom make headlines because they occur every day, are far greater. The same mechanism works on trends. Improvements tend to be gradual and diffuse, deteriorations are often abrupt, and so a society that is slowly getting better at something can easily believe, from its news, that it is getting worse.", "It would be a mistake to answer this by demanding more good news. Stories chosen because they are cheerful would be as unrepresentative as stories chosen because they are alarming, and readers sensibly distrust outlets that seem to be managing their mood. Nor can journalism simply abandon the unusual. A fire in a crowded building matters, and the fact that most buildings do not burn is no reason to stay silent about the one that did. A press that reported only what is typical would be not more accurate but merely less useful, since the typical is, almost by definition, what its readers already expect. Novelty is a legitimate test of what deserves attention; the error lies in letting it serve as the only test.", "The more promising remedy is to report the denominator alongside the numerator. A story about a crime can say whether such crimes are rising or falling; a story about a drug's side effect can say how many people take the drug without harm. A newsroom could also give slow developments a regular place, treating a ten-year change in literacy or infant survival as worthy of the front page even though nothing happened on the day it was printed. None of this asks reporters to cover less; it asks them to say more about the scale of what they cover. Such measures will not make the news a faithful miniature of the world, and they should not try to. Their aim is more modest: to ensure that what is exceptional is presented as exceptional, so that readers can tell the difference between what is striking and what is typical."]
difficulty_reason: A clear thesis stated early, concrete examples and an explicit remedy; the one concession is signposted.

subtopic: Reader-funded journalism gains independence from advertisers but risks a two-tier public in which the quality of what one knows depends on what one pays.
paragraphs: ["For most of the twentieth century, readers of newspapers paid only a fraction of what their papers cost to produce. The rest came from advertisers, who were buying not journalism but attention, and the arrangement was so familiar that few people thought about it. Readers believed that they were buying a newspaper; in commercial terms, they were the product being sold. When advertising money migrated to online platforms that could target audiences more precisely, many news organisations turned to the readers themselves and asked them to subscribe. The change has been widely welcomed, and with some reason. A publication that lives on subscriptions answers to the people who read it rather than to the firms that want to sell them things, and it has less incentive to chase the cheap, fleeting clicks on which online advertising depends.", "Yet the subscription model carries a cost that its admirers tend to pass over. Advertising, whatever its faults, made news cheap for the reader and therefore widely shared. A wall that admits only paying readers divides the public into those who can afford careful reporting and those who cannot, or will not, pay for it. The second group does not stop reading. It turns to whatever is free, and what is free is increasingly material that is cheap to produce: opinion, aggregation, rumour and content funded by people with something to promote, whether a product, a cause or a candidate. The result is a two-tier system in which the quality of what one knows depends partly on what one spends.", "This matters more for news than for most products because the value of good reporting does not stay with the person who buys it. A voter who is misinformed about a local budget affects the outcome for neighbours who read every line of it, and a neighbourhood in which most residents rely on rumour about a planning dispute will reach worse decisions, which the careful reader who paid for accurate coverage must then live with. In this respect news behaves less like a private purchase and more like public health: the well-informed are not fully protected if those around them are not.", "The conclusion to draw is not that news should go back to an advertising model that has largely collapsed, nor that we should pretend that journalism can be given away without someone paying for it. Free news was never really free; its price was simply hidden in the cost of the soap and cars its advertisers sold. The question is how to keep the independence that reader revenue brings while limiting the exclusion it creates. Some answers are familiar: lifting the wall for stories of urgent public importance, cheaper access for students and libraries, and public or philanthropic support for reporting that markets will not fund. None is sufficient alone. But a news system should be judged not only by the quality of its best journalism but by how many people that journalism actually reaches."]
difficulty_reason: Plain chronology and a clearly signposted 'Yet' turn; the stance is stated directly in the last paragraph.

subtopic: The reporter's habit of giving both sides suits disputes over values but misleads on lopsided questions of fact, where minority views should be placed rather than excluded.
paragraphs: ["Among the habits that journalists learn early is the instinct to give both sides. When a council proposes a new road, the reporter calls the residents who want it and the residents who do not; when a minister defends a policy, the opposition is asked to respond. The habit is a good one wherever the disagreement is about values or interests, because there the reporter has no standing to declare a winner, and readers are entitled to hear the competing cases at comparable length. To do otherwise would be to editorialise under the cover of reporting, settling a political question by the simple device of quoting only one side.", "Difficulties arise when the same habit is carried over to questions of fact on which the evidence is heavily one-sided. Suppose that nearly all the researchers who study a question have reached one conclusion, and a handful dissent. A report that sets one scientist from each camp side by side, allotting them equal time, is scrupulously fair to the two individuals and seriously misleading about the state of knowledge. The reader, reasonably assuming that a newspaper does not stage contests between unequal parties, infers that the field is evenly split. Repeated over many reports, the impression hardens into a belief that the experts are hopelessly divided, and a reader may then feel free to choose whichever answer is more congenial. The format has communicated a falsehood that neither speaker uttered.", "The obvious objection is that journalists are poorly placed to judge which scientific views are sound, and that the history of science contains majorities that turned out to be wrong. Both points are true, and neither rescues the practice. The reporter is not being asked to decide who is right, only to describe accurately how opinion within a field is distributed, which is itself a matter of fact that can be checked. And the occasional vindication of a lone dissenter is not a reason to present every dissenter as half the story; most minority positions in science are minority positions because the evidence has gone against them. If a dissent later prevails, it will be because the evidence changed, and the reporting can change with it.", "What the critique of false balance requires, then, is not the exclusion of minority views but their placement. A dissenting researcher can be quoted, and quoted fairly, as a dissenter, with the reader told plainly how far that view departs from the field. What the reader should not be given is the impression, created by symmetry alone, that the dissenter speaks for half of those who know the subject. Nor does the critique apply where science is genuinely unsettled; there, presenting rival hypotheses side by side is exactly right. The skill it demands is harder than either reflexive balance or reflexive deference: it is the skill of knowing which kind of question one is reporting on."]
difficulty_reason: Claim, objection and reply structure with a two-sided conclusion; the stance rejects two opposite errors.

subtopic: Audience metrics record real choices but measure the pull of headlines, not the value of journalism, and treating them as a verdict slowly thins out important coverage.
paragraphs: ["Newsrooms once knew remarkably little about their readers. An editor could see how many copies were sold, but not which articles were read, how far, or by whom; judgements about what the public wanted were made on instinct, on letters to the editor and on the preferences of the editor's own circle. Today a screen in the corner of the room can show, minute by minute, how many people are reading each story, and a headline can be tested in two versions on live audiences, the weaker one retired within the hour. Critics regard this as the moment journalism surrendered to the crowd. The charge deserves a more careful answer than either its proponents or its targets usually give.", "The first thing to say is that the numbers are not lies. A click records a real decision, made by a real person, to open one article rather than another. What it records, however, is narrower than it appears. It measures the pull of a headline at the instant of choice, not the worth of what follows, and still less whether the reader was better informed for having read it. A story that disappoints everyone who opens it can outperform one that rewards every reader, provided its headline promises more. When a newsroom treats these figures as a verdict on its journalism, it is reading a measure of curiosity as if it were a measure of value. Curiosity matters, and a story that nobody opens informs nobody, but it is only one of the things a newspaper exists to serve.", "The damage done by this misreading is gradual. No editor decides to abandon difficult subjects; it is only that, week after week, the stories that perform poorly on the screen are given less space, fewer reporters and less prominent positions, and the subjects they belong to slowly thin out. Each individual decision is defensible, since space is limited and something must give way, and that is precisely why the cumulative effect is so rarely noticed until it is well advanced. Coverage of committee hearings, foreign elections and the routine work of public agencies is especially vulnerable, not because readers have rejected it but because the measure in use was never designed to register its value.", "It would be naive to conclude that newsrooms should switch the screens off. The instincts the screens replaced were not neutral; they reflected the tastes of a narrow group of editors, who often mistook their own interests for the public's. Some organisations now try to measure better things, such as how long readers stay, whether they return and whether they subscribe. These are improvements, though each can be gamed in its turn. The deeper lesson is that no figure, however refined, can settle what a public needs to know. Metrics can tell editors what readers choose; deciding what deserves to be offered remains a judgement that cannot be handed to the instruments."]
difficulty_reason: Defends the data while attacking its misuse, so the stance is two-sided; the causal claim in paragraph 3 is implicit.

subtopic: Investigative reporting is undersupplied because its costs are certain and its benefits diffuse, and its chief value, deterrence, depends on a steady presence rather than occasional scoops.
paragraphs: ["An investigation that changes a law or ends a career is remembered for its result, and the result makes it look like a sound investment. The reporting behind it rarely looks that way while it is under way. A team may spend months requesting documents, cultivating reluctant sources and checking figures, only to discover at the end that the story cannot be stood up, or that it is smaller and duller than it seemed. No publication can know in advance which of its inquiries will succeed, so the cost of the one that does must also cover the many that quietly fail. Editors who have watched a promising inquiry collapse after half a year learn caution, and caution, in a publication under financial pressure, usually means fewer inquiries.", "This uncertainty would matter less if the rewards of success flowed back to the publication that paid for it. Mostly they do not. Once a finding is published, rivals can report it within hours, and the citizens who benefit from a cleaner tendering process or a safer bridge are seldom the readers who bought the paper that exposed the problem. In the language economists use, the work produces benefits that spill over to people who did not pay for them, and goods of that kind tend to be supplied in smaller quantities than a society, if it could choose collectively, would want.", "The most important of those benefits is also the least visible. Officials who know that their accounts might one day be examined behave differently from officials who are sure that they will not be. A local administration that expects a reporter to read its contracts has a reason to keep them clean, and the corruption that never takes place leaves no story behind it. The contractor who decides not to inflate an invoice, because a reporter once asked awkward questions about a neighbouring council, will never appear in any account of what journalism has achieved. Investigative journalism therefore works partly as a deterrent, and like other deterrents it is judged unfairly by its visible output; a quiet year may be evidence of its success rather than of its irrelevance.", "Admirers of the form sometimes overstate its virtues. Investigations can be mistaken, and a reporter convinced of wrongdoing may read ambiguous evidence in only one direction, with real costs for the people named. Nor is every exposure a public service; some are driven more by rivalry or an appetite for scandal than by any public interest. But the case for supporting such work does not depend on its infallibility. It depends on presence. Deterrence works only if the possibility of scrutiny is continuous; a single celebrated exposure every decade, however brilliant, does less to discipline the powerful than a modest but permanent habit of looking. Those who fund journalism, whether readers, donors or the public purse, should therefore value a steady capacity for inquiry above the occasional prize-winning scoop."]
difficulty_reason: Economic reasoning about spillovers and an invisible benefit; the stance turns on a distinction between presence and brilliance.

subtopic: A retracted news claim survives because it fills a gap in the reader's account of events, so corrections must replace a false explanation rather than merely deny it.
paragraphs: ["When a news organisation discovers that it has published something false, the conventional remedy is a correction: a short notice, often printed some days later and some pages away from the original, stating that the earlier report was wrong. Few people defend the correction as adequate, but the usual complaint, that corrections are too small and too late, misses the more interesting difficulty. Even a correction that is prominent and prompt may fail, and it may fail because of what a retraction asks the mind to do. The problem, in other words, is psychological before it is editorial, and editorial remedies that ignore this are likely to disappoint.", "Consider a report that a fire in a warehouse was caused by paint and chemicals stored carelessly in a back room. A day later the paper announces that no such materials were present. The reader is now asked to give up the only explanation offered for the fire and to put nothing in its place. Minds do not handle this well. People tend to understand events as chains of cause and effect, and a chain with a link removed does not simply grow shorter; it breaks. An account with a missing link is uncomfortable, and when asked later why the warehouse burned, many readers reach for the explanation they were told to discard, not because they disbelieve the correction but because the correction left them with no story at all. The false claim survives because it was doing work that the retraction did not take over.", "If this is right, the remedy lies less in the size of the correction than in its content. A retraction that supplies an alternative account, stating what did cause the fire, or at least what the investigators now think likely, gives the reader somewhere to go. Where no alternative is yet known, the correction can at least explain why the original claim was made and why it seemed plausible, so that the discarded belief is accounted for rather than merely forbidden. There is a familiar worry that repeating a false claim, even in order to deny it, will make it more familiar and so more believable. The worry is reasonable, but it should not lead editors to issue vague notices that never say what was wrong; a denial that does not name its target cannot replace anything.", "None of this makes corrections easy, and it does not excuse the haste that produces most errors in the first place. A newsroom that publishes a confident causal story before the facts are in has created a problem that no notice can fully undo, since the first explanation a reader meets enjoys an advantage that later ones must work to overcome. Readers who met the false cause first will often have repeated it to others, built further conclusions upon it, and forgotten where they heard it. The lesson for reporters is therefore double: be slower to supply a cause, and, when one has been supplied wrongly, be quicker to supply a better one."]
difficulty_reason: A single extended example carries a psychological argument; the author weighs and partly rejects a competing worry.

subtopic: Journalistic objectivity is defensible as a method of verification that disciplines partial reporters, not as a claim of personal neutrality, and much criticism targets its degraded outward form.
paragraphs: ["Few words in journalism are now used with as much suspicion as objectivity. To its critics it names a pose: the pretence that reporters, alone among human beings, can step outside their own experience and describe the world from nowhere in particular. Put that way, the ideal is plainly impossible, and the critics are right to reject it. But it is worth asking whether that is the ideal anyone ever seriously defended. In at least one influential strand of its history, objectivity was proposed not as a description of the journalist but as a remedy for the journalist's limitations. Precisely because reporters could not be trusted to be neutral, the argument ran, they needed a method that would restrain what their partiality could do to the record.", "The method in question resembled, in a modest way, the procedures of empirical inquiry. A claim was to be checked against more than one source; documents were to be preferred to recollection; and the reporter was to say where each piece of information came from, so that a reader or a rival could test it. On this understanding the objectivity belonged to the procedure, not to the person, much as a laboratory's results are trusted not because its scientists lack ambitions but because their work is arranged so that others can repeat it. A reporter with strong opinions could practise the method; indeed, the method existed for such reporters, since a reporter without opinions, if one could be found, would hardly need it.", "What happened over the following decades was a quiet substitution. The discipline of verification, which is laborious and often invisible to the reader, was gradually overshadowed by a set of outward signs that were easier to display: a flat tone, a reluctance to draw conclusions, the habit of pairing every assertion with a counter-assertion. These signs were meant to signal fairness, but they could be produced without any verification at all. A story could quote two officials making incompatible claims, check neither, and still look objective. The appearance had detached itself from the practice it was supposed to indicate, and in some cases it obstructed that practice, since a reporter who had established that one of the officials was wrong was discouraged from saying so.", "Much of the current attack on objectivity is in fact an attack on this degraded form, and to that extent it is justified. Where it goes wrong is in the alternative it sometimes proposes. If the remedy for false neutrality is for journalists to report openly from their convictions, readers are left to choose among the convictions of different reporters with no common procedure by which to test any of them. The proposal also concedes too much to the degraded form, accepting that objectivity simply is the flat tone and the paired quotation, and then discarding the whole inheritance on that basis. Candour about one's commitments is a virtue, but it is not a substitute for evidence; a frank partisan who has not checked the facts is no more reliable than a disguised one.", "It should be conceded that method does not solve everything. Verification governs how a story is reported, not which stories are chosen, and the choice of what to investigate remains shaped by the interests and blind spots of those who make it. No procedure can remove that influence, and a newsroom that believes its method has made it neutral will be blind to it. Yet the concession limits the claim rather than defeating it. The case for objectivity understood as method is not that it makes journalism impartial but that it makes journalism answerable: it allows a reader who suspects a report to find out where it came from and whether it holds."]
difficulty_reason: History of an idea with a reported critique, a partial endorsement of it, a rejection of its remedy and a final self-limiting concession; the author's position must be separated from two others.

subtopic: The lament for a lost common forum misreads the past; what democracy needs is not a single audience but shared standards for settling disputes of fact across many publics.
paragraphs: ["A familiar lament holds that the public has broken into pieces. Where citizens once read the same few newspapers and watched the same evening bulletin, they now inhabit separate streams of information, each tuned to its audience's prior beliefs, and the common ground on which democratic argument depends is said to have eroded. The complaint is heard from commentators of every persuasion, each of whom tends to blame the media favoured by the other side. The lament contains a real worry, but it rests on a picture of the past that deserves scrutiny, and the remedies it suggests follow from the picture rather than from the worry.", "The ideal of a single forum in which a whole society reasons together has an attractive genealogy. Its admirers point to the coffeehouses, reading societies and pamphlet wars of early modern Europe, where private individuals gathered to discuss public affairs as equals. Yet the gatherings so admired were open in principle and narrow in practice, confined largely to those with the leisure, literacy and standing to take part. The mass audiences of the broadcast era were broader, but their breadth was purchased by a different narrowing: millions listened, while very few were permitted to speak, and the range of views considered respectable was set by a small number of editors and producers. What looks in retrospect like common ground was in part a common silence about matters that the gatekeepers did not think worth raising.", "None of this means the old arrangement had no merit. A shared stock of reported facts, however selectively assembled, gave opponents something definite to disagree about. Two people who had heard the same bulletin could argue over what to do about a strike or a drought without first arguing over whether it had happened. That is the genuine loss the lament points to, and it should not be dismissed. But it is worth being precise about what was lost. It was not chiefly that everyone attended to the same things, which was never a requirement of self-government and was always enforced partly by exclusion. It was that disputes about fact could be settled, or at least narrowed, by appeal to procedures and sources that people on both sides accepted.", "Seen this way, the fragmentation of audiences matters less than the fragmentation of standards. Many publics can coexist in a healthy democracy, each attending to its own concerns, provided that when they collide they can appeal to shared ways of establishing what is true. A society in which different groups read different things but accept the same rules of evidence is plural, not broken. A society whose groups no longer recognise any common method for testing claims is in difficulty even if they all watch the same programme. The second condition is the more dangerous because it is harder to see: a shared screen can conceal the fact that its viewers no longer agree on what would count as showing that something is so.", "The distinction has practical consequences. Nostalgia for the mass audience tends to recommend the impossible, the restoration of a few dominant outlets with the authority to define reality for everyone, and it risks restoring the exclusions along with the authority. The more plausible task is to build connections between publics rather than to merge them: institutions trusted across divides to verify claims, and habits of reporting that show their evidence so that readers who distrust the reporter can still examine the work. Such arrangements are less comforting than the image of a nation gathered around one screen, but they ask for something a plural society can actually provide. Nor need the connections be grand. A local paper that publishes the documents behind its reporting on a disputed planning decision, so that both sides can read them, does a small part of the work that the lament imagines only a national institution could do."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief through a history of an idea, with a concession that relocates the loss; the decisive distinction between audiences and standards is abstract.

subtopic: The cycle in which polite replacement terms acquire the contempt of the words they replaced shows that renaming cannot reform attitudes alone, though it still buys a useful interval of courteous speech.
paragraphs: ["Every generation of reformers discovers that words wear out. A term introduced to replace a cruder one, chosen precisely because it carried none of the old contempt, acquires that contempt within a few decades, and a new term is proposed to replace it in turn. Students of language sometimes call this cycle a treadmill, and the image is apt: a great deal of effort is expended, and the speaker seems to remain in the same place. Words for bodily functions, for old age, for poverty and for conditions of the mind have all passed through several such rotations, each new coinage arriving clean and departing stained.", "The usual explanation is that the stain was never in the word. Attitudes towards the thing named are what give a word its colouring, and so long as those attitudes persist, any word that reliably points at the thing will soon absorb them. On this view the replacement of terms is a kind of displacement activity, a way of feeling that something has been done while the underlying attitude goes untouched. Critics who hold this view tend to conclude that the whole enterprise of renaming is futile, and some go further and call it dishonest, since the fresh term flatters the speaker as much as it spares the listener.", "The first half of this argument seems to me largely right, and the second half too hasty. It is true that a new word cannot by itself change what people feel about the thing it names. But the treadmill is not simply a record of failure. A replacement term, for the years before it darkens, often gives people a way of speaking about a subject without signalling contempt, and in that interval conversations become possible that were not possible before. A parent can ask a teacher about a child's difficulty in terms that do not insult the child; an official form can ask about a condition without reading like an accusation. These are small goods, but they are not nothing, and they are purchased cheaply.", "What the treadmill does show is that renaming cannot carry the whole burden of reform. A society that changes its vocabulary for poverty while leaving the poor exactly as they were will find that its new word sours as fast as the old one, and perhaps faster, since the gap between the gentle name and the harsh reality invites irony. The cycle slows, where it slows at all, when the thing named stops being a mark of shame. The word then has nothing to absorb. Renaming is best understood not as a substitute for that change but as a temporary courtesy that can accompany it."]
difficulty_reason: A clear critique-and-concession structure with concrete examples and an explicitly stated authorial position in paragraphs 3 and 4.

subtopic: Listening is an effortful skill that public life neglects to teach, and the case for teaching it rests less on fairness to speakers than on its practical usefulness to listeners.
paragraphs: ["Public life has an elaborate culture of speaking and almost none of listening. Schools hold debating contests, organisations train their staff in presentation, and the history of rhetoric is largely a history of techniques for the person holding the floor. Listening, by contrast, is treated as what happens automatically when someone else is talking, a passive condition rather than an activity. Nobody is coached in it, and nobody wins a prize for it.", "This neglect would matter less if listening were in fact passive. It is not. To follow an argument one disagrees with, a person has to hold its parts in mind long enough to see how they connect, resist the urge to compose a reply while the speaker is still in the middle of a sentence, and notice the difference between what was said and what one expected to hear. Each of these is effortful, and each can be done well or badly. Anyone who has watched a meeting in which three people answer a point that nobody made has seen what happens when it is done badly.", "One objection is that a culture of listening would favour the patient over the right. If every view must be heard out in full, the argument runs, then bad ideas gain a hearing they have not earned, and those who are merely persistent will exhaust everyone else. There is something to this. Listening is not the same as agreeing, and a meeting that cannot end because everyone must be fully heard is not a model of deliberation. But the objection mistakes the purpose. Careful listening is valuable less because it is fair to the speaker than because it is useful to the listener: a person who has understood an opposing view can answer the strongest form of it, and can sometimes discover that the disagreement was smaller than it looked.", "Nor is it obvious that listening must be slow. Much of the time lost in public argument is lost to misunderstanding, to replies aimed at positions no one holds and to corrections of those replies. A discussion in which each participant first restated the other's point before answering it might take longer at each step and less time overall. If that is so, the case for teaching listening is not a plea for patience but a practical one, and it is odd that institutions so devoted to efficient communication have left half of communication untaught."]
difficulty_reason: Plain vocabulary and a signposted claim, objection and reply structure; the stance is stated directly.

subtopic: Online incivility depends less on whether speakers are named than on whether their identities persist, so real-name rules are a blunt remedy whose costs fall on vulnerable speakers.
paragraphs: ["It has become a commonplace that the internet would be a more civil place if people had to speak under their own names. The reasoning is simple: a person who cannot be identified bears no cost for cruelty, and a person who bears no cost will be cruel more often. Proposals to require verified identities on public platforms rest on this reasoning, and it has an obvious appeal to anyone who has read the comments beneath a news article.", "The reasoning is not wrong so much as incomplete. Anonymity does loosen some restraints; people say things to a faceless audience that they would not say across a table. But the restraint that matters most in face-to-face life is not the fear of being named. It is the expectation of meeting the same people again. A villager who insults a neighbour must live beside her the next day; a commuter who insults a stranger on a train usually need not, and commuters are not famous for their courtesy. What disinhibits is less the absence of a name than the absence of a future in which one's words will have to be lived with.", "Seen this way, the relevant distinction online is not between named and anonymous accounts but between identities that are durable and identities that are disposable. A pseudonym used for years in a small forum accumulates a reputation as surely as a name does, and its owner has much to lose by squandering it. Many such forums are known for patient and generous discussion, though few of their members could be identified by an outsider. Conversely, people posting under their real names on large platforms frequently behave badly, perhaps because the audience is so vast and transient that no particular reader's opinion of them seems to count.", "None of this shows that identity requirements would do nothing. They might deter some of the worst abuse, and they would make legal remedies easier to pursue. But they carry costs that fall unevenly. The people with most to fear from being named are not usually the trolls; they are the employee describing misconduct at work, the young person asking about a matter their family would punish, the dissenter in a place where dissent is dangerous. A policy that removes their cover in order to inconvenience the cruel has chosen a blunt instrument where a finer one was available: designing spaces in which identities, named or not, persist long enough to matter."]
difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief that turns on a conceptual distinction (durable versus disposable identity) and includes a concession in paragraph 4.

subtopic: What spreads in an internet meme is a template rather than a message, so share counts measure the vitality of a form, and any persuasive force lies in a frame's familiarity rather than in argument.
paragraphs: ["Imagine a photograph of a cat staring with great solemnity at an empty food bowl. In its first appearance the caption beneath it complains, in the cat's voice, about a late breakfast. Within days the same photograph carries hundreds of other captions: a student staring at an exam paper, an investor staring at a falling share price, a voter staring at a ballot. The cat, and the bowl, have stopped meaning anything about cats. They have become a frame into which almost any experience of disappointed expectation can be placed.", "This is the ordinary life of an internet meme, and it is worth noticing what has actually spread. It is not a message, since the messages are all different and many contradict one another. What has spread is a template: a recognisable structure with a slot in it, together with a tacit rule about what kind of thing goes in the slot. Those who share the meme are not endorsing a claim; they are demonstrating that they know the form and can fill it aptly. The pleasure is the pleasure of a good fit, much like the pleasure an audience once took in a skilled performer's handling of a familiar tale, where the interest lay less in what happened than in how well the expected moves were made.", "This has consequences for how memes are read by those who study public opinion. It is tempting to treat the reach of a political meme as a measure of agreement with it, as if each share were a small vote. But a template can carry a sentiment its sharers do not hold, simply because the sentiment fits the slot neatly, and a meme that mocks one side may be passed along by the other side in an inverted version that keeps the frame and reverses the point. Counting shares, in such cases, measures the vitality of the form far more reliably than the distribution of belief.", "It would be too quick to conclude that memes persuade nobody. Repetition has effects, and a frame that is used often enough can make one way of seeing a situation feel natural before anyone has argued for it. If the cat's bowl is used a thousand times to describe a particular government's policies, the idea that those policies are a disappointment may come to seem like common knowledge. But the persuasive power, where it exists, lies in the frame's quiet familiarity rather than in any argument, and it is precisely because memes do not look like arguments that their influence is so hard to measure and so easy to misread."]
difficulty_reason: A hypothetical case leads to a general claim about measurement, followed by a qualifying final paragraph that must be held against paragraph 3.

subtopic: The logician's dismissal of the speaker's character and the rhetorician's reliance on it can be reconciled: character is legitimate evidence where arguments cannot be inspected, but only in the domain where credibility was earned.
paragraphs: ["Two attitudes to the character of the speaker run through the study of persuasion, and they are hard to reconcile. The first, familiar from introductory logic, holds that an argument stands or falls on its own terms. Who makes it is irrelevant; to reject a claim because of the person advancing it is to commit a fallacy, and to accept a claim because of the person is the same error in a friendlier mood. The second attitude is older. Aristotle counted the character of the speaker among the means of persuasion, alongside appeals to the emotions of the audience and to the argument itself, and he did not present it as a regrettable weakness of listeners. A speaker who seems sensible, honest and well disposed towards the audience is, on this view, more worthy of belief, and an audience is right to take that into account.", "The logician's attitude is correct for a particular situation: one in which the listener can examine the argument fully. A proof in geometry is no better for coming from a famous mathematician. But most of the claims on which people must act are not like proofs. A patient cannot check a diagnosis, a juror cannot repeat the forensic analysis, and a citizen cannot audit the statistics behind a policy. In such cases the listener is not choosing between evaluating the argument and evaluating the speaker; the argument is largely out of reach, and the speaker's record, competence and incentives are the best evidence available. To attend to them is not a lapse in reasoning but reasoning under a division of intellectual labour that no one can escape.", "If this rehabilitates the appeal to character, it also shows where that appeal goes wrong. Credibility is earned in a domain. The physician's record is evidence about diagnoses, not about tax policy, and the honesty of a popular broadcaster is evidence that he reports what he believes, not that what he believes is true. Much modern persuasion works by carrying trust from the place where it was earned to a place where it has no bearing: the athlete who recommends an investment, the scientist who pronounces on matters far from her field. The listener who accepts such claims is not wrong to rely on character in general; she is wrong about which character she is relying on.", "The two attitudes, then, are less opposed than they first appear. The logician is right that character cannot make a bad argument good, and the rhetorician is right that, where arguments cannot be inspected, character is often all a listener has to go on. What a careful audience needs is neither a rule against attending to the speaker nor a habit of trusting the likeable, but the narrower discipline of asking what, exactly, the speaker's credibility is credibility about."]
difficulty_reason: A comparison of two views that ends in a reconciliation; the reader must track which view is credited with which half of the truth.

subtopic: The symbols and punctuation conventions of typed messages are a written prosody that restores lost cues of tone, but because they are local and unstable they relocate misreading rather than end it.
paragraphs: ["Spoken irony rarely needs announcing. A slight drag on a word, a flattened pitch, a pause before the punchline: listeners pick up such cues without noticing that they have done so, and the speaker relies on them without noticing either. Writing, however expressive in other respects, strips most of them away. For centuries this mattered less than it might have, because the written forms people used for personal exchange, letters above all, were slow, composed and long enough to establish their own tone over several paragraphs. A letter writer who wished to be ironic had room to prepare the reader for it.", "The short typed message removes that room while keeping the pace of speech. Exchanges happen in seconds, between people who often know each other well enough to joke, in fragments too brief to carry their own context. The result is a familiar variety of communicative accident. A remark meant as affectionate teasing arrives as a rebuke; a dry agreement reads as sincere enthusiasm, or the reverse. The writer, who heard the intended tone in his own head as he typed, is often the last to see that it was not on the screen.", "Writers have not, however, accepted this deprivation quietly. Over the past few decades they have built, without any committee to guide them, a supplementary system of signals: the small faces and symbols that can be appended to a sentence, the strategic use of capitals and repeated letters, even the presence or absence of a full stop, which among some groups of writers has come to make a short reply sound curt. It is common to lament these devices as a decline in the standards of written language. That complaint misses what they are for. They are not a lazy substitute for vocabulary but a written prosody, an attempt to restore precisely the cues that typing removed.", "Yet the new system has a weakness that spoken prosody largely lacks. The meaning of a rising tone is shared across most speakers of a language; the meaning of a particular symbol or a missing full stop is settled within smaller circles and changes quickly. A face that one group uses to soften a criticism may strike another as mocking, and a message read across a gap of age or community can misfire precisely because the writer took care to mark its tone. The invention of written prosody, in other words, has not abolished misreading so much as relocated it, from the gap between voice and text to the gap between the conventions of different readers."]
difficulty_reason: Problem and partial solution with a turn in the last paragraph; the reader must separate the problem of paragraph 2 from the new problem of paragraph 4.

subtopic: The vagueness of political slogans is a structural requirement of coalition-building rather than mere evasion, but it defers disappointment, and the fault worth condemning is not generality but a slogan that means something different to each audience.
paragraphs: ["Critics of political language have long treated the slogan as its lowest form. A slogan, they point out, asserts nothing that could be checked. Words such as renewal, fairness, security or change are compatible with almost any programme, and a campaign that rallies behind one of them has, in effect, declined to say what it will do. On this account the vagueness of the slogan is a species of evasion, and the remedy is to demand specifics: costed proposals, timetables, named measures that a voter can hold against the candidate once the votes have been counted.", "There is a good deal of sense in this, but it rests on a picture of the voter as an individual buyer comparing the contents of rival packages. Politics in most large societies does not work like that. A party seeking a majority must assemble people whose interests and hopes overlap only partly: the worker and the small employer, the city and the countryside, the young and the retired. A precise programme would divide them at once, since each specific measure pleases some members of the coalition at the expense of others. A slogan holds them together by offering a phrase into which each can read a version of what he or she wants. Its emptiness is not a failure of communication; it is what allows a heterogeneous coalition to communicate with itself at all.", "To see the slogan in this way is not to absolve it, for the difficulty has merely been postponed. A coalition assembled on an open phrase must, once it wins, translate the phrase into decisions, and each decision closes off some of the readings that brought supporters in. Those whose reading is closed off do not usually feel that a compromise has been struck; they feel that a promise has been broken, and in a sense they are right, since the slogan let each of them believe that it had been made to them. The disillusionment that so regularly follows electoral victory is often attributed to the cynicism of politicians, but a good deal of it is built into the structure of the appeal. Vagueness borrows support from the future, and the future presents the bill.", "Nor is the critics' remedy as clean as it looks. A detailed platform has its own dishonesty, of a quieter kind. It implies a control over events that no government possesses, and its specific commitments are routinely overtaken by a recession, a war or some crisis that no one foresaw. A voter who holds a government to the letter of such a platform may end up rewarding rigidity over judgement. Specificity, in other words, can be as much a performance as vagueness is, a display of seriousness staged for an audience that has learned to distrust slogans.", "What, then, should a careful listener ask of political language? Not that it abandon general phrases, which coalitions cannot do without, nor that it supply a detailed plan for every contingency. A more useful question is whether the speaker, pressed on how the slogan would decide a real conflict between its own supporters, can name the principle that would settle it. A slogan backed by such a principle is simply a commitment stated at a high level of generality, and it can be held to account at that level. One that dissolves into a different answer for each audience that asks is merely a mirror, and it is the mirror, not the generality, that deserves the critics' contempt."]
difficulty_reason: Five paragraphs that move from a reported critique through a structural defence, a cost, a counter-critique and a test; the author's position is reached only by holding all of them together.

subtopic: Engagement-ranked feeds neither invent outrage nor merely mirror it: they amplify an old appetite by confusing reaction with endorsement and reshape the supply of anger by training those who post.
paragraphs: ["Two stories are told about the anger that seems to pervade online discussion, and each is convenient for someone. In the first, the ranking systems that decide what appears in a feed have manufactured outrage, turning otherwise reasonable people into combatants. In the second, told chiefly by those who build such systems, a feed merely reflects its users: it shows people what they engage with, and if what they engage with is furious, the fault lies in human nature, not in the code. The first story flatters users, who become the victims of a machine; the second flatters engineers, who become the neutral servants of a public. Neither is quite right.", "Against the first story, it must be granted that outrage is old. Pamphleteers, broadsheets and street-corner orators discovered long before any computer that indignation sells, and audiences have always lingered over a scandal longer than over the correction that followed it. A ranking system that favours whatever holds attention did not invent this appetite. It found the appetite already there, and it could hardly have succeeded so quickly if it had not. Any account that treats the present climate as wholly unprecedented must therefore explain why the appetite it deplores appears so reliably in the commercial history of every earlier medium of mass communication.", "But the second story trades on an ambiguity in the word 'want'. A feed ranked by engagement learns what people react to: what they click, what they pause over, what they reply to in anger. Reaction is not the same as endorsement. A person may linger over a provocative post in the way a driver slows to look at an accident, and may say, if asked afterwards, that she wishes she had seen less of such material. A system that learns only from the lingering will give her more of it, and will describe the result as giving her what she wants. It is giving her what she wanted in the moment of reaction, which may be the opposite of what she wants on reflection.", "The older media of indignation differed in a further way that the mirror story overlooks. A newspaper editor chose what to print, but the feedback that reached him was slow and coarse, a matter of sales figures and letters to the editor. A feed reports, to every person who publishes in it, exactly how each post performed, often within minutes. Those who write for such an audience learn quickly which tone is rewarded, and many adjust accordingly, not because they are cynical but because they would like to be read. The ranking system therefore does not merely distribute a fixed supply of anger; it shapes the supply, by teaching producers what pays. A mirror that trains the face in front of it is not a mirror.", "It does not follow that the remedy is simply to rank posts by what people say, on reflection, that they value. Reflective preferences are harder to measure, easier to misreport and, when a platform infers them, open to the charge that the platform has substituted its own judgement for the user's. These are real objections, and they counsel modesty about any redesign. But they cut both ways. A system that optimises for momentary reaction has also made a judgement about what its users really want; it has simply made that judgement silently, and in favour of the version of the user that is easiest to count. Neutrality, in this domain, is not an available option; the only choice is between an explicit conception of the user's interests and an implicit one."]
difficulty_reason: Two rival accounts are each partly rejected, a key distinction (reaction versus endorsement) is introduced, and the final paragraph turns an objection back on the status quo; the stance is indirect.
